US-119-HCONRES109.s: The resolution would let Emancipation Hall in the Capitol Visitor Center be used on June 24, 2026, for a ceremony to dedicate the Semiquincentennial Congressional Time Capsule. It affects the House and Senate, and the Architect of the Capitol would set the conditions for any setup work for the event.

US-119-HCONRES112.s: This concurrent resolution says people with disabilities face barriers to access and calls for more physical access to federally funded facilities. It would make universal and inclusive design a guiding idea for future infrastructure bills and projects. It affects federal infrastructure work and people who use those facilities, especially people with disabilities.
US-119-HCONRES112.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-15)

US-119-HCONRES114.s: This concurrent resolution would recognize the pay gap faced by Black women and its effect on women, families, and the country. It also would reaffirm Congress’s support for equal pay for equal work and for narrowing the gender wage gap. A concurrent resolution is a formal statement from both chambers of Congress.

US-119-HCONRES119.s: This concurrent resolution would celebrate the 65th anniversary of the Peace Corps and honor its volunteers. It would recognize their work in global peace, friendship, and community development. The measure affects the Peace Corps and the people who have served in it.

US-119-HCONRES123.s: This resolution would recognize that Latinas are paid less than White, non-Hispanic men and say this affects women, families, the economy, and the country. It would also reaffirm support for equal pay and for closing the gender wage gap. The resolution was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

US-119-HCONRES124.s: This concurrent resolution would direct the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities against the Houthis in Yemen that Congress has not authorized. It refers to the War Powers Resolution, a law about when U.S. forces can be put into hostilities. The measure affects U.S. military activity connected to the conflict in Yemen.

US-119-HCONRES125.s: This resolution would support designating November 9 through November 15, 2026, as National Caregiving Youth Week. It would recognize children under 18 who help care for family or household members and encourage more awareness of their needs. It would also urge schools, health workers, and researchers to help identify these youth and connect them with support.

US-119-HJRES1.s: The resolution would propose a change to the Constitution that requires the Supreme Court to have nine justices: one chief justice and eight associate justices. It would affect how the Court is set up.
US-119-HJRES1.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-01-03)

US-119-HJRES104.s: This joint resolution became law and nullified a Bureau of Land Management land-use rule for the Miles City Field Office in eastern Montana. It would open certain federal land there to coal leasing. The change affects land managed by the Bureau of Land Management in Montana.

US-119-HJRES105.s: This joint resolution would cancel a Bureau of Land Management rule for the North Dakota Field Office’s land-use plan. That plan guides how BLM-managed land is used, including limits on oil, gas, and coal leasing. It became Public Law 119-49 on December 11, 2025.
US-119-HJRES105.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-07-10)

US-119-HJRES106.s: This law cancels a Bureau of Land Management rule for the Central Yukon area in Alaska. The rule had set land use plans for that area and changed some protected lands. It affects federal lands managed by the Bureau of Land Management there.
US-119-HJRES106.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-07-14)

US-119-HJRES130.s: This joint resolution overturns a Bureau of Land Management rule for the Buffalo Field Office in Wyoming. It would return the area to the 2015 land plan and make federal coal available again for future leasing. The measure became law as Public Law 119-51.

US-119-HJRES131.s: Became law. It cancels a 2024 land-use decision for the Coastal Plain area in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. That means the area would again be opened for oil and gas leasing, with at least 400,000 acres made available for a lease sale under current law.

US-119-HJRES140.s: Became law. It opens about 225,504 acres of National Forest System land in Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties, Minnesota, to mineral and geothermal leasing. The law cancels a land withdrawal order that had blocked that leasing for 20 years and removed protections for the area.

US-119-HJRES142.s: Signed into law, this resolution cancels a District of Columbia tax law and puts DC tax rules back in line with federal tax law. It restores several tax breaks, including a larger standard deduction, a $6,000 deduction for people 65 and older, and deductions for some tips, overtime pay, and car loan interest. It also affects DC changes to the child tax credit and some business tax write-offs.

US-119-HJRES20.s: This joint resolution became law and blocked a Department of Energy rule on energy-saving standards for consumer gas-fired instant water heaters. It affects the federal rules for these water heaters and cancels the amended standards DOE had adopted. The law took effect when it was signed on May 9, 2025.

US-119-HJRES200.s: The resolution would block a proposed U.S. military sale to Turkey of certain defense items and services. It covers support for integrating, installing, modifying, testing, and certifying F110-GE-129E/F engines for the TF-X aircraft. It would affect the proposed sale to Turkey and the defense articles and services named in the notice to Congress.

US-119-HJRES203.s: The resolution would direct the Federal Trade Commission to investigate possible antitrust problems in the fire truck manufacturing industry and report back to Congress within 1 year after adoption. The report would cover things like price fixing, serial acquisitions, and monopolization, plus the effects on fire fighters, fire departments, states, towns, and small businesses. It would also ask for ideas for new laws or other fixes.

US-119-HJRES210.s: This joint resolution would cancel the EPA decision that let California update its rules for pollution from ocean-going ships at berth. It would also end the approved change that expanded engine emission cuts to more types of vessels. The measure affects California air rules and ship operators covered by those rules.

US-119-HJRES213.s: This joint resolution would cancel EPA approval for California to change its rules for commercial harbor craft, which are work boats such as fishing and harbor vessels. It would affect California regulators and owners or operators of covered vessels. The changes at issue include new emission limits, new compliance dates, and a wider group of vessels covered by the rules.
US-119-HJRES213.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-08-10)

US-119-HJRES215.s: This joint resolution would block a Homeland Security rule about how long certain nonimmigrant academic students, exchange visitors, and foreign media representatives may stay in the United States, and how they can ask to stay longer. If Congress approves it, the rule would have no force or effect. It affects people in those visa groups and the agency that issued the rule.

US-119-HJRES217.s: This joint resolution would state that Congress disapproves of the proposed civilian nuclear cooperation agreement between the United States and Saudi Arabia. It concerns the agreement submitted to Congress under section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954.

US-119-HJRES218.s: The resolution would change the Constitution to end the electoral college and have the President and Vice President chosen by direct vote. People in the states and the District of Columbia would each cast one vote for a pair of candidates. The pair with the most votes would win, and the change would take effect one year after the first day of January following ratification.

US-119-HJRES219.s: The resolution would propose a constitutional amendment saying federal judges must be natural born U.S. citizens. It would also remove any current judge who is not a natural born citizen two years after the amendment is ratified. The change would affect judges in the Supreme Court and lower federal courts.

US-119-HJRES220.s: The resolution would propose a Constitution change to create a national referendum process, where people could vote on laws or on repealing existing laws. To get on the ballot, a petition would need enough signatures from at least 25 states and from across the country, collected within 18 months. If a measure got 60% support, it would become law without going to the President, and Congress would face limits on changing it for 2 years unless two-thirds of each House agrees.

US-119-HJRES221.s: The resolution would propose a constitutional amendment giving Congress power to set rules on campaign contributions and spending in federal elections. It would also let states set similar rules for state elections, while requiring those rules to be applied the same way to all citizens and citizen groups. It would bar noncitizens, foreign governments, and their agents from giving money or using it to affect elections in the United States.

US-119-HJRES24.s: The law cancels new federal energy-saving rules for certain walk-in coolers and freezers. It removes the new standards for walk-in non-display doors and walk-in refrigeration systems. It became Public Law 119-7 on May 9, 2025.

US-119-HJRES25.s: The law blocks an IRS rule that would have required some people who help with digital asset sales in decentralized finance, or DeFi, to report certain sale details to the IRS. It affects brokers and others handling these crypto-based transactions. It became Public Law 119-5 on April 10, 2025.

US-119-HJRES35.s: The law cancels an EPA rule on waste emissions charges for oil and gas facilities. That charge was part of the Methane Emissions Reduction Program and applied to some facilities that go over set pollution limits. It became Public Law 119-2 on March 14, 2025.

US-119-HJRES42.s: The law cancels a new Energy Department rule on energy-saving rules for certain appliances and equipment. It ends updated certification, labeling, and enforcement requirements for some consumer products and commercial equipment, like washers, dishwashers, and computer room air conditioners. It became Public Law 119-8 on May 9, 2025.

US-119-HJRES60.s: This joint resolution became law and cancels a National Park Service rule on motor vehicles in the Glen Canyon National Recreation Area. It allows off-road vehicles in certain areas of the park, including parts of the Orange Cliffs Special Management Unit. The park area is in northern Arizona and southeastern Utah and includes Lake Powell.

US-119-HJRES61.s: The law cancels an EPA rule on air pollution from rubber tire manufacturing. It removes new limits on hazardous air pollutants for the rubber processing part of that industry. It became Public Law 119-14 on May 23, 2025.

US-119-HJRES75.s: The law blocks new federal energy standards for commercial refrigerators, freezers, and refrigerator-freezers. It removes a 2025 Energy Department rule that would have required those products to meet tougher efficiency standards by January 22, 2029. It affects makers and users of this equipment.

US-119-HJRES87.s: The resolution became law and cancels an EPA notice that approved California waivers for several vehicle pollution rules. It affects California air rules for heavy-duty vehicle and engine standards, truck rules, airport shuttles, and zero-emission power train certification. It became Public Law 119-15 on June 12, 2025.

US-119-HJRES88.s: This joint resolution became law and canceled a federal decision that let California keep its Advanced Clean Cars II rules. Those rules set new standards for low-emission and zero-emission vehicles. It affects California vehicle pollution rules and the federal approval for them.

US-119-HJRES89.s: Lawmakers approved this joint resolution, and it became law. It cancels the Environmental Protection Agency decision that let California set new emissions rules for certain new heavy-duty vehicles and diesel engines starting with the 2024 model year. The change affects California's air pollution standards for those vehicles and engines.

US-119-HR1.s: This law changes taxes, spending, and the federal debt limit, and it also affects many federal agencies and programs. It changes some SNAP food aid rules, including how benefits are figured and who must meet work rules. It became law on July 4, 2025.

US-119-HR10020.s: The bill would add a Medicare home care benefit for people on Medicare who need help with daily tasks at home. It would cover up to 20 hours a week of help like bathing, dressing, meal prep, medicine reminders, and light housework tied to health and safety. The bill would also raise Part B premiums to cover the new benefit and would apply to services furnished on or after the first day of the first plan year beginning more than 2 years after enactment.

US-119-HR10035.s: This bill would change several federal employment laws so that some people who work for an employer under an independent contract are treated as employees. It would amend laws on job discrimination, pay, disability rights, and genetic information nondiscrimination. The change would affect independent contractors who provide work for an employer under those terms.

US-119-HR10036.s: The bill would direct the Government Accountability Office to study how federal job cuts and other workforce reductions affect public services people get from agencies. The study would look at things like benefit processing, call wait times, office hours, backlogs, and how well agencies can answer questions from Congress on behalf of constituents. GAO would report its findings to Congress and make the report public.

US-119-HR10052.s: The bill would make it unlawful to knowingly disrupt or block people from taking part in a scheduled religious service near a house of worship, within 100 feet of an entry during the hour before and after the service. It would affect people near places of worship and could lead to civil fines and lawsuits. The bill also lets the U.S. Attorney General or a state attorney general bring a civil case.

US-119-HR10061.s: The bill would expand federal work on wildfire prevention, recovery, and response. It would support prescribed fire, forest restoration, community wildfire defense grants, smoke monitoring, wildfire research, and new tools for detection and mapping. It would also set new steps for wildland firefighter pay, leave, health, retirement, and workforce support.

US-119-HR10062.s: This bill would provide supplemental funding to increase the number of AmeriCorps and other national service positions by at least 500,000. It would also raise the living allowance for each national service participant to 200 percent of the poverty line and adjust it each year after 2027 for inflation. The bill would change the cost per member service year for national service programs as well.

US-119-HR10073.s: This bill would create a grant program to help conserve critically endangered species in foreign countries. It would let foreign wildlife authorities and other qualified people or groups apply for financial assistance for projects like habitat protection, research, law enforcement training, and public education. The bill would also set up a fund for the program, require reports on grant results, and limit the use of grant money for captive breeding except when it is for release into the wild.

US-119-HR10078.s: This bill would require any increase or suspension of the federal debt limit to be matched by spending cuts over the next 10 years. A presidential request to raise the debt limit would have to include proposed legislation with spending reductions at least equal to the amount of the requested increase. It would also bar the House and Senate from considering debt limit bills unless they include the required spending cuts, with some Senate waiver rules.

US-119-HR10083.s: The bill would renew funding authority for a grant program for advanced drinking water technology under the Safe Drinking Water Act. It would change the covered years from 2022 through 2026 to 2027 through 2031, affecting that grant program and the agencies that run it.

US-119-HR10085.s: This bill would amend the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act to give more flexibility for incumbent worker training programs. It would change the law’s set-aside amounts from 20 to 30 and from 10 to 15 for certain training and transitional jobs funds. It would also require states to report outcomes for these programs and allow a local board to serve as a one-stop operator if the chief elected official and Governor approve it and conflict-of-interest rules are followed.

US-119-HR10095.s: The bill would change the Foreign Service Act so Foreign Service members who are ordered to take required leave could get daily pay and related travel help, including lodging and other benefits. It would affect members of the Foreign Service who must take that leave.

US-119-HR10101.s: The bill would update the Foreign Service Act so the Secretary of State would improve outreach and recruiting at nontraditional colleges and schools, like community colleges and career and technical colleges. It would call for regular info sessions and prep help for people interested in Foreign Service jobs and other entry programs. It would also widen recruitment outreach to students enrolled full-time or at least half-time, including those at community colleges and similar schools.

US-119-HR10115.s: The bill would change the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act to expand who can file claims tied to nuclear testing and related cleanup or response work. It would raise some payment amounts to $150,000 and add payment for certain out-of-pocket medical costs linked to the covered disease. It would also let the Attorney General accept written affidavits, or sworn statements, as proof for some work, location, or disease claims.

US-119-HR10125.s: The bill would bar people from trading stocks, commodities, swaps, or similar contracts while using nonpublic information from certain social media accounts controlled by government officials. It would also bar social media platforms from giving special early access to posts from those accounts, with some listed exceptions. Platforms that break that rule could face a civil penalty equal to the revenue they got from that access.

US-119-HR10126.s: This bill would direct the Secretary of Defense to include projected demand for foreign military sales, including sales already in progress, in industrial base assessments, munitions production planning, sustainment planning, and decisions on production rate increases and capacity expansion. It would affect Defense Department planning for the defense industrial base, major defense acquisition programs, and defense articles.

US-119-HR1013.s: This bill would change federal securities laws to expand how certain 403(b) retirement plans are treated. It would apply to some 403(b) plans, including ones subject to ERISA, plans where an employer agrees to act as a fiduciary for investment choices, and governmental plans. It also makes related changes to the Investment Company Act of 1940, the Securities Act of 1933, and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

US-119-HR10131.s: The bill would stop the Archivist from closing certain federal records centers and archive facilities that were already open before the law takes effect. It would also bar unreasonable limits on public access to those places. In some cases, it would forbid rebuilding or changing a facility if that would move records for more than 180 days.

US-119-HR10136.s: The bill would require the Agriculture Secretary to transfer the Crossett Experimental Forest in Arkansas to the state if Arkansas asks for it within 180 days after enactment. The state would have to pay the transfer costs and keep the land as the Crossett Experimental State Forest for research, education, and demonstration work, with access for the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture. If the state does not meet the required use and care rules, the land could be returned to the United States.

US-119-HR10146.s: The bill would require certain AI tools used by the public to clearly say when their answers include sponsored content, like paid promotions, affiliate links, or content shaped by a business deal. It would also bar these tools from hiding required disclosures or pretending sponsored content is just normal AI output. The rule would take effect 12 months after enactment and would be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission, with some actions also allowed by states and injured users.

US-119-HR10155.s: The bill would change retirement rules for some reserve members by treating certain past active-duty service as service as a regular member of an Armed Force. That could help some people qualify for a lower retirement age. The change would apply to qualifying active-duty service performed after January 28, 2008.

US-119-HR10163.s: The bill would make the Commerce Department the main adviser to the President on U.S. quantum technology and related supply chains. It would also have Commerce support U.S. business leadership in quantum technology, including by helping draw private investment and by working to build a trusted supply chain for key parts. Commerce would also have to publish reports with a strategy for this work.
US-119-HR10163.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-08-27)

US-119-HR10164.s: The bill would direct the Commerce Department to lead work on biomanufacturing and to help make U.S. biomanufacturing more competitive. It would also have the department study supply chain weak spots, domestic production capacity, and barriers to bringing biomanufactured products to market, then share a public report and web resource. The bill would affect federal agencies and private companies involved in making, supplying, or using biomanufactured products.

US-119-HR10168.s: The bill would direct the Housing and Urban Development Department to start a pilot program within 1 year to take back and give out again unused HUD-VASH rental help for veterans. It would target housing agencies that have not been using that aid and would make the reworked assistance available to veterans who are homeless or at risk of homelessness. The program would end after 5 years, and the department would have to send Congress a report after 3 years on how well it is working.

US-119-HR10173.s: The bill would reauthorize the National Science Foundation’s Research Experiences for Undergraduates program, which gives undergrads research jobs and training in science and engineering. It would expand rules for who can take part, with extra focus on students from schools with fewer research chances, first-generation college students, and other underrepresented groups. It would authorize $100 million each year from fiscal years 2027 through 2032 for the program.

US-119-HR10174.s: The bill would stop U.S. courts from enforcing certain foreign court judgments, fines, orders, or demands that are tied to foreign censorship laws. It would also let a U.S. person ask a federal court to rule that such a judgment cannot be enforced here. The bill defines foreign censorship laws as foreign laws that restrict or punish speech or force disclosure in ways that would conflict with First Amendment protections.

US-119-HR10176.s: The bill would bar seafood products from China from being bought, served, or sold in dining spots in the Capitol and other congressional dining facilities. It would also require the offices that run those facilities to set rules within 180 days if the bill became law. Suppliers would have to name every country where the seafood was caught, raised, made, or processed and keep records to back that up.

US-119-HR10180.s: The bill would let the National Institute of Standards and Technology director assess trends in artificial intelligence system abilities, including whether AI can help make new AI systems. It would also set rules for agreements with developers of frontier AI systems, which are leading-edge systems, before pre-deployment testing. Those agreements would have to allow the director to ask for details about how AI was used to help build the system and include testing for that ability.

US-119-HR10183.s: This bill would set U.S. policy toward Serbia and call for sanctions on people who the President says hurt peace, democracy, human rights, or anti-corruption efforts in the Western Balkans. It would require reports and a strategy on Russian and Chinese influence in Serbia, and it would limit U.S.-Serbia strategic talks unless key issues like elections, corruption, and press freedom are addressed. The bill would also allow more U.S. help for Serbia only after the President certifies that Serbia has made major progress, and it would end five years after enactment.

US-119-HR10197.s: This bill would require covered entities that sell nucleic acid sequences in interstate or foreign commerce to verify buyers, find out the purpose of the purchase, check whether a sequence is a covered sequence, and refuse sales based on risk criteria. It would also require these entities to notify the Secretary in some cases, keep records, and have independent checks of compliance. The Secretary would issue guidance, keep and update a list of covered sequences, and could enforce the requirements with records requests, investigations, and civil actions.

US-119-HR10210.s: This bill would regulate the use of artificial intelligence in the review of claims by group health plans and health insurance issuers. It would require certain adverse benefit determinations involving clinical judgment to be made by a licensed health care professional using independent judgment, not by an artificial intelligence system or its output. If AI is used in a review, the notice would have to say so and identify the professional who made the decision, and records about the AI system would have to be kept and made available on request. It would also treat the use of AI in utilization review as a treatment limitation.

US-119-HR10223.s: The bill would make ending tuberculosis a goal of U.S. foreign aid and let the government support work to prevent, diagnose, treat, and eliminate TB around the world. It would push aid toward countries with high TB rates, with focus on better testing, treatment, prevention, supplies, and research. It would also set global TB goals for 2027 to 2030 and require yearly reports to Congress on progress and spending.

US-119-HR10227.s: The bill would set new rules for some health plans on insulin costs starting with plan years on or after January 1, 2028. It would require coverage of selected insulin products with no deductible and limit cost-sharing to $35 per 30-day supply, or less in some cases, and it would also bar prior approval or similar limits except for safety or quantity rules. It would direct a government study of uninsured people who use insulin and create a grant-funded resource center and hotline to help uninsured people find affordable insulin assistance.

US-119-HR10233.s: The bill would continue a federal program that supports mosquito and other vector-borne disease surveillance and control. It would keep funding at $100 million a year from 2026 through 2030 and let the agency use some funds for training and technical help. It would also let the government plan for stockpiling emergency supplies used to control these diseases.

US-119-HR10235.s: This bill would amend Social Security rules for widows and widowers in two-income households. It would change how widow and widower insurance benefits are figured, using the greater of the deceased person’s benefit amount or 75 percent of certain combined benefits, with a cap in some cases. It would also keep Social Security benefits from counting above current-law levels when figuring income for Supplemental Security Income eligibility and payment amounts.

US-119-HR10238.s: The bill would require the Small Business Administration to give small businesses information and tools to improve their cybersecurity. It would also give small businesses seeking federal contracts help with the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification program, a security rule for some Defense Department contractors. The agency would also have to send Congress a yearly report on small businesses that contact it for cybersecurity help.
US-119-HR10238.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-10-13)

US-119-HR10257.s: The bill would require the U.S. Postal Service to give a single, unique ZIP Code to each of the listed communities. It would cover many places in several states, including towns, villages, and townships. The change would have to be made within 1 year after the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR10273.s: The bill would change federal wage rules for farm workers by adding overtime pay after set weekly hours, with the hours phasing down from 55 to 40 over several years. It would also remove some current farm work exceptions in labor law and change family-work and small-farm rules. The changes would apply at different times based on employer size, with smaller employers getting later start dates.

US-119-HR10275.s: The bill would require the Interior Department, through the U.S. Geological Survey, to conduct geothermal studies for Puerto Rico. The work would include high-detail maps, checks on groundwater risk, and checks on earthquake risks tied to enhanced geothermal systems. It would also require reports to House and Senate committees within 1 year after enactment and every 2 years after that until the study is done.

US-119-HR10279.s: The bill would name a U.S. Postal Service building at 9995 Southeast Federal Highway in Hobe Sound, Florida, as the "Special Operations Chief Petty Officer Aaron Carson Vaughn Post Office Building." It would affect that single post office location.
US-119-HR10279.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-09-03)

US-119-HR10280.s: The bill would change how the national suicide prevention lifeline is run. It would add grants for local crisis call centers, fund a national suicide prevention media campaign, and provide money for health center building projects and crisis care sites. It would also change some Medicaid rules for crisis services.

US-119-HR10291.s: The bill would require certain people who represent the federal government before a foreign government to pass a background check before getting access to classified information. They would also have to file yearly financial disclosure forms and could not take deals that directly benefit them from a foreign government they dealt with for the United States. The Office of Government Ethics would report these filings and any violations to Congress and the public each quarter, and people who break the rules could face removal, loss of clearance, or criminal penalties.

US-119-HR10299.s: The bill would name the U.S. Postal Service facility at 83 East Park Street in Alamo, Tennessee, the "Kenneth Nolen Davis Post Office." It affects that post office in Alamo, Tennessee.
US-119-HR10299.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-09-04)

US-119-HR10304.s: The bill would update safety rules for small drones, or small unmanned aircraft systems. It would require manufacturers to give the first user a safety statement when the drone is first turned on, and the user would have to confirm they read and understand it. The Federal Aviation Administration would have to create and keep up to date a model safety statement with rules, airspace limits, safety tips, and possible penalties for unsafe use.

US-119-HR10306.s: The bill would make a technical fix to a water rights settlement for the Shoshone-Paiute Tribes of the Duck Valley Reservation. It would change how interest is paid on the Development Fund and allow an added amount for fiscal years 2027 through 2033. The money could come from funds already set aside to carry out Indian water rights settlements.

US-119-HR1031.s: This bill would establish the Fort Ontario Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park in New York as a unit of the National Park System. The park would be created only after the Secretary of the Interior determines that enough land has been acquired for a manageable park unit. Its purpose is to preserve, protect, and interpret the stories of the 982 World War II refugees housed at Fort Ontario. The Secretary could acquire land, enter agreements for interpretive and educational services, and must complete a general management plan.

US-119-HR10323.s: The bill would lower the standard workweek in federal wage law from 40 hours to 32 hours. It would also keep overtime pay rules for hours worked above that limit and would phase in the change over several years after it takes effect. Employers could not cut an affected worker’s total pay rate or benefits just because of this change.

US-119-HR10324.s: The bill would direct the Agriculture Department to create and keep a database of isotopic signatures for processing tomatoes, which are tomatoes used for paste or other processed foods. It would also support research on testing methods, and let federal agencies, schools, research stations, and private groups request the database information. The department would work with Customs and Border Protection on import checks and send Congress a report within 2 years of enactment.

US-119-HR10326.s: The PROOF Act would require states to give the Justice Department information it asks for to investigate or prosecute fraud in certain federally funded programs. It would cover Medicaid, SNAP, TANF, some coronavirus aid to states, and other state programs the department says are at risk for fraud. The Justice Department could use the information only for fraud law enforcement and would have to report each year to Congress on its requests, investigations, and convictions.
US-119-HR10326.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-09-10)

US-119-HR10329.s: The bill would require the Small Business Administration to work with other agencies and publish learning materials about foreign actions that can hurt small businesses. Those materials would explain the harmful conduct, give tips to protect sensitive information and supply chains, and offer guidance on cybersecurity and data protection.
US-119-HR10329.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-10-09)

US-119-HR10330.s: The bill would add new rules for IRS tax inquiries and exams of universities. It would require a high-level Treasury official to have a written reason before an inquiry starts, require written notice to the school, and give the school a chance for a conference before an exam. It would also set time limits, add approval steps before some tax changes or assessments, and limit repeated inquiries for the same school.

US-119-HR10334.s: The bill would require the IRS, or another approved checker, to confirm that an electronic filing ID is active and allowed before a federal tax return or other document can be filed online. It would also require the IRS to build a system to check these IDs in real time and to verify them before first use and at set intervals. An electronic filing ID is a number the IRS gives to people or businesses that are allowed to file tax forms for others.
US-119-HR10334.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-09-10)

US-119-HR10345.s: The bill would require the United States to rejoin the World Health Organization within 30 days after it becomes law. It would also require the government to work with the organization right away on the Ebola outbreak in Central and Eastern Africa. It authorizes whatever money is needed to pay U.S. dues and help with the response effort.

US-119-HR10350.s: The bill would require certain financial firms to report suspected financial abuse of seniors within 5 days and send key details about the person and the suspected abuse. It would also let the firm put a hold on a suspicious transaction for up to 30 business days, with possible 30-day extensions, and tell a trusted contact when appropriate. The changes would take effect 180 days after enactment.

US-119-HR10352.s: The bill would let the Small Business Administration back more loans under the 504 Loan Program if its loan guarantees could go over the yearly cap, up to 115% of that limit. The 504 Loan Program helps small businesses get financing through a certified development company for expansion or upgrades. The agency would have to tell Congress before using this authority, and it could use it only once each fiscal year.
US-119-HR10352.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-10-09)

US-119-HR10353.s: The bill would require the Small Business Administration to post quarterly reports on its website about Small Business Investment Companies, or SBICs. Those reports would include data like how much SBA-backed financing SBICs get, how many are approved, and how many jobs their investments create or keep. SBICs are private companies that invest in small businesses using debt and stock-like funding.
US-119-HR10353.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-10-09)

US-119-HR10355.s: The bill would require the Small Business Administration to keep its disaster loan outreach materials accurate, up to date, and the same across all disaster field offices. It would also make the agency update those materials with current rules on who can apply and what the loan terms are. Before any public release, the agency would have to check that the materials are current and review them every year for consistency.
US-119-HR10355.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-10-09)

US-119-HR10356.s: This bill would require the Secretary of Health and Human Services to update the moms.gov website with a directory of resources for pregnant and postpartum women and women parenting young children. The site would let users find resources by ZIP code, distance, and topic, and it would allow outreach by phone or email if users give consent. The bill would also create grants for states to build or support resource systems, and it would bar listed resources and grant recipients that are "prohibited entities."

US-119-HR10357.s: The bill would change federal tax rules for digital assets, including how small fees paid with digital assets are taxed and how gains and losses are counted for some widely traded digital assets. It would also add rules for digital asset lending, dealer and trader treatment, charitable gifts, mining and staking income, broker reporting, and a voluntary disclosure program. Some parts would apply to transactions after December 31, 2027.

US-119-HR10359.s: The bill would make permanent the power of the Health and Human Services Secretary to give priority review vouchers for products that treat rare diseases in children. A priority review voucher is a token that can speed up the review of another drug application.

US-119-HR10362.s: The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to create and keep updated standards for finding, tracking, and securing AI agents, which are software systems that can act with little human help. It would also direct federal buying rules to require contractors and agencies that use or buy AI agents, or systems that work with them, to follow those security rules. The bill defines terms and sets rules for inventories, identity checks, logs, and control over AI agent activity.

US-119-HR10366.s: The bill would withhold 10% of certain federal surface transportation money from a state if the state does not pass rules limiting how automated license plate readers can be used. The rules would allow use only for toll systems, or for stolen vehicles, missing or endangered people, people with felony warrants, or vehicles tied to a felony case. The money cut would start on the first day of a fiscal year that begins after the second fiscal year after the law takes effect.

US-119-HR10371.s: The bill would direct a Small Business Administration office to set up policies and steps to meet current reporting rules for veteran-owned small businesses. It would require an annual report on the needs of small businesses owned and controlled by veterans, including service-disabled veterans. The report would also include ideas to improve their access to government help.
US-119-HR10371.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-10-09)

US-119-HR10374.s: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Secretary to keep the Medicare Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration going for 2027 through 2029 in a way like 2026. It would also keep it going in 2030 and later years unless the Secretary finds ending it would not raise premiums for people in Medicare Part D prescription drug plans. The Secretary would have to issue updated rules for how the program works for 2027 within 30 days after the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR10375.s: The bill would change the Small Business Administration’s 504 loan program, which helps small businesses get financing for building projects and upgrades through a local group called a certified development company. It would add new goals, including job training and helping areas hit by a declared disaster, and it would give these groups more room to fix loan papers and move up to 10% of a project’s cost. It would also let some small businesses lease more of a renovated building to other tenants and remove a rule that these groups must show they cannot get credit elsewhere.
US-119-HR10375.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-10-09)

US-119-HR10394.s: The bill would set new rules for Medicare Advantage plans on prior approval and claim denials. Starting with plan years on or after January 1, 2028, if a plan approves care, or if care does not need prior approval, the plan could not later deny it for lack of medical need, reopen the decision in most cases, or change the claim code to cut payment. These rules would affect Medicare Advantage plans and people enrolled in them.

US-119-HR10395.s: The bill would set up a pilot program at the Energy Department to support at least 3 domestic projects that refine, process, or recycle critical materials. It would use financial tools like price support to help these projects and to study how they affect supply chains and markets. The Energy Secretary would also have to issue rules, pick projects, and send annual reports to Congress.

US-119-HR10397.s: The bill would create a restitution program run by the Attorney General to pay compensation for harm and losses tied to sexual violence. It would let certain survivors, or the personal representative of someone who died, file a petition with the U.S. Court of Federal Claims for sexual assault, abuse, sex trafficking, or exploitation in the cases listed in the bill. The court would assign special adjudicators to decide if compensation is owed and how much.

US-119-HR10398.s: This bill would change how Medicare pays Federally qualified health centers for certain services. It would require the Secretary of Health and Human Services to adjust payment rates, collect cost and service data, and convene a working group to study payment changes. It would also change payment rules for telehealth services and set guidance and review steps for payments to these centers for Medicare Advantage enrollees.

US-119-HR10405.s: The bill would require states that get certain cancer control funding to include at least two pediatric cancer experts on their cancer control coalitions. It would also direct the Health and Human Services Secretary to create a pediatric cancer advisory committee to give advice, best practices, and funding ideas for childhood and adolescent cancer care. The committee would meet with state groups each year, report to Congress within 2 years after its first meeting, and then end 2 years after that first meeting.

US-119-HR10409.s: The bill would require the Department of Veterans Affairs to update its suicide prevention and firearm safety training within 180 days, and then update it at least once a year. It would apply to certain VA workers, some outside care providers who work with veterans, and family caregivers who get VA support. The training would also have to be posted on a VA website for the public.

US-119-HR10410.s: This bill would create a national graduate nurse education program under Medicare. Eligible hospitals could receive payments for the reasonable costs of qualified clinical education for advanced practice registered nurses, if they have written agreements with nursing schools and community-based care settings. The bill also sets reporting rules for hospitals and directs the Secretary to send money from Medicare trust funds to run the program.

US-119-HR10415.s: The bill would let the Agriculture Department give competitive grants to certain colleges and universities to provide free meals, including snacks, to low-income students. Eligible schools would have to apply, do outreach, and may get help with meal program setup and student outreach. Grants could last up to 2 years, and schools could use the money for meals, outreach, and some equipment.

US-119-HR10416.s: The bill would set up a process at the Commerce Department for U.S. businesses and groups to ask for home construction products to be excluded from some import duties. It would require faster decisions for certain key products, allow some past imports to be adjusted after an exclusion, and call for public posting and quarterly reports on decisions. The bill defines these covered products as many items used to build or furnish homes, with some exceptions.

US-119-HR10417.s: The bill would require the Department of Veterans Affairs to tell people when they are dealing with an artificial intelligence system instead of a human employee. The notice would also say the general purpose of the AI use. It would apply to veterans, their survivors, dependents, caregivers, and other people seeking VA benefits or services, and it would take effect within 180 days after enactment.

US-119-HR10418.s: The bill would require the Department of Veterans Affairs to create and run a technology platform to modernize the disability claims process. It would set rules for using automation and artificial intelligence, including human review and final decisions by VA staff, and it would require data sharing across VA health, benefits, and Defense systems. The bill would also require reports and briefings to Congress, and the program would end on October 1, 2028.

US-119-HR10419.s: The bill would direct the Department of Veterans Affairs to start a pilot program that helps rural veterans get dental care through local providers, including mobile clinics and nonprofit groups. It would cover services like exams, cleanings, fillings, dentures, and urgent care, and it would require outreach, a public provider list, and rules for payment and claims. The bill also sets aside $5 million for fiscal year 2027 and $20 million a year for fiscal years 2028 through 2030, and it would create a VA working group to study rural veteran dental access.

US-119-HR10421.s: The bill would change federal education law to give more support to elementary and secondary schools. It would cover things like arts and history lessons, new ways to test students, school safety, teacher pay and training, mental health help, and school meals. It would also address preschool, public school funding, and support for students facing money or other barriers to learning.

US-119-HR10426.s: The bill would set up a public online database with state and local data on sexual assault evidence kits and how long labs take to test them. It would also create FBI training programs for people who test these samples, support new testing methods, and give some states up to a 10% grant boost if they use an online tracking system for kits. The bill also calls for a report on the needs and backlog in public forensic science, with updates starting 1 year after enactment and every 3 years after that.

US-119-HR10429.s: This bill would rename the U.S. Postal Service facility at 901 Lake Street in Oak Park, Illinois, as the "Detective Allan Reddins Post Office Building." Any law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other federal record that refers to that facility would use the new name. It affects that post office and federal references to it.

US-119-HR1043.s: This law directs the Interior Department to transfer about 3,400 acres of federal land in La Paz County, Arizona, to the county for fair market value, if the county asks for it. The land transfer must leave out areas with major cultural, environmental, wildlife, or recreation resources. The county and later owners must protect tribal artifacts and work with the Colorado River Indian Tribes on any artifacts found, and the county must pay the costs of the transfer.

US-119-HR10436.s: The bill would direct the Department of Education to set up a grant program to help train future teachers to teach English learners well. Grants would go to partnerships between colleges and either high-need school districts or high-need early childhood programs.
US-119-HR10436.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-09-16)

US-119-HR10437.s: The bill would create a grant program for family literacy services for English language learners and their families. It would fund one-year grants of at least $150,000 and no more than $1,000,000 to groups that help families improve English and reading skills, with priority for families with greater need. It would also provide training and support for grant winners and require yearly program reviews. The bill would authorize $75 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2031.

US-119-HR10438.s: The bill would let the Education Department give up to five grants for dual language immersion programs. These programs would help low-income children, including English learners and minority children, in high-need schools from preschool through 5th grade. The grants would go to groups of local schools, early childhood programs, and technical help groups working together.
US-119-HR10438.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-09-16)

US-119-HR10443.s: The bill would update the federal AbilityOne procurement program, which helps the government buy goods and services from nonprofits that employ blind people or people with significant disabilities. It would change key definitions, set new rules for adding or removing items from the procurement list, and require public notice before those changes. It would also require new rules within one year for approving or ending a nonprofit's authority to provide items or services, and it would focus on employee training and wages.

US-119-HR10444.s: The bill would set rules to protect physicians and other licensed health professionals and place limits on how medical practices and management services organizations can be run. It would bar some corporate entities from owning or controlling a medical practice, and it would restrict noncompete, nondisclosure, and nondisparagement agreements in some cases. It would also limit a management services organization’s control over hiring, pay, scheduling, billing, and clinical decisions in a medical practice.

US-119-HR10448.s: The bill would remove certain data center property from a tax break called bonus depreciation, which lets businesses write off costs faster. It would also keep covered data centers and related property from counting as qualified opportunity zone business property. The changes would apply to property placed in service or acquired in tax years beginning after the date the bill is enacted.

US-119-HR10455.s: The bill would create grants to help cover the gap between college costs and other aid for students at certain colleges. It would support state and federal partnerships to help eligible students at in-state public colleges attend debt free, and it would give grants to historically Black colleges and universities and other minority-serving schools for this purpose. It would also make some Dreamer students, who were brought to the U.S. before age 16 and meet certain school rules, eligible for federal student aid.
US-119-HR10455.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-09-16)

US-119-HR10456.s: The bill would have the Interior Secretary remove the current plaque at the Lincoln Memorial and install a new one about Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech. It would apply the rules for commemorative works to the new plaque's design and placement. The bill would also allow donations for the plaque and let federal money be used for its removal, design, purchase, and installation.

US-119-HR10463.s: The bill would let some combat-injured military retirees get both their disability compensation and their retired pay at the same time. It mainly affects disability retirees with combat-related disabilities, including those with 20 years or more of service and those with less than 20 years, using different payment rules. It authorizes $9.4 billion and would apply to payments for months beginning on or after January 1, 2027.

US-119-HR10465.s: The bill would change the rules for approving hyperscale data centers on public lands. It would treat these approvals as major federal actions under the National Environmental Policy Act, which means a full environmental review, a at least 45-day public comment period, and one public hearing in the affected community. The review would also have to look at water use, power use, drought effects, and water sources, and the Bureau of Land Management could not use a fast-track exemption. Applicants would also have to submit a workforce plan with job estimates, how many construction jobs may go to state residents, whether workers would be paid prevailing wages, and expected permanent jobs.

US-119-HR10473.s: The bill would provide at least $15 million a year from fiscal years 2027 through 2032 to help gather evidence, track, rescue, and help children from Ukraine who were taken to Russia. It would also require sanctions on foreign people the President finds helped with the transfer, deportation, indoctrination, or militarization of these children, and it would bar them from U.S. entry and freeze certain property. In addition, it would authorize at least $10 million a year for Ukraine- and nearby region-language broadcasts by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty and Voice of America, and it would require reports to Congress from the Secretary of State and the U.S. Agency for Global Media.

US-119-HR10476.s: The bill would require health coverage for annual glaucoma screenings for certain people, including adults age 40 or older with certain ancestry or risk factors, and adults age 60 or older. It would apply this coverage to private insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, and federal worker health plans, with different start dates in 2027. The bill would also create grant programs for glaucoma screening, follow-up care, and research, with $10 million authorized for each program for fiscal years 2027 through 2028.

US-119-HR10478.s: The bill would direct the Department of Veterans Affairs to run a pilot program with qualified pension assistance groups to help veterans and surviving spouses prepare claims for pension benefits, including aid and attendance. The help would include checking eligibility, gathering records, and preparing and tracking claim paperwork. The program would be limited to selected VA regions and would end on December 31, 2031.

US-119-HR10495.s: The bill would add tougher criminal penalties for certain fraud tied to romance scams that target people age 60 or older. It would also require training for some financial institutions and retailers, including help for gift card purchases over $500, and new reporting steps when a senior customer shows signs of possible fraud. Covered financial institutions would have to report warning signs, keep records of these events, and set up procedures to help protect senior customers.

US-119-HR10497.s: The bill would require Congress to approve, before any deployment, the use of troops or armed persons at polling places to repel armed enemies of the United States. It would also require advance notice to congressional leaders and set a fast review process for a joint resolution, which is a bill passed by both chambers. The bill would limit federal funds for using troops or armed persons to access certain election records, and that section would end on January 20, 2029.

US-119-HR10498.s: The bill would have the government calculate the economic cost of the Iran war each year starting in fiscal 2027. It would move an equal dollar amount from unused Defense Department funds to the Treasury, then send equal payments to eligible U.S. taxpayers and their dependents. The payments would go out by October 30 each year, and any payment notice could not show the name, signature, or image of an elected official.

US-119-HR10504.s: This bill would bar past marihuana use from being used by itself to deny a person a security clearance or Federal employment based on suitability. It would also require Federal agencies to set up a public process to review certain denials made on or after January 1, 2008. If a person asks for reconsideration, the agency would have to review the decision within 90 days and determine whether it was based solely on past marihuana use.

US-119-HR10507.s: The bill would direct the Comptroller General to study and report to Congress by December 31, 2028, on expanding a terrorism-related legal rule so more people could seek payments when a terrorist attack caused injury but not death. It would look at how many more people could qualify, how much extra money would be needed, and what law changes would best make that happen, including for psychiatric injuries. The report would also list certain funds, forfeitures, and payments collected by the United States since December 18, 2015, tied to terrorism-related violations and cases over $5 million.

US-119-HR10513.s: The bill would direct the Housing and Urban Development Secretary to set up a grant program for eligible groups to help pay early planning costs for new or rebuilt affordable housing on land owned by faith-based organizations. Those costs could include design work, environmental reviews, studies, legal work, and help with financing plans. It would authorize $100 million for fiscal year 2027, and the program would run for 5 years after it starts.

US-119-HR10522.s: The bill would bar covered federal health agencies from using federal money for biomedical research on live dogs or cats. It would also cover spending that mainly supports that research, like staff pay, building upkeep, and office help. Groups that get these funds would have to try to place unneeded dogs and cats with rescue groups or others, and could euthanize them only if a vet says it is needed for the animal’s welfare or public safety. The ban would start 180 days after enactment, and HHS could allow a limited waiver in certain emergencies.
US-119-HR10522.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-09-21)

US-119-HR10530.s: Would create a federal program to support educators and educator training programs. It would focus on teacher preparation, mentoring, and career support, especially for high-need schools and local school agencies. It also defines many terms used in the bill, such as educator, educator preparation program, and high-need local educational agency.

US-119-HR10532.s: The bill would require some research facilities that receive federal funding to make reasonable efforts to transfer retired dogs and cats to an adoption group. A veterinarian would have to certify certain cases before the animal could be euthanized. It would apply to live domestic dogs and cats used for research, testing, breeding, or education.

US-119-HR10534.s: This bill would let the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development offer capital assistance and loans for distressed multifamily housing projects. It is aimed at owners, sponsors, and HUD-approved purchasers of eligible projects to help pay for necessary physical improvements and keep the housing affordable. To get loan help, the recipient would have to agree to a 30-year affordable housing use agreement and accept rental assistance contract renewals when offered.

US-119-HR10536.s: The bill would direct the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to study the dumping of certain waste in and around the San Pedro Basin off California. It would require research, monitoring, and possible cleanup studies, and it could provide grants for related deep seafloor contamination studies. The bill would also allow $6 million each year from fiscal years 2028 through 2034 for this work.

US-119-HR10542.s: The bill would have the Agriculture Secretary study how to fight pasture mealybug, an invasive insect that harms plants and grazing land. It would look at how far the pest has spread, its effects on livestock and crops, and how well the U.S. can detect, contain, and respond to it. The secretary would also report the findings and suggest actions to Congress within set time limits after the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR10543.s: The bill would create an Office of Prison Education inside the Bureau of Prisons. It would set up a federal prison education program for people in federal prisons, with classes like literacy, high school, job training, apprenticeships, and college-level study. The office would also do research, share best practices, and help state prison systems improve education programs, including for incarcerated veterans and people with disabilities.

US-119-HR10544.s: The bill would expand federal efforts on ovarian cancer awareness, genetic risk checks, genetic counseling and testing, and access to specialty care. It would also require many health plans to cover certain genetic tests, early detection steps, and risk-reducing care for people at higher hereditary risk, with an effective date for those coverage rules starting 1 year after enactment. The bill also sets up grants, outreach, and reporting rules, and it authorizes $20 million each year from fiscal years 2027 through 2031 for part of the program.

US-119-HR10545.s: This bill would amend the Voting Rights Act to prohibit intimidating, threatening, or coercing election officials and election workers while they do their duties. It would also create a presumption of intimidation in some cases when a person displays or carries a visible firearm, imitation firearm, or antique firearm near voting or election-related activity. State and local law enforcement officers acting within their official duties would not be subject to that presumption, and the National Guard would not be exempt.

US-119-HR10551.s: The bill would direct the Education Secretary to create a program that gives education help to dependents of certain public service workers. It would cover tuition, fees, and books at a public college or approved job training program, for up to 4 academic years. The workers must be full-time first responders, teachers, or social workers with at least 20 years of service.

US-119-HR10554.s: The bill would let the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children share certain information with the Department of State and the Department of Homeland Security. It says the sharing would be for screening and vetting, meaning checking people before they are allowed in or processed. The change would affect those two departments and the center.

US-119-HR10555.s: The bill would let the Department of Veterans Affairs provide care, treatment, and rehab services to veterans with serious mental illness and to homeless veterans, even if they do not qualify for hospital, nursing home, or domiciliary care. It would allow those services to be given directly or through community treatment sites, including halfway houses. The change would take effect 90 days after the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR10563.s: The bill would bar federal agencies and federal workers from using biometric surveillance, which means software that identifies people from face, voice, or other body traits, unless Congress gives clear permission in law. It would also block use of certain federal public safety grants for state or local governments that use biometric surveillance, starting with the first fiscal year after enactment. The measure would affect federal agencies, federal workers, and state and local governments that receive those grants.

US-119-HR10566.s: This bill would change federal election law to require extra disclosure for certain political ads and other communications paid for by covered independent expenditure committees. These communications would have to include a list of the top funders and the amounts they gave. The rule would apply to communications that expressly advocate for or against a clearly identified candidate, or that count as electioneering communications.

US-119-HR10568.s: The bill would require the Homeland Security Department’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, to protect genetic data and other sensitive body-based data. It would treat certain genetic data systems as critical infrastructure and call for training for federal staff on how to protect them. It would also have CISA work with biotechnology companies and other stakeholders on security rules and incident reporting.

US-119-HR10569.s: This bill would change homeland security law to have the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency work on protecting biotechnology and biomanufacturing infrastructure. It would direct the agency to help with analyses, outreach, and protection efforts for this kind of infrastructure when no sector-specific agency is assigned. It would also require the agency to submit a work plan and later reports to Congress about stakeholders, outreach, and implementation.

US-119-HR10571.s: The bill would create a federal grant program to help states put newborn screening in place for conditions on the federal recommended screening list. State health leaders or state agencies could apply for the grants. It would set aside $35 million each year from 2027 through 2031 for these grants and require yearly reports to Congress on progress and results.

US-119-HR10574.s: The bill would expand federal support for fusion energy research, development, and demonstration work. It would also create a program for private groups or groups with public partners to show fusion power technologies that could make electricity, heat, hydrogen, or radioisotopes. The bill also includes funding levels for several fusion programs, including $800 million for fiscal year 2027 for fusion materials and fuel-cycle work, $100 million for supply chain work, and $2 billion for the fusion milestone program.

US-119-HR10582.s: The bill would create a federal business tax credit for part of the pay given to workers for movie and TV production services done in the United States. It would apply to certain film and TV projects that meet set size, cost, and filming rules, and it would exclude some kinds of programming like news and live sports. The credit would start at 20% and could rise to 30% if certain conditions are met, and it could be sold to another company for cash.
US-119-HR10582.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-09-24)

US-119-HR10586.s: This bill would require the President to consult with Congress within 72 hours of starting to consider leaving NATO, and to send Congress a report within 48 hours of starting a withdrawal action. It would let Congress stop the withdrawal with a joint resolution, and the withdrawal would end after 30 days unless Congress approves it. It also sets fast committee and court steps for members of Congress to challenge a withdrawal action.

US-119-HR10587.s: The bill would move $1 billion to the Health and Human Services Department to help fund the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which helps low-income households pay energy costs. It would also stop certain funds from being used for the Board of Peace and instead direct them to this energy aid program. The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the House Appropriations Committee.

US-119-HR10590.s: The bill would start a pilot program where the Department of Veterans Affairs makes direct home loans to veterans in rural areas so they can buy land and build a new home. The loans would have 1% interest, and the home would have to be the veteran’s main residence for at least 24 months; the bill also calls for provided blueprints, help with permits, and the use of domestic wood products in the build. It would set aside $5 million for fiscal year 2027, and the loan authority would end five years after the law takes effect.

US-119-HR10591.s: The bill would set up and authorize the EPA’s Safer Choice Program, a voluntary program that identifies products made with safer chemical ingredients. It would let the EPA certify products, allow use of the Safer Choice and Design for the Environment labels, and set rules for review, public reports, and a public product database. It would affect manufacturers, retailers, and other groups that want to take part in the program.

US-119-HR10593.s: The bill would permanently authorize the Payment in Lieu of Taxes program, which sends federal payments to help local governments that have land the government owns. It would change the law so the program can operate each fiscal year instead of only through fiscal year 2019.

US-119-HR10594.s: The bill would direct the Secretary of Homeland Security to run at least one prize contest to improve how people understand artificial intelligence systems and at least one to make them more resistant to attacks. It would involve work with other federal officials and experts, and it would cover AI products used in government or industry. The bill also authorizes $10 million for fiscal years 2027 through 2031 and would require a report to Congress after the first contest ends.

US-119-HR10595.s: The bill would make certain private funds share legal responsibility for debts of companies they buy and control. It would also add limits on payouts, buybacks, outsourcing, and some tax rules, while creating new worker protections if a company goes bankrupt. The bill would also require more fee and return disclosure for private funds and add rules for risky corporate debt.

US-119-HR10596.s: The bill would renew a grant program that helps schools replace drinking water fountains. It would also raise the program amount to $7 million for each fiscal year from 2027 through 2029. The change would affect schools that apply for these grants.

US-119-HR10597.s: The bill would require group health plans and group or individual health insurance to cover over-the-counter birth control that the Food and Drug Administration has approved for use without a prescription. It would also tell federal agencies to clarify that this coverage includes those products and, in some cases, one covered prescription version for each group of similar drugs. Retailers that sell these products would not be allowed to block access to them or to accurate information about them.

US-119-HR10600.s: This bill would amend the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 to let federal foreign assistance funds be used for comprehensive reproductive health care services, including abortion services, training, and equipment. It would also state U.S. policy to include safe abortion and family planning in foreign assistance programs. The bill would affect federal foreign assistance programs, as well as governments and service providers that work with them.

US-119-HR10604.s: The bill would direct the Army to place a monument in Arlington National Cemetery for the crew members of Zeus 95 who were killed in action on March 12, 2026. If no spot can be found there, the monument would go outside the cemetery entrance. The design would need approval from the Army and Air Force, and the Air Force would pay the full cost to prepare, build, install, and maintain it.

US-119-HR10617.s: The bill would create a grant program for veterinary medicine work-based learning in high schools in states with veterinarian shortages. It would let schools, colleges, extension programs, clinics, associations, and some other groups apply for competitive grants to build or grow these programs. The grants would support student training tied to careers in animal care, food safety, and related fields.

US-119-HR10621.s: The bill would raise the state share of money recovered in Medicaid fraud cases from 10 percentage points to 25 percentage points. It would affect states that bring actions under Medicaid false-claim rules. The change would apply to amounts recovered in state actions brought on or after the date the law is enacted.

US-119-HR10622.s: This bill would require the Small Business Administration to review at least 10% of contracts each fiscal year for compliance with required subcontracting plans. It would also require the Administrator to make sure different types of contracts and plans are included in those reviews. The bill would require a report that describes how contractors complied with subcontracting plans, how many compliance reviews were done, and any other actions taken on noncompliance.

US-119-HR10628.s: The bill would change when biosimilar drugs can be chosen for Medicare price talks. It would give some biosimilar products more time before they can be included, and it sets rules for when the health secretary can delay or speed up that process. The change would apply to initial price applicability years beginning with 2027.

US-119-HR10634.s: The bill would bar the demolition of memorials that honor a U.S. President and were designated by Congress, unless Congress later gives permission. It would affect those presidential memorials and the people or agencies that manage them.

US-119-HR10642.s: The bill would set sanctions on certain foreign people and groups tied to building, financing, or supporting Israeli settlements or outposts in the West Bank or Gaza. It would also direct U.S. financial officials to issue guidance to banks and other financial firms, and it would bar imports of goods made in those settlements or outposts starting 120 days after enactment. The ban would not cover some personal baggage, and the bill would end 10 years after it becomes law.

US-119-HR10648.s: The bill would require the Department of Veterans Affairs to provide inpatient mental health treatment to eligible veterans through the Veterans Community Care Program or at a VA medical center. It would require that care be given within 24 hours after the veteran asks for it or a provider orders it. It would also require VA to post a wait-time report every six months for veterans seeking this care.

US-119-HR10652.s: The bill would reauthorize the San Gabriel Basin Restoration Fund. It would also raise the fund's cap from $146.2 million to $250 million. The change would affect work tied to restoring the San Gabriel Basin.

US-119-HR10654.s: The bill would require an honorable discharge for service members who are separated only because of pseudofolliculitis barbae, a skin condition that can cause razor bumps. It would also keep those members from being denied veterans benefits just because they did not meet the usual minimum active-duty service time. It applies to members of the Armed Forces and to benefits run by the Department of Veterans Affairs.

US-119-HR10655.s: The bill would direct the Department of Veterans Affairs to study how cannabis affects veterans with chronic pain or post-traumatic stress disorder. It would also allow clinical trials if the department finds it can meet the needed criteria, and it would track things like pain, sleep, mood, and substance use. The work would focus on veterans in VA care, and the bill says participation would not change other VA benefits.

US-119-HR10656.s: The bill would direct the Department of Homeland Security, working with U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the State Department, to put up and keep warning signs near land border crossings on the southern border. The signs would warn travelers about nearby areas or routes listed as dangerous in State Department travel advisories, and they would be placed where drivers and pedestrians can see them and updated as advisories change. It would also require reports to Congress and says no extra money would be authorized for the work, so agencies would use existing funds.

US-119-HR10658.s: The bill would require the Secretary of Commerce to give Congress a yearly report on how much the United States depends on imported biomanufacturing inputs. It covers inputs used in certain fermentation methods, biomass processing equipment, and large fermentation tanks.

US-119-HR10660.s: The bill would create a grant program to help local governments pay for needed accommodations for local elected or appointed officials with disabilities. The grants could cover things like office changes, special software, sign language interpreters, transportation for work events, and other assistive tools, and eligible local governments would have to provide at least 25% in nonfederal matching funds. It would focus on rural places, small jurisdictions, and some places with higher poverty, and it would authorize $5 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2033.

US-119-HR10664.s: The bill would direct the Education Department to give competitive grants to eligible colleges and universities. The money would support academic counseling and other services for students who are survivors of sexual assault and other violence.
US-119-HR10664.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-10-01)

US-119-HR10665.s: This bill would require colleges and universities that receive federal financial assistance under title IV to designate an independent advocate for campus sexual assault prevention and response. Employees who receive a report of sexual assault would have to tell the survivor about the advocate, including the advocate’s contact information and services. The advocate would help survivors get medical care, counseling, legal information, and help with reporting or campus processes, and would keep their privacy and confidentiality except where state law requires otherwise.

US-119-HR10666.s: The bill would extend the Frontier Community Health Integration Project Demonstration from a 5-year period to a 10-year period. It would affect that health care demonstration under Medicare rules. The change would take effect on December 31, 2026.

US-119-HR10667.s: The bill would change federal disaster rules after a major disaster is declared. It would let certain vessels get an exemption from some shipping rules for 180 days to help bring disaster aid, and it would end some wage rules for repair work tied to the disaster.
