It would also create a recovery board to review disaster recovery and make recommendations, and it would update rules for disaster repairs, environmental reviews, and planned technology upgrades to damaged facilities.

US-119-HR10669.s: The bill would require Congress to approve any federal land withdrawal over 5,000 acres, with some exceptions for short-term public land orders and for national security needs. It would also set new limits on how large a national monument can be, change what kinds of things can qualify for one, and place new rules on nearby private land and water rights. These changes would affect federal agencies, landowners, and national monument designations.

US-119-HR10670.s: The bill would bar Chinese AI models from being used on federal government devices and software systems, and it would also stop executive agencies from buying those models or software that uses them. It would require federal standards and guidelines for removing covered apps from government technology within 60 days after enactment. The bill includes exceptions for law enforcement, national security, and security researchers, and it allows case-by-case waivers for national security reasons.

US-119-HR10671.s: The bill would reauthorize a Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency program that sends security warning notices about weak spots in computer systems. It would apply to covered utilities, including some water and wastewater utilities and certain public water and treatment works operators. It would also add rules for sharing and protecting private information, automatic cyber hygiene services, and help with incident response, and the program would end five years after that section takes effect.

US-119-HR10673.s: The bill would direct the Transportation Department to update rules so certain freight containers, vehicles, and rail cars carrying lithium-ion batteries must show an outside placard, or sign, that can be seen from all sides. It would affect battery shippers and transportation businesses, and it would require the department to study compliance costs and consult with law enforcement, first responders, and industry groups. The department would also have to brief Congress after changing the rules and review them over time.

US-119-HR10674.s: This bill would establish the National Institutes of Clean Energy as an agency of the Department of Energy. It would invest in clean energy science, climate science, innovation, and research and development to reduce emissions and build climate resilience. The bill would also support research on clean energy projects, frontline communities, job loss and job creation, and workforce development. It gives priority to projects at public universities, land-grant colleges and universities, minority-serving institutions, and in areas that have seen the worst job losses.

US-119-HR10675.s: The bill would set up programs to work with allied countries on critical minerals, energy, manufacturing, and technology supply chains. It would also create exchange and cooperation programs, a list of foreign mining entities tied to forced labor or environmental harm, and steps to help foreign partners buy U.S.-made cyber and digital technology. Other parts would address trade, development aid, and shipbuilding competition with China.

US-119-HR10676.s: The bill would expand Medicaid health coverage for current and former foster youth, with a focus on dental care. States would have to cover screening, testing, and treatment services, including dental care, for foster youth under age 26. States would also set a special payment rate for these dental services, and the federal government would help pay the extra cost; the rules would take effect 80 days after enactment.
US-119-HR10676.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-10-01)

US-119-HR10677.s: The bill would change Medicaid, the health coverage program for low-income people, for former foster youth. It would require states to cover some former foster youth until age 26 even if they were placed with a kin caregiver or left foster care before age 18, and it would remove a rule that they had to be in Medicaid while in foster care. States would also have to set up outreach and enrollment programs for former foster youth.
US-119-HR10677.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-10-01)

US-119-HR10679.s: The bill would let a voter meet a state ID rule for federal elections by signing a sworn written statement saying who they are and that they are registered to vote. It would also require states to provide this form for in-person and mail voting, and not force those voters to use a provisional ballot, except for certain first-time voters who register by mail. The change would apply to elections on or after the date the bill is enacted.

US-119-HR10680.s: The bill would direct the Health and Human Services Secretary to set up a grant program to help community health centers improve food access. It would let partnerships between a community health center and a nonprofit food group apply for grants for things like a food space, a food vehicle, or related costs. Each grant could be up to $500,000, and the department would have to share reports on the program’s results and effect on patients.

US-119-HR10681.s: The bill would create a National Critical Minerals Council in the President’s office to help guide a national plan for critical minerals and materials. It would bring together several federal agencies to coordinate policy, budgets, research, and projects tied to mining, processing, reuse, and recycling. The council would also work with schools, companies, tribes, and other groups, and it would have to send a report and later brief Congress on its progress.

US-119-HR10682.s: The bill would change the tax code so professional sports franchises are treated the same as other businesses under a limit on tax deductions for some employee pay. It would also make a technical change to the same tax rule. The changes would apply to tax years starting after December 31, 2026.

US-119-HR10683.s: The bill would give the Federal Aviation Administration more money for airport and air traffic control projects in fiscal year 2027. It would create a grant program for up to 3 older hub airports to fix, rebuild, or modernize their main terminals, with federal aid covering up to 90% of project costs. It would also fund air traffic control system upgrades and airport grants for terminal and other airport improvements, affecting airports and the FAA.

US-119-HR10684.s: The bill would update the Energy Policy Act of 2005 to support Department of Energy research, development, demonstration, and commercial use of bioenergy and renewable chemicals and materials. It would define terms like bioenergy, biomass, biomanufacturing, and biorefineries, and set up work on feedstocks, scale-up testing, data tools, sustainability, workforce training, and coordination with other agencies and groups. It would also require at least four small-scale process development or scale-up facilities and a grant program for new bioenergy ideas, plus demonstration projects for integrated biorefineries.

US-119-HR10685.s: The bill would let certain Hong Kong residents who got Deferred Enforced Departure apply to become lawful permanent residents, which means they could get green cards. It would also cover some of their spouse, children, and unmarried adult sons and daughters if they meet the listed rules. While an application is pending, they could not be detained or removed and would be allowed to work in the United States.

US-119-HR10686.s: The bill would direct the Department of Homeland Security, through FEMA, to set up a pilot grant program within 1 year after enactment. It would give grants to covered entities to help design and run community-based catastrophe insurance, which is insurance for losses from natural disasters or hazards. The program would focus on helping communities fill insurance gaps, support the private insurance market, and encourage risk-reduction steps.

US-119-HR10687.s: The bill would change how the Energy Secretary can use emergency power orders under the Federal Power Act. It would require more public explanation and reporting about why an order is issued, its expected costs, and its effects on utilities and customers. It would also bar orders that stop or delay a power plant from retiring, unless a special emergency is met and the grid operator asks for that delay in writing.

US-119-HR10691.s: The bill would bar the federal government from using automatic license plate readers, except where another law clearly allows it, and would also ban federal funds from being used to buy or use them. It would cut certain grants to state and local governments unless they already have a law or policy that bans these readers to the same or a greater degree. It also sets rules for toll use, data retention, and penalties for violations.

US-119-HR10695.s: The bill would set new security rules for submarine cables that land in or operate in the United States. It would direct the Federal Communications Commission to create standard and extra security measures, and to use a faster process for cable license reviews in some cases. The rules would apply to companies and others seeking to build or run these cables, including some foreign-linked projects.

US-119-HR10698.s: The bill would require the Homeland Security Secretary and the Attorney General to share evidence with state and local police after an incident involving an Immigration and Customs Enforcement or Customs and Border Protection officer or employee shooting, injuring, or killing someone. It would also let those police access the scene, once they arrive, to do their normal investigative work, as long as safety and evidence needs are met. The shared records could include body camera video, surveillance video, radio and dispatch records, photos, forensic evidence, and witness statements.

US-119-HR10699.s: The bill would require states to provide secured drop boxes for voted absentee ballots in federal elections. It would set rules for where they must be placed, how many are needed, and make them accessible to people with disabilities and people with limited English. The new rules would apply to the regularly scheduled federal general election in November 2026 and later elections.

US-119-HR10700.s: The bill would change a federal voting law to make voting easier for people with disabilities and older people. It would set up new federal help and rules for states, including accessible election websites, plain-language and translated voting information, and support for absentee and in-person voting. It also would address access for Native Americans, Alaska Natives, and people with limited English.

US-119-HR10701.s: The bill would let the Federal Trade Commission start civil cases on its own to collect certain civil penalties, instead of always relying on another party to do so. It would affect the FTC and people or businesses covered by laws the FTC enforces.

US-119-HR10703.s: The bill would change a federal retirement law to let a worker or beneficiary sue on behalf of a benefit plan in some cases and seek relief for the plan. If the plan wins or settles, the recovered money would count as plan assets, and the person bringing the case would get between 0.5% and 1% of the amount recovered, plus other court-awarded costs or expenses. It would affect people in employee benefit plans covered by that law.

US-119-HR10704.s: This bill would direct the Secretary of Labor to award grants to eligible entities to help recruit, retain, and advance direct care workers. The grants would support strategies for direct care workers in home and community-based settings and other related jobs. Applicants would have to describe the area served, the need for direct care services, planned training or career planning, wages or benefits, supportive services, and how they will remove barriers to participation. The bill also requires the Labor and Health and Human Services departments to work together on the grant program.

US-119-HR10707.s: The bill would let the Health and Human Services Department give grants to states and territories to help internationally trained doctors work in the U.S. while they finish required exams. It would support programs where they work under a licensed doctor for a limited time, and it could help pay exam costs. It would also let some of these doctors be left out of a Medicare resident training cap used to set medical education payments.
US-119-HR10707.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-10-01)

US-119-HR10711.s: The bill would require the Secretary of State to report to Congress on staffing at U.S. embassies and consulates, visa wait times, and the effect of social media screening on visa processing. It would also require monthly public posting of visa wait times and the reason for those times on a State Department website. The bill would direct the Secretary to make a plan to add staff and find other ways to cut visa delays.

US-119-HR10713.s: The bill would set up a process for federal employees to ask to telework and for agencies to review those requests. If a request is denied, the worker could appeal inside the agency, and some requests would be treated as approved if no decision is made within 90 days. It would also require agencies to update and post their telework rules and would block federal funds from being used to carry out a 2025 order or directive that would end remote work and require in-person work.

US-119-HR10714.s: The bill would require diplomatic and consular posts to review and update their emergency action plans at least once a year, after each emergency, and when conditions change. It would also require better emergency evacuation information for U.S. citizens abroad, including more access to crisis forms and regular contact with next of kin. The Secretary of State would have to report to Congress on these evacuation procedures within 30 days and on airline price gouging during emergency evacuations within 90 days.

US-119-HR10717.s: The bill would change military health law to provide wigs to TRICARE beneficiaries who have alopecia, including hair loss caused by chemotherapy. It would affect people covered by TRICARE who have this kind of hair loss. The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the House Armed Services Committee on October 1, 2026.

US-119-HR10718.s: The bill would create a temporary way for former federal workers to ask for their personnel records, fix missing or wrong personnel and benefits papers, and get help with benefits coverage details. It applies to people who left federal jobs on or after January 20, 2025, and they could make requests for 4 years after the bill becomes law. Federal offices would have to help find and share the needed records.

US-119-HR10719.s: The bill would set rules for AI chatbots that minors can use. It would require a non-personified default setting, limit prompts that push minors to turn that setting off or lie about their age, and give parents or schools control in some cases. It also would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to seek public input and issue voluntary technical guidance.

US-119-HR10723.s: The bill would direct the State Department, working with the Attorney General, to try to set up a U.S.-Mexico rapid response plan for serious crimes against U.S. citizens in Mexico. It would affect U.S. and Mexican authorities, and it could include quick notice, better communication, evidence sharing, and contact points for victims and families. The bill would also require progress and status reports to Congress after the plan is pursued and after it is set up.

US-119-HR10728.s: The bill would change Medicaid rules so some limits on state-directed payments would not apply to certain maternity, labor, and delivery services. It would affect rural hospitals, Indian Health Service or Tribal hospitals, and hospitals where at least half of births are qualifying births. The change would apply to payment periods starting on or after July 4, 2025.

US-119-HR10730.s: The bill would change the health insurance premium tax credit, which helps people pay for coverage, and it would start for tax and plan years after December 31, 2025. It would also add help for some people in the Medicaid coverage gap, change some Medicaid funding rules for states, and set open enrollment dates for coverage starting in 2026. In addition, it would add fraud checks and penalties for agents and brokers who help enroll people in exchange plans.

US-119-HR10732.s: The bill would bar candidates for federal office, and some close people tied to them, from trading in contracts based on the outcome of their own elections. It would also require the Federal Election Commission to keep a public list of federal candidates and notify them of these rules when they file. The changes would apply to conduct on or after the date the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR10733.s: The bill would create a Science Advisory Board at the Department of Justice. The board would include 26 experts from schools and criminal justice fields, and it would advise the Attorney General on research, policy, and program work. It would also require a report to Congress within 90 days after enactment and every year after that.

US-119-HR10734.s: This bill would amend Title IX to set standards for when an education provider is liable for harassment on the basis of sex. It covers harassment by employees, agents, or other people if it affects a person’s ability to take part in or benefit from an education program or activity. It would also let an aggrieved person bring a civil action and recover equitable and legal relief, including damages and attorney’s fees.

US-119-HR10735.s: The bill would change federal crop insurance rules so a livestock pilot program would include bred cattle, replacement heifers, and cull cattle starting with crop year 2027. It would affect farmers and ranchers who use that program for cattle coverage.

US-119-HR10737.s: The bill would change EPA science rules to require more openness, including public disclosure of some board members’ financial ties and yearly reports. It would bar federally registered lobbyists from certain science board roles and set rules for recusal, or stepping aside, when there is a conflict. It would also require EPA to use a scientific integrity training program for agency staff within 180 days after enactment.

US-119-HR10740.s: The bill would keep temporary protected status available for certain people from Ukraine after the current designation ends. It would apply from October 20, 2026, through July 1, 2029, for Ukrainian nationals and some people who last lived in Ukraine, if they meet the listed residence, presence, and registration rules. It would also require the Department of Homeland Security to process these requests, including work permit requests, and decide them within 90 days.

US-119-HR10741.s: The bill would create new federal child care grants and support programs for states, tribes, child care providers, workers, and families with children under 6 who are not yet in kindergarten. It would set aside large federal funds for child care help, facility upgrades, home-based care training, research, and wage support for child care workers. It would also create a support benefit for stay-at-home parents and a program to pay family, friend, and neighbor caregivers.

US-119-HR10743.s: The bill would change how the Homeland Security Department’s Nonprofit Security Grant Program pays out grants. It would require those grants to be given in advance, not as money paid back after costs are already covered. It affects nonprofit groups that receive these security grants.

US-119-HR10744.s: The bill would change the federal meat inspection law to let some small red meat producers and processors sell meat directly to consumers without federal inspection. It would cover direct sales on the farm, at farm stands, farmers markets, and similar places, if the meat is labeled "Exempt--21 U.S.C. 623" with the producer's name and address. The exemption would apply only to producers under certain yearly slaughter limits for cattle, swine, sheep, and goats, and it would not override more lenient state laws.

US-119-HR10745.s: The bill would change federal child welfare and foster care rules to bar using certain federal funds to support removing children from parents over sex-rejecting interventions. It would also add rules for custody cases and create a private right of action, which is a way for a person to sue in court, for some violations. The changes would affect parents, children, and state child welfare agencies that use these funds.

US-119-HR10748.s: The bill would require the Defense Secretary, with the State Secretary’s approval, to send Congress a report on security cooperation with Western Balkan countries within 180 days after it becomes law. The report would cover ties with Russia, China, the United States, and NATO, plus each country’s role in NATO’s Partnership for Peace program if it applies. It would also include an assessment of the Russian Humanitarian Center in Nis, Serbia, and any links to Russian intelligence agencies.

US-119-HR10749.s: The bill would let the Agriculture Department make payments to growers of high-value crops, including citrus, for lost income or lower crop quality or output after events like drought, wildfire, hurricanes, floods, tornadoes, winter storms, or smoke exposure. It would affect farmers who grow these crops. The department could also use block grants to states and territories to run the program.
US-119-HR10749.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-10-05)

US-119-HR10751.s: The bill would change federal Indian health law so certified dental therapists could provide care in Indian health programs under tribal or board certification standards, even if state rules say otherwise. It would also say the Community Health Aide Program funding should not be reduced when a national program is set up. It affects Native American health programs and the people who provide dental care in them.

US-119-HR10752.s: The bill would set up an artificial intelligence task force inside the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency at the Department of Homeland Security. The task force would help guide the agency’s work on safe and secure AI, including cyber risks, workforce gaps, privacy, civil rights, and civil liberties. It would also give briefings to House and Senate homeland security committees every 6 months, and the task force would end 5 years after the law takes effect.

US-119-HR10753.s: The bill would direct the Housing and Urban Development secretary to set up a program to move unused Tribal HUD-VASH housing vouchers to tribes and housing entities that need them, if they choose to take part. Tribes and tribally designated housing entities could tell the department they have extra vouchers or need more, including by digital, phone, or mail notice. The department would also have to send Congress a report within 180 days after the law takes effect.

US-119-HR10756.s: The bill would renew the Regional Ocean Partnerships program and update how it is run. It would change some wording in the law, require reports, and extend funding years through 2031. It also sets funding amounts for fiscal years 2028 through 2031 and bars these partnerships from using federal money to develop new rules, model rules, or compliance programs.

US-119-HR10757.s: The bill would limit U.S. money for contributions to the United Nations. It would block those funds until the President tells Congress that the U.N. Security Council has named Hamas and Lebanese Hezbollah as terrorist groups. It would affect federal spending on U.N. contributions.

US-119-HR10758.s: The bill would direct the Veterans Affairs Secretary to start a grant program for certain state veterans agencies. The grants would help expand structured outdoor recreation programs for veterans, and each approved state entity would get at least $200,000 for the year if funds are available. It also authorizes $10 million each fiscal year to run the program.

US-119-HR10759.s: This bill would create a tariff-funded aid program for U.S. manufacturers, farmers, workers, and supply chains that are hurt by tariffs and foreign retaliation. It would offer refundable tax credits, low-interest loans, investment credits, and emergency bridge financing to help with domestic production, jobs, training, and supply chain changes. People or businesses seeking aid would need to show real tariff-related harm and agree to keep the supported work in the United States.

US-119-HR10761.s: The bill would change the federal campus safety law for colleges that receive federal funds. It would require more public reporting on sexual assault and related cases, add clearer definitions, and put more campus safety and complaint information on a public website. It would also require each school to set up support steps for survivors, including trained violence specialists and victim-focused interview methods.

US-119-HR10762.s: The bill would require sellers of used cars sold at auction, through a dealership, or in a private resale to keep the airbag system working or clearly tell buyers in writing and with a sign that it is missing or disabled. It would also let the Federal Trade Commission and states enforce the rule. For covered cars made on or after September 1, 1997, a seller who hides this problem could face civil penalties and criminal charges.

US-119-HR10764.s: The bill would set special court steps for certain settlements or awards for some executive branch people and related entities. For claims of $250,000 or more, or for nonmoney relief, the case would go to a three-judge federal court in Washington, D.C., and any appeal would go to the D.C. Circuit court. The settlement proposal would have to be filed, published, open for public comment, and reviewed by the court before approval.

US-119-HR10765.s: The bill would direct the Smithsonian to collect, preserve, and display artifacts in a permanent exhibit at the National Museum of American History about Donald J. Trump’s two presidencies. It would also direct the National Park Service to remove certain signs near the museum and add a congressional sign in some cases. The bill authorizes $5,000,000 for this work.

US-119-HR10766.s: The bill would require the Defense Secretary to update the Pentagon’s Critical Asset List within 180 days to add assets tied to the Golden Dome missile defense system. It would also require a matching update to the Defended Asset List, which is the list of assets to protect first. The changes would cover space-based sensors and interceptors, some ground missile defense sites, and other support systems. The Defense Secretary would also have to send Congress a report within 270 days.

US-119-HR10769.s: The bill would let states approve certain facilities in the land next to or along federal-aid highways. It covers electric vehicle charging, renewable energy, power lines, and broadband lines or conduit, which is a pipe or channel for cables. It would affect states and groups that build or run these facilities.

US-119-HR10770.s: The bill would limit some rebate deals for prescription drugs in the 340B program from January 1, 2027, through December 31, 2028. It would stop drug makers from using agreements that make covered health care groups pay more than the allowed price first and then get a rebate later. It would also delay the 340B Rebate Model Pilot Program until January 1, 2029.
US-119-HR10770.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-10-09)

US-119-HR10771.s: The bill would direct FEMA to set up a grant program for higher education institutions to create or expand emergency preparedness and disaster response work. Eligible schools include many types of colleges and universities, such as historically Black colleges, Tribal colleges, and career schools. Grants would be from $250,000 to $5 million, and the bill authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2031.

US-119-HR10772.s: The bill would let the Defense Innovation Unit at the Defense Department evaluate and invest in Ukrainian defense technologies. It would also let the unit take steps so the United States can directly use those technologies, including ones developed and improved in Ukraine's fighting. It would affect the Defense Innovation Unit and U.S. defense efforts.

US-119-HR10773.s: This bill would change the tax code rules for scholarship groups and private and religious K-12 schools. It would say governments cannot control those groups or schools through this section of the tax law, and cannot block scholarship money from being used at those schools because of their religious status. It would also bar governments from discouraging parents from using those scholarships at private, nonprofit, or faith-based schools.

US-119-HR10774.s: The bill would ban taking, importing, exporting, or breeding certain whales and orcas for public display. It would block federal permits for those actions and make it illegal to export them unless they are going to a marine mammal sanctuary or back to the wild. It would also bar breeding or artificial insemination of these animals when their young would be used for public display.
US-119-HR10774.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-10-09)

US-119-HR10775.s: The bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to set up a task force within 90 days after it becomes law. The group would study how automated accounts, or bots, affect social media, public debate, and elections. It would then send its findings to Congress and relevant federal agencies within 1 year after the task force is formed.

US-119-HR10776.s: The bill would change parts of the Marine Mammal Protection Act on when people can take, or harm, marine mammals under allowed exceptions. It would also change how agencies set conditions for those activities, including rules for monitoring and reporting, and say those conditions should not change the basic design, place, size, length, or timing of the activity. The bill would add a rule that decisions under the law must use the best scientific and commercial data available, without added caution-based assumptions.

US-119-HR10777.s: The bill would make certain federal orders and memorandums about fighting transnational cybercrime count as law. It would affect federal efforts to combat cyber-enabled crime, fraud, and related schemes. It also covers a memo on expanding cyber capabilities to fight this kind of crime.

US-119-HR10778.s: The bill would create a tax credit for health care facilities that use certain low-emission anesthetic gases. It would apply to hospitals and some surgical centers, and it would also cover some costs to retrofit mobile anesthetic machines so they can use those gases. The credit would apply to amounts paid or incurred after December 31, 2026, and would end for amounts paid or incurred after December 31, 2029.

US-119-HR10779.s: The bill would name the U.S. Postal Service building at 1905 Route 112 in Medford, New York, the "Gunnery Sergeant Ruben Santos Post Office Building." It affects that specific post office facility.

US-119-HR10780.s: This bill would change how Congress plans and passes federal spending bills. It would require some appropriations bills to be grouped in set ways, add a spending reduction account to those bills, and create new budget rules for executive spending and impoundment, which is when money is delayed or held back. It would also set up automatic continuing appropriations for some programs during a funding lapse, with 14-day extensions, starting in fiscal year 2027 and later.

US-119-HR10781.s: The bill would ask the President to name one month each year as National American History and Founders Month. It would also ask state, local, and territorial leaders to issue their own yearly proclamations and encourage programs, ceremonies, and activities that support civics education and knowledge of U.S. history. The proposal affects the President and governments in the states, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories and possessions.

US-119-HR10782.s: The bill would extend the Clean School Bus Program by changing its covered years from 2022–2026 to 2027–2031. It would affect the federal program that helps replace school buses with cleaner ones.

US-119-HR10783.s: The bill would let a defendant who wins a federal defamation or libel case get reasonable lawyer fees and court costs paid by the person who sued. It applies to cases over a communication about sexual assault, harassment, or discrimination, if the statement was factual and made without malice. A judge could limit the award in special cases.

US-119-HR10785.s: The bill would reauthorize the SCORE program, which helps small business owners and people who want to start a business with free counseling, mentoring, coaching, and workshops. It would also add new rules for how the program is run, including reporting, accounting, privacy, and online services. The bill would authorize $17 million for each of fiscal years 2027 and 2028.

US-119-HR10786.s: The bill would change federal higher education rules so some colleges and universities would have to make U.S. citizen students pass the U.S. naturalization test before graduating. The test would have to be given by a faculty member, with no books or notes. It would apply to certain institutions covered by the Higher Education Act.

US-119-HR10787.s: The bill would keep Medicare competitive buying rules from covering urological and ostomy supplies for 5 years, from January 1, 2028, through January 1, 2033. It would also create an expert panel and a pilot project to study how these supplies affect patient access and health results. People who use these supplies, along with suppliers and Medicare officials, would be affected, and the bill would bar suppliers from pushing people to switch brands without being asked.

US-119-HR10788.s: This bill would change some surprise medical billing rules for private health insurance. It would change how the payment amount is figured, set new rules for payments and audits starting in 2028, and affect health plans, insurers, providers, and air ambulance services. It would also limit some dispute steps for bills under these rules.

US-119-HR10789.s: The bill would block new oil and gas leasing, preleasing, production, and related work in the Eglin Gulf Test and Training Range. It would not change valid leases already in place when the law takes effect. The ban would end if the Secretary of War tells Congress that the range is not of critical use.

US-119-HR10790.s: The bill would change the rules for the Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board. It would require at least one board member to have experience in trades or industrial labor, and it would also set rules for filling vacancies, removing members, and the chair’s role. It affects the board’s members and presidential nominations.

US-119-HR10791.s: The bill would bar federal money from going to any state or local government that celebrates Indigenous Peoples Day instead of Columbus Day. This would apply starting one year after October 12, 2026, and on each later Columbus Day. It also says Congress thinks October 12 should keep being observed nationwide as Columbus Day.

US-119-HR10792.s: The bill would add new protections for people who report possible violations tied to the Federal Trade Commission. It would bar retaliation against whistleblowers, block some gag rules and arbitration deals from being enforced against them, and let some whistleblowers sue for reinstatement, back pay, and other damages. It would also create a reward program that could pay whistleblowers a share of money collected in covered FTC cases.

US-119-HR10793.s: The bill would change how the Defense Department can pay for installation support services and intergovernmental support agreements. It would let the Secretary of Defense use funds from any Defense Department source for these agreements, and it would add a rule for the repair, construction, maintenance, and operation of a facility on an installation. It would also require the department to create a data system, a public searchable database, and periodic reports to Congress on these agreements and their use.

US-119-HR10794.s: The bill would create a grant program for states to improve access to WIC, the nutrition program for women, infants, and children. States could use the money for outreach, better data sharing, online applications, and other steps to help people enroll and stay in the program. It would authorize $50 million each year from fiscal year 2027 through 2031, and each participating state would get at least $200,000 when possible.

US-119-HR10795.s: The bill would direct the State Department to try to set up a U.S.-Sudan partnership on farming and minerals. If Sudan meets certain steps on civilian protection, stability, and basic rule, the United States could provide farm and mining tools and help in exchange for minerals from Sudan. It would affect U.S. foreign policy and Sudan’s agriculture and mining sectors.

US-119-HR10796.s: The bill would require the Secretary of Defense to name one person or office to coordinate U.S. defense technology work with Israel. It would cover research, testing, buying, and joint work in areas like missile defense, cyber defense, artificial intelligence, and counter-drone systems. It would also require briefings and yearly reports to Congress on progress.

US-119-HR10797.s: The bill would direct the Air Force to run a Defense Department program for safe, long-range air transport of people who have, or may have, high-risk infectious diseases. It would also set training, safety, equipment, and care standards for military medical teams and for transporting these patients. The program would begin by October 1, 2027, and could also support other federal, state, local, civilian, and academic partners when needed.

US-119-HR10798.s: The bill would create a grant program for clinics, hospitals, health departments, and nonprofit health providers to treat people with silicosis and teach workers in high-silica jobs about it. The grants could pay for outreach, screening, diagnosis, treatment, patient help, and breathing rehab. It authorizes $10 million for each fiscal year from 2027 through 2031.

US-119-HR10799.s: The bill would change the wage rule for some H-1B workers who are exempt from the usual wage test. It would replace the $60,000 floor with a level set at twice the national average wage index, which is a measure of average wages. Employers that use this H-1B category would be affected.

US-119-HR10800.s: This bill would set a process for naming a country as a safe third country in asylum cases and for reviewing those decisions. It would let a person challenge a removal to that country by showing certain risks or problems, and they would be released from detention while the review goes on. It would also require the Secretary of State to issue standards for safe third countries within 180 days and to certify to Congress that a country meets those standards before it is named safe.

US-119-HR10801.s: The bill would end covered federal elementary and secondary education programs by no later than June 30, 2027, and move any unused money into new school savings accounts. The Treasury would set up a School Freedom Account for eligible students, with federal deposits starting for school years beginning on or after July 1, 2027. Parents could use the money for approved school costs, or choose to send the federal share to the public school their child attends. It would also create a later account for higher education and job training when the student finishes secondary school or ages out of public school.

US-119-HR10802.s: The bill would direct federal agencies to look for ways to help people register to vote and vote more easily. It would also require plans to improve federal voting websites, make Vote.gov easier to use and available in more languages, and help federal workers, service members, overseas citizens, people in federal custody, people with disabilities, and Native American communities access voting services. Some agencies would have to report back to the President and Congress with plans or recommendations within set time limits.

US-119-HR10803.s: The bill would abolish the Department of Homeland Security and create a new Department of Community Safety. It would move some emergency and cybersecurity duties into the new department, and shift some other duties to the Transportation, Treasury, and Justice departments. It would also change immigration and border work by ending immigration detention, changing enforcement powers, and creating programs to help asylum seekers and immigrants with community-based support.

US-119-HR10804.s: The bill would set penalties for investor-owned electric utilities that do not meet state performance standards. If a utility fails to meet those standards, it would have to give residential customers a bill credit starting at $100 a year, with the amount increasing by $100 each year until the utility complies. If a state regulator does not follow the order, the Energy Secretary could withhold grants, loans, loan guarantees, and technical help from that state agency.

US-119-HR10805.s: The bill would change federal communications law so elementary schools, secondary schools, and public libraries that get universal service support could not block internet access to LGBTQ resources if they want to keep discounted service rates. It defines LGBTQ resources as information about topics like homosexuality, bisexuality, transgender identity, gender identity, and sexual orientation. The bill was introduced in the House and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

US-119-HR10806.s: The bill would tighten Medicare screening and oversight for home health agencies, including more checks for agencies seen as high risk for fraud. It would also require more frequent surveys in some cases and add training and review rules for groups that accredit these agencies. The bill would change how Medicare home health payment amounts are set starting in 2027 by using more reliable data and by blocking certain payment adjustments tied to the Patient-Driven Groupings Model.

US-119-HR10807.s: The bill would bar federal money from being used to buy, run, or support automated mass surveillance systems, such as license plate readers, biometric tracking, and facial recognition. It would also stop federal agencies from getting or using data from those systems, require some systems to be removed within 30 days, and require the data to be deleted within 7 days. States and local governments would have to certify they do not use these systems to qualify for some federal crime-fighting grants.

US-119-HR10808.s: The bill would let people add an extra $2,000 to a health savings account when a child is born or adopted. It would apply for each qualifying child under age 18, and married couples could split the extra amount between them. The change would apply to tax years starting after December 31, 2026.

US-119-HR10809.s: The bill would change federal power law so large data centers and high-density computing sites must pay the full added electric costs they cause. Those costs could not be passed on to other utility customers, and utilities would have to get financial backing before building or upgrading power equipment for these sites. The rules would apply to new covered loads, which are sites using at least 20 megawatts of power, while older approved arrangements would stay in place.

US-119-HR10810.s: The bill would create a National Patient Safety Board within the Department of Health and Human Services to help prevent and reduce patient safety events. It would let patients, providers, and others report safety problems, including anonymously, and would have the board study data and share reports. The board would also work with federal agencies and some private groups to find causes and suggest fixes.

US-119-HR10811.s: The bill would let some transit projects get a larger federal share of costs if the project leader gives small businesses nearby certain help during construction disruptions. That help would include a point of contact, regular updates, and extra signs to guide customers. It applies to new rail or guideway projects, core capacity upgrades, and small start projects.

US-119-HR10812.s: The bill would have the Library of Congress keep track of its Armenian American materials and make digitized copies of them when allowed by funding and copyright rules. It would also use these materials in education collections and send a report to Congress within 1 year after enactment. The bill would affect the Library of Congress and people who use its collections, and it would call for an exhibit and event in 2026 celebrating Armenian American heritage.

US-119-HR10813.s: The bill would let certain partnerships choose a special process to settle open tax disputes tied to donations of conservation easements. It applies to eligible partnership donations made in tax years ending on or before December 31, 2025, and can affect the partnership, its partners, and related pass-through entities. If the election is made, the partnership would pay a settlement amount and related tax and penalty amounts, and that payment would resolve the federal income tax issues tied to the part of the deduction above the allowed limit.

US-119-HR10814.s: The bill would require political ads that use generative AI images or video to include a clear notice saying so. It would also expand federal election ad rules to cover some paid online ads and set rules for large online platforms and ad vendors. The changes would apply to communications made on or after January 1, 2027, and the Federal Election Commission would have to report to Congress every two years after the law takes effect.

US-119-HR10815.s: The bill would create a new tax credit for certain child care providers that spend money to improve access and innovation for children with developmental disabilities. The credit would cover up to $10,000 in eligible costs each year for providers that meet state law and local rules. The change would apply to amounts paid or incurred after December 31, 2026, and the credit would end for amounts paid or incurred after December 31, 2031.

US-119-HR10816.s: The bill would bar the Defense Department from naming or renaming facilities, aircraft, ships, or other assets after a sitting president. It would also block Defense Department funds from being used for that purpose. Any Defense asset already named for the current president would have to go back to its earlier name when the law takes effect.

US-119-HR10817.s: The bill would state that Congress thinks the Navy should name an aircraft carrier the "Doris Miller" to honor Mess Attendant Third Class Doris "Dorie" Miller. It gives a short history of Miller’s service at Pearl Harbor, where he saved his captain, fired an anti-aircraft gun, and helped evacuate sailors. The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the House Armed Services Committee.

US-119-HR10818.s: The bill would change the tax code so some income earned by firefighters and emergency medical services workers would not count as taxable income. It would cover up to the first $100,000 of ordinary income each year for certain full-time firefighters with at least 5 years of service and some qualified volunteer first responders. The change would apply to tax years that begin after the date the law is enacted.

US-119-HR10819.s: The bill would direct the Secretary of State to seek an agreement with India within 180 days to create a U.S.-India interparliamentary group that would help both countries work on shared interests. If the agreement is reached, Congress would appoint up to 12 members to represent the United States, and the group would meet at least once a year with Indian lawmakers. It would also have to file an annual report on spending, and the bill would allow up to $100,000 a year for its costs.

US-119-HR10820.s: The bill would require certain federal financial regulators to hand over and later post records tied to Jeffrey Epstein and related people or entities. It would also order those agencies to start investigations into covered banks and other financial firms, and into senior leaders at those firms, for possible banking, securities, money laundering, or criminal law violations. The bill also calls for possible bans, civil penalties, and criminal referrals, and sets deadlines of 90, 120, and 180 days after enactment for some of the required steps.

US-119-HR10821.s: The bill would raise the standard FDIC deposit insurance limit from $250,000 to $750,000 and then adjust that amount each year for inflation using the Consumer Price Index, rounded down to the nearest $10,000. It would apply 180 days after enactment. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the National Credit Union Administration would also have to study the right insurance amount and report to Congress within 1 year.

US-119-HR10822.s: The bill would limit how government agencies can use automated license plate reader systems. It would generally require a warrant based on probable cause to search records, with a narrow emergency exception, and it would bar use for tracking people based on political or religious ties or for some civil fines and immigration enforcement. It would also require fast deletion of records, limit how vehicle details can be stored and searched, and require logging and public reporting by agencies and vendors.

US-119-HR10823.s: The bill would let the Interior Secretary run a voluntary grant and help program for habitat restoration in the Oregon and Washington coastal zone and the Columbia River Basin. It would give grants and technical help to public agencies, tribes, nonprofits, private landowners, and other approved groups for projects that improve habitat and water for shorebirds, waterfowl, and other wetland birds. The bill would authorize $10 million each year from fiscal years 2026 through 2030, and the Secretary would report to Congress within 180 days after enactment and every year after that.

US-119-HR10824.s: The bill would direct the Health and Human Services Secretary to create a national stroke education program for emergency medical services clinicians within 2 years. The program would teach EMS workers how to spot stroke signs, give care before the hospital, and take patients to the right stroke center. It would also allow grants to state and local EMS agencies, give priority to underserved and rural areas, and require reports to Congress on the program’s results.

US-119-HR10825.s: The bill would bar certain joint fundraising committees that include federal candidates and super PACs, which are independent groups that can spend money on ads, from paying for broadcast, cable, satellite, or paid online ads. If they broke this rule, the spending would count as a coordinated campaign expense and as a contribution to the candidate. It would take effect when enacted.

US-119-HR10826.s: The bill would let U.S. citizens sue immigration officers or other law enforcement officers who enforce immigration laws if they are arrested or detained without a warrant or probable cause on or after January 20, 2025. If they win, the court would award $500,000 plus $100,000 for each day of detention, along with lawyer fees and other court-ordered relief. It also would end some unused immigration enforcement funds.

US-119-HR10827.s: The bill would require the Secretary of State, with the Director of National Intelligence, to send Congress a report naming senior Syrian officials and related people who are credibly alleged to have helped with serious human rights abuses against religious and ethnic minorities. It would also ask for a finding on whether targeted penalties, like blocking property or visa limits, should be used under existing U.S. law. The bill says the United States supports accountability for abuses in Syria and the protection of minority communities.

US-119-HR10829.s: The bill would require the Federal Trade Commission’s Elder Justice Coordinator to set up a website and hotline for people who are victims of fraud and scams aimed at older adults. It would have to be ready within 180 days after the law takes effect and work 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. The site would also show the hotline number and give help and resources from several federal agencies.

US-119-HR10830.s: The bill would direct the Comptroller General to study pattern books, which are approved sets of building plans used to speed housing approvals. The study would look at how they affect housing supply, permit speed, and building costs, and it would also look for barriers and better ways to use them, including in rural areas. The Comptroller General would consult with local governments and other public and private groups, then send Congress and post a report within 18 months after the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR10831.s: The bill would change how oil and gas lease money from acquired lands is shared, and it would give states a larger share. It would amend two federal laws that cover mineral leasing on those lands. The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the House Natural Resources Committee.

US-119-HR10832.s: The bill would update U.S. plans to support internet access and secure online tools for people in Iran. It would direct federal agencies to review and update that strategy, ask the FCC to consider avoiding cuts to satellite coverage over Iran, and expand cybersecurity training and digital safety tools for journalists and other civil society groups in Iran. It would also authorize $15 million for each of fiscal years 2027 and 2028 for this work.

US-119-HR10833.s: The bill would let the Secretary insure mortgages for certain first-time homebuyers who meet income and homebuyer rules. It would cover some single-family homes, set loan and interest limits, and require homebuyer counseling. It would also set upfront and yearly insurance charges and provide interest rate help for lower-income borrowers.

US-119-HR10834.s: The bill would tell the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to start a review of fuel economy rules if gas prices rise at least five times faster than inflation over a 180-day period. It would affect vehicle fuel economy standards and the agency that sets them. It would also raise two penalty amounts in federal law from $0.00 to $25 and $50.

US-119-HR10835.s: The bill would add a program under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act to fund demonstration and pilot projects for training in advanced manufacturing. It would use grants or contracts for schools, local boards, and other eligible groups working with manufacturers. The projects would focus on workers with limited experience, including unemployed, dislocated, rural, and other underrepresented workers.

US-119-HR10836.s: The bill would change military justice rules to ban live TV or online broadcast of military executions. It would also bar making video of those executions available to the public after they happen. The rule would apply to executions under the military justice system and would take effect when the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR10837.s: The bill would bar people with a final conviction for bribery, certain ethics crimes, or a Foreign Agents Registration Act violation from holding certain executive branch jobs for 10 years. It would also require job holders to certify they are not barred, and the Office of Personnel Management would screen candidates and issue guidance to agencies. The bill sets penalties for violations, including removal from office and fines.

US-119-HR10838.s: The bill would give a 10-year time limit for bringing cases over false statements, hiding facts, or fraudulent claims made in matters tied to Congress. It would apply to work done by Congress, such as committee investigations, reviews, and oversight matters. The change would apply only to offenses committed on or after the date it takes effect.

US-119-HR10839.s: The bill would require federal agencies to make plans to reduce heat buildup at federal properties and facilities in areas with ozone pollution problems. The plans would look at steps like adding trees, shade, cool roofs, and cooler paving, and would also include costs, timelines, and funding. Agencies would update the plans every 2 years, and the General Services Administration would report yearly to Congress on progress.

US-119-HR10840.s: The bill would require the Comptroller General to study how the Department of Veterans Affairs keeps non-clinical staff, like support workers, at VA health care facilities and to report the findings to Congress within one year after it becomes law. The report would compare facilities with different retention results and look at things like size, location, staffing, pay, benefits, working conditions, workload, training, and hiring practices. It would also review practices at facilities with higher retention and analyze an anonymous survey of non-clinical staff, including people leaving VA jobs.

US-119-HR10841.s: The bill would bar people who build or use artificial intelligence from using it to trick, threaten, or stop people from voting in federal, state, or local elections. It would also require clear labels on certain AI-made election content, like altered images, fake voice clips, or voting info, and the Federal Trade Commission would enforce these rules. It would apply to developers and users of these systems, and some parts would take effect 60 days after enactment or 60 days after the FTC issues rules.

US-119-HR10843.s: The bill would change copyright rules for visual artists, especially for photos, drawings, and other art works. It would let artists register groups of photos together, use third-party photo registries, and use deferred registration, which means some works could be registered later while still getting an earlier effective date. It would also require the Copyright Office to set up online tools, keep electronic deposits, and create lower fees and subscription options for these kinds of works.

US-119-HR10844.s: The bill would change Medicare payment rules for services provided by mobile stroke units, which are vehicles that bring stroke care to patients. For items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2027, it would treat them as outpatient department services for payment, and some rural cases would get a 5% higher payment. It would also exclude these services from inpatient operating costs.

US-119-HR10845.s: The bill would require the Homeland Security secretary, with Customs and Border Protection and the General Services Administration, to send Congress a report on how air, land, and sea ports of entry are run. The report would cover staffing levels, delays, temporary duty moves, lane openings at land ports, border tools and their effects on rights, trade impacts, and needed buildings or tech. It would also require a briefing to Congress after each report.

US-119-HR10847.s: The bill would set the rank of the top military lawyers in the Army, Marine Corps, Navy, and Air Force, and it would raise some deputy roles to higher ranks when needed. It would affect Judge Advocates General and Deputy Judge Advocates General in those services. It would also set the Marine Corps staff judge advocate to the Commandant at the rank of lieutenant general in some cases.

US-119-HR10849.s: The bill would change a Defense Department program that helps small businesses with procurement, which means getting goods and services for the government. It would say the help is for confidential procurement assistance and raise some funding limits from $1.5 million to $2 million and from $750,000 to $1 million. It would also let the Secretary change those dollar limits in some cases and notify Congress within 30 days.

US-119-HR10850.s: The bill would require a federal health IT office to create a national, machine-readable framework for cancer screening recommendations and update it each year. It would also require certified health technology to use that framework to help show when a person is due for a screening, while following privacy rules. The bill would direct federal health officials to guide certain health plans on using this technology and would let a research institute support related studies and pilot projects.

US-119-HR10851.s: The bill would set a federal standard for states to consider ways to promote portable solar devices that plug into a home outlet and help cut electricity use. It would also create a grant program for states to give point-of-sale rebates of up to $1,000 for low- and moderate-income households, with extra focus on renters, multifamily residents, and high-energy burdened communities. The bill would require a voluntary label showing expected electricity cost savings and would direct a federal safety standard for these devices. It also sets some tenant protections, state review timelines, and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2032.

US-119-HR10852.s: The bill would add tax credits for making mass timber products, which are wood products like cross-laminated timber and glue laminated timber. It would also give a 20% credit for research expenses tied to mass timber products. The changes would apply to property placed in service after the bill becomes law, and the research credit would apply to amounts paid or incurred after that date.

US-119-HR10853.s: The bill would require the Homeland Security secretary to give Yemen temporary protected status. That status would let eligible people from Yemen stay in the United States for a set time. The designation would last until 3 months after January 20, 2029.

US-119-HR10854.s: The bill would direct the Secretary of Energy to set up a program that tracks public safety power shutoff events, which are planned outages used to lower wildfire or other safety risks. Covered electric utilities would have to report details like where the outage happened, how long it lasted, how many customers and critical services were affected, and what hazards led to it. The Energy Department would publish quarterly public summaries and share the information with emergency and state agencies, while keeping certain reported details protected.

US-119-HR10855.s: The bill would create an East Coast Bivalve Research Task Force to study shellfish like clams, oysters, mussels, and scallops in East Coast states. The group would review existing research, find gaps in knowledge, and look at issues like harvest changes, habitat, climate change, disease, and the economy of bivalve fishing and farming. It would be set up by the Secretary of Commerce within 90 days after enactment and include federal, state, tribal, industry, and academic members.

US-119-HR10856.s: The bill would change the low-income housing tax credit rules so certain low-income housing units could not qualify if they are occupied by some noncitizens who do not meet the listed immigration rules. States could also choose a different rule that lowers the housing credit amount by 5 percent instead. The changes would start for tax years and calendar years after December 31, 2027.

US-119-HR10858.s: The bill would create a National Blood Cancer Program at the Health and Human Services Department. It would fund grants for state, local, tribal, and other groups to raise awareness, train health workers, and help people with blood cancer and their caregivers. It would also fund colleges and medical centers to study better tests and treatments, and it would require yearly reports to Congress.

US-119-HR10859.s: The bill would require the Defense Secretary to make a strategy for adding biotechnology threats from foreign adversaries into defense planning, with a focus on China. It would also require intelligence and defense officials to submit reports on China’s use of biotechnology for military use and on foreign biotech investments in the United States. The bill would create a contact group to monitor these risks and brief Congress on its work.

US-119-HR10860.s: The bill would stop the Department of Defense from buying or using certain robotic systems tied to China. It would block new contracts for those systems within 1 year of enactment, bar use in sensitive military settings within 2 years, and limit lease funding, with some rules taking effect 1 year and 3 years after enactment. The Secretary of Defense could give short waivers in some cases and would have to tell Congress about them.

US-119-HR10861.s: The bill would require the Defense Department to audit its systems and infrastructure for certain cellular modules and assess the cyber risk they pose. It would also require reports to Congress on the findings, mitigation steps, costs, and timelines, with a separate review by the Comptroller General. The rules would apply to Defense Department systems, including government and contractor-operated systems that connect to Defense networks or use Defense information.

US-119-HR10862.s: The bill would direct the Pentagon’s Inspector General to review how the military departments try to prevent suicide, suicide attempts, and suicidal thoughts among service members. The review would look at data, command response plans, mental health team capacity, training, and access to mental health resources. The Inspector General would have to send a report to Congress by April 30, 2027.

US-119-HR10863.s: The bill would set up a pilot program at the Department of Veterans Affairs to give grants to nonprofit groups that provide dogs or cats to eligible veterans. Those groups would also help pay for starter supplies, spaying or neutering, and initial shots and medicine for the pets. The program would end after fiscal year 2028, and up to $1,000,000 would be available for fiscal years 2027 through 2028.

US-119-HR10864.s: The bill would direct the Interior Secretary to transfer the San Carlos Irrigation Project electric system and related assets in Arizona to other agreed-upon parties. It would require the transfer plan to be made with federal, state, tribal, local, and private partners, and the new owners would pay the transfer costs unless Congress provides funds. It would also let the government make contracts for other Bureau of Indian Affairs electric systems, with notice to Congress before any contract is signed.

US-119-HR10865.s: The bill would require states to give notice and reasons after they decide where to place a child who has been removed from a parent’s custody. It would also let certain people ask for the reasons in writing, let the child’s lawyer ask a court to review the decision, and require that review to start within 7 days and be held on the record. The new rules would take effect at the start of the first fiscal year after the bill becomes law, with a later start allowed if a state needs new state laws to comply.

US-119-HR10866.s: The bill would stop the Treasury Department from granting waivers or general licenses that would let Russian energy products be imported. It would also cancel a current Russia-related license for diesel fuel transactions and block future similar deals. In addition, it would require U.S. intelligence agencies to provide certain intelligence support to Ukraine and to report any break in that support within 24 hours.

US-119-HR10867.s: The bill would make it unlawful to import most sloths into the United States. It would allow some imports for research if the animal is dead, or for a covered zoo or similar facility as part of a breeding program, if the person shows the sloth was not taken from the wild after the law takes effect. People who break the rule could face fines, loss of federal wildlife-related permits, and seizure of the sloth.

US-119-HR10868.s: The bill would bar federal education money from being used for instructional materials with sexually explicit content in kindergarten through 12th grade. It would also require school districts that get federal funds to let parents or guardians review the materials their children can access. The changes would start with the first full fiscal year after the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR10869.s: The bill would increase funding for state programs that help pay for cleanup of emerging contaminants in drinking water and wastewater systems, including PFAS. It would raise one program’s funding to $1 billion a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2031 and create a new grant program for state water pollution funds to use for this cleanup work. At least 25% of those grants would go to small or disadvantaged communities and systems serving fewer than 25,000 people.

US-119-HR10870.s: This bill would extend Special Victim's Counsel services, a military legal help service, to people hurt by domestic violence. It would also change related Defense Department rules and require a briefing to Congress on how the new policies are being carried out. The changes would take effect two years after the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR10871.s: The bill would require military relocation information to include help with food access and child care for service members who get orders to move to a new base. It would add details about nutrition aid, local support services, and child care options, including Defense Department help and community programs. It applies to members of the armed forces receiving permanent station change orders.

US-119-HR10872.s: The bill would create a National Auto Theft Bureau in the Justice Department. It would gather auto theft information, help law enforcement share it in real time, and give training and advice to police, private companies, and the public. It would also set up a pilot program for state and local police, with $10 million authorized for fiscal year 2027.

US-119-HR10873.s: The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST, to work with private AI companies on ways to define and stop certain AI distillation attacks. It would also create an AI Cybersecurity Roundtable to develop voluntary standards and best practices for using AI to help protect computer systems. NIST would publish these standards and best practices on its website after they are ready.

US-119-HR10874.s: The bill would make Medicare drug plan premium help and cost-sharing help available to low-income people in Puerto Rico and other U.S. territories. It would also change how some Medicare and Medicaid payment amounts are figured for those places. The Medicare help changes would take effect on January 1, 2027, and the other changes would take effect when the law is enacted.

US-119-HR10875.s: The bill would lower the age to qualify for Medicare from 65 to 50, with some enrollment and premium rules updated to match. It would also create automatic enrollment steps for people who become eligible under the new age rule. Some changes would take effect 6 months after enactment, while a few would start on the day the law is enacted.

US-119-HR10876.s: The bill would change Medicare rules for mental health care and affect Medicare patients and behavioral health providers. It would end a 190-day lifetime limit for some inpatient psychiatric care starting October 1, 2027, and block payment cuts for people admitted after an involuntary commitment order under state law. It would also raise Medicare payment for certain behavioral health integration services in 2027 through 2029, require technical help for primary care practices that add these services, and provide money for that help through fiscal year 2031.

US-119-HR10877.s: The bill would give brewers a tax credit for donating spent grain, which is the leftover grain from beer making, for local farm use. The credit would be 8 cents per dry pound of spent grain, with a yearly cap of $35,000 and other limits tied to the beer tax owed. It would cover use in compost, soil improvement, mushroom growing, and animal feed within 100 miles of the brewery, and would apply to beer removed after December 31, 2026.

US-119-HR10878.s: The bill would create an independent Truth and Accountability Commission in the legislative branch. It would investigate alleged abuses of public office and other misconduct by U.S. officers and employees since January 20, 2025, and could also look at related private people and companies. The commission would make its findings public and could refer possible lawbreaking to federal or state authorities.

US-119-HR10879.s: The bill would bar noncompete agreements for workers and contractors whose cash pay is under $100,000 a year, with that amount rising with inflation after 2026. It would also require written notice that such agreements cannot be enforced and let the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general enforce the rule. The bill says stronger state protections can still apply, and it does not stop agreements to protect trade secrets or other confidential business information.

US-119-HR10880.s: The bill would create a free online form run by the General Services Administration so people could send a new address to certain federal agencies at once. It would require those agencies, including the IRS, Social Security, Veterans Affairs, and the Postal Service, to update their records if the notice is valid, and it would let people get confirmation that the notice was received. The program would be temporary and would end after 5 years, or sooner if it is not set up within 3 years after enactment.

US-119-HR10881.s: The bill would require the Commerce Secretary to send Congress a report on the number, prices, and ownership costs of different kinds of new vehicles, and it would also require more reports on key minerals, gasoline-heavy drivers, and electric vehicle charging use. It would make the clean vehicle tax credit, the used clean vehicle credit, and the alternative fuel refueling property tax credit permanent, and it would raise the credit amounts and change some income limits. These tax credit changes would affect people and businesses that buy or install eligible clean vehicle and fuel charging property.

US-119-HR10882.s: The bill would make male breast cancer count as service-related for certain veterans when the Department of Veterans Affairs decides on disability pay. That means some veterans with male breast cancer could be more likely to qualify for VA disability compensation. It was introduced in the House and sent to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee.

US-119-HR10883.s: Would change tax rules for certain home swaps. It would let some homeowners avoid tax on gains or losses when they exchange a principal home for another like-kind home, if they owned and used the home as their main residence for the past 30 years. The change would apply to exchanges completed after December 31, 2026.

US-119-HR10885.s: The bill would require food delivery apps and other delivery services to have a written partnership agreement with a restaurant before they can take orders for that restaurant. If a restaurant asks and there is no agreement, the service would have to remove the restaurant from its online platform and stop handling its orders within 10 days. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rule, and it would apply to orders placed 180 days after the law takes effect. It would also make an FTC rule on impersonating government and businesses carry the force of law.

US-119-HR10886.s: The bill would require the Office of Personnel Management to publish a yearly public list of federal workers who are also citizens or nationals of another country, or who owe allegiance to another country. The list would include the other countries, the worker's federal agency, and the job title and yearly pay. It would apply to federal government employees who have dual citizenship or similar ties to another country.

US-119-HR10887.s: The bill would make it unlawful for brand-name drug makers to pay generic drug makers to delay market entry. It would also ban payments between biologic drug makers and makers of biosimilar or interchangeable products for the same kind of delay. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce these rules, and the bill would also allow some settlements that only include certain items, like a right to market early, litigation costs up to $7.5 million, or a promise not to sue.

US-119-HR10888.s: The bill would direct the NOAA Administrator to run a National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science program. It would support research, monitoring, grants, and technical help for coastal, ocean, and Great Lakes habitats, affecting federal, state, Tribal, and local coastal managers, plus research partners. It would authorize $75 million each year from fiscal years 2027 through 2033.

US-119-HR10889.s: The bill would create a new tax credit for individuals for personal fuel costs. It would cover money spent on gasoline, diesel, or charging an electric vehicle for personal use. The change would apply to amounts paid or incurred after December 31, 2026.

US-119-HR10890.s: The bill would create a new income tax deduction for individuals for personal motor fuel costs. It would cover gas, diesel, and the cost to recharge an electric vehicle for personal use, and it would also be available to people who do not itemize deductions. The changes would apply to amounts paid or incurred after December 31, 2026.

US-119-HR10891.s: The bill would change tax rules so people who lose money to theft tied to fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation could deduct those losses. It would also let them take that deduction even if they do not itemize other deductions. The change would apply to losses after the date the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR10892.s: The bill would require makers of certain household appliances to put a label or tag on each product and post the same details online. The label would show the appliance’s estimated performance life, the yearly cost of routine care, which features need Wi-Fi or software updates, how long updates will be provided, and how to report that the appliance has reached the end of its life. It would apply only to certain appliances named by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rule.

US-119-HR10893.s: The bill would stop the Homeland Security secretary from using personal information collected by FEMA to help enforce immigration laws. That information includes details like a name, address, Social Security number, or other identifying records. It would apply to information gathered when FEMA gives disaster or emergency help under federal disaster law.

US-119-HR10894.s: The bill would bar federal funds from being used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to get personal information collected by a private group after a natural disaster. A private group could share that information only if ICE gets a court warrant. It would affect DHS and ICE, and it covers information like names, addresses, Social Security numbers, and medical or job records tied to a person.

US-119-HR10895.s: The bill would have the Education Department create a grant program for civic education and service learning in public elementary and secondary schools.
