It would give grants to state and local school agencies, colleges, and nonprofit groups to train teachers, build civics lessons, and run student projects like mock hearings and community service, and it would authorize $400 million each fiscal year. It would also set up an Office of Civic Education, an advisory committee, and a center to study and improve these programs.

US-119-HR10896.s: The bill would end the diversity immigrant visa program, which is part of the U.S. immigration system. It would remove that category from the immigration law and make related changes to other parts of the law. It would affect people who apply for visas through that program.

US-119-HR10897.s: The bill would set new safety rules for ride-hailing apps. It would require a digital check so riders and drivers can confirm who they are before a trip starts, and it would let riders opt out in some cases. It would also require driver background and work-status checks, and it would ban the sale of fake or unauthorized ride-hailing signs.

US-119-HR10898.s: The bill would require the President’s pay agent to study and then set pay areas for the Orlando and Tampa metro areas. It would affect federal pay for workers in those places. If enacted, these steps would need to happen within 1 year.

US-119-HR10899.s: The bill would let the President provide aid to people and households after a long power outage, even if no major disaster is declared. It covers needs like medical and dental costs, lodging, moving costs, and some personal property costs. It applies only to outages caused by covered events, such as major storms, fires, floods, explosions, terrorism, or cyber events, and only when at least 10% of people in a local area lose power for 72 hours or more.

US-119-HR10900.s: States and local governments that get certain Justice Department grants would have to report to the Attorney General on misuse of automated license plate readers by police. The report would cover law-breaking use, related convictions, and any discipline taken, and the reports would be posted online. If a government did not file the report or did not take corrective action, its future Byrne or COPS grant money could be cut.

US-119-HR10901.s: The bill would require the Housing and Urban Development Department to set up a grant program for states to help speed up support for builders of affordable housing. States could use the money to combine housing finance offices, make the aid process simpler, help builders with applications, and improve rules like permits and zoning. It would authorize $90 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029, and each state that joins could get at least $500,000 a year, subject to available funds.

US-119-HR10902.s: The bill would tie some federal transit money to steps meant to reduce crime and improve safety on public transit. It would affect transit agencies and state or local governments, and it would start some funding cuts in fiscal year 2028 if certain local laws do not treat fare evasion as a crime, bar people convicted of violent crimes like assault from transit, or require a bail bond for some people charged with crimes. It also would let transit funds pay for things like better lighting, cameras, emergency phones, cybersecurity, fare controls, transit police, and other safety projects.

US-119-HR10903.s: The bill would direct the Department of Veterans Affairs to try to lease space for a Vet Center in Socorro, New Mexico. The lease would need to start no later than December 31, 2027. It would affect veterans in the Socorro area who may use the center.

US-119-HR10904.s: The bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to lead a group of federal agencies to track and report on market concentration and monopoly activity in certain parts of the economy. It would require public reports on things like top firms' market share, supply chain bottlenecks, and possible pricing coordination, with graphs and charts for the public. The sectors covered could include basic goods and services such as food, fuel, rent, drugs, and phone service.

US-119-HR10905.s: The bill would bar large grocery stores and their online shops from using a shopper’s personal data, facial scans, or similar data to set different prices. It would also ban dynamic pricing, which means changing prices based on when or what kind of shopper is expected to buy. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce it, and it would take effect 1 year after it becomes law.

US-119-HR10906.s: The bill would create and expand tax credits for mass timber buildings, biomass facilities, carbon capture, and some fuel made from biomass. It would also change rules for forest products, timber, and biomass used in energy and building projects, and it would set new grants and fund programs for wood research and use. Several parts would apply after the bill becomes law, with some starting dates tied to when buildings are placed in service or when guidance is issued.

US-119-HR10907.s: The bill would add new civil remedies and longer time limits for certain election interference crimes tied to federal elections. It would also limit when law enforcement can seize ballots or election equipment and require chain-of-custody records if seizure happens. States could get grants to set up ballot tracking programs, with $50 million authorized for fiscal year 2027.

US-119-HR10908.s: The bill would create Universal Savings Accounts with tax rules for deposits, withdrawals, and extra contributions. It would also require health plans and insurers to give prior approval decisions in writing and through a secure portal within 30 days, and to share procedure codes, prices, and covered services with insurance contracts. It would bar some changes to drug tiers or covered services during a plan term and would set rules tied to in-network and out-of-network provider payments.

US-119-HR10909.s: The bill would change how deaths in custody are reported under the 2013 law. It would require more detailed reports to the Director of the Bureau of Justice Statistics, including more facts about each death, and it would call for a public database and yearly reports. It would also direct the National Institute of Justice to study the data and report its findings to Congress.

US-119-HR10910.s: The bill would change the Animal Welfare Act to add extra protections for companion animals kept at certain pet businesses, like boarding, daycare, training, grooming, and overnight care. It would define “sentient being” as a household companion mammal, such as dogs, cats, and rabbits, and it would exclude livestock and other listed animals. It would also let the owner of a harmed, neglected, or dead animal sue in federal court to seek damages, court costs, and lawyer fees.

US-119-HR10911.s: The bill would create a voluntary swine health program run by the Agriculture Secretary with states and the swine industry. It would certify certain pig facilities that meet rules for disease safety, tracking, and monitoring for diseases like African swine fever and classical swine fever. It would also require the final rule to be finished within 1 year after enactment and would authorize $4.5 million each year from fiscal 2027 through 2031.

US-119-HR10912.s: The bill would speed approval for certain U.S.-made defense items bought by NATO members, Australia, Japan, South Korea, Israel, or New Zealand and then sent to Ukraine. It covers 155mm artillery shells, Excalibur shells, HIMARS munitions, and GMLRS munitions, and it would require Ukraine to agree not to pass them on without U.S. consent. The President would have to notify Congress before the transfer, and the time limit for Ukraine to take custody could be extended in one-year steps through December 31, 2035 if Russia’s invasion is still ongoing.

US-119-HR10913.s: The bill would change food safety law so food for people that contains any amount of butylated hydroxyanisole, butylated hydroxytoluene, or tert-butylhydroquinone would count as adulterated, meaning not meeting the law’s food standard. It would apply to food put into interstate commerce 2 years after enactment. The Food and Drug Administration would have to write rules within 2 years, and the Health and Human Services secretary would have to send Congress a report within 3 years.

US-119-HR10914.s: The bill would extend and update a grant program that helps socially disadvantaged, veteran, and beginning farmers and ranchers get outreach and technical help. It would run the program from 2027 through 2031 and allow more use of interpretation and translation services to help people access Agriculture Department programs. It would also require new data reports on farm program use by county and state, including race, ethnicity, and gender, with privacy protections.

US-119-HR10915.s: The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to study cloud security and publish new rules and advice for cloud-based systems. It would also create a voluntary cloud security certification program for private companies, with public listings of certifications and tiered levels. The bill would affect cloud service providers, federal agencies, and owners and operators of critical infrastructure.

US-119-HR10916.s: The bill would require the Agriculture and Interior secretaries to make a joint plan to expand the use of aquatic restoration and conservation in wildfire risk work and post-fire recovery on federal lands. It would look at science, staff training, and ways to use these efforts in fuel reduction projects, grant-funded work, contracts, and stewardship agreements. The plan would be due within 1 year after enactment, and the secretaries would then send a report to Congress.

US-119-HR10917.s: The bill would direct the Agriculture Secretary to start a pilot program for forest restoration projects on National Forest System land and nearby land. It would also support work to help communities better handle wildfire, including critical infrastructure, microgrids, home retrofits, and wildfire detection equipment. The bill limits the pilot to 20 agreements and up to $250 million over 10 years, with no more than $50 million for any one agreement.

US-119-HR10918.s: The bill would change the Clean Air Act rules for certain oil and gas sites. It would stop the Environmental Protection Agency from requiring some owners and operators to continuously monitor the net heating value, or related measures, of certain combustion control devices like flares. It would also set limits on how long some wells may send gas to a flare or control device during malfunctions or service breaks.

US-119-HR10919.s: The bill would require certain safety net health providers to pay no more than the 340B ceiling price for covered outpatient drugs when they buy them. It applies to certain covered entities and sole community hospitals. The change would take effect on the date it is enacted and would apply to drugs bought on or after that date.

US-119-HR10920.s: The bill would renew a federal grant program for state professional licensing boards. The grants would help them create and carry out rules that lower state barriers to telemedicine, or health care delivered by phone or video. It would extend the program for fiscal years 2026 through 2031.

US-119-HR10921.s: The bill would make Medicare cover custom-made breast prostheses after a mastectomy, including replacements. It would apply to services provided on or after the date the act is enacted. This would affect Medicare patients who have had breast removal surgery.

US-119-HR10922.s: The bill would make state officers and employees liable if they know about fraud in certain benefit programs and fail to help stop it. It would let the Attorney General bring a civil case and seek money damages, with higher amounts when the loss is over $500,000. It would also set required prison terms for certain fraud crimes tied to covered benefits, with longer terms for bigger losses and for repeat offenses.

US-119-HR10923.s: The bill would change the Controlled Substances Act to use newer medical and public health standards. It would create a new system for how controlled substances are placed into schedules, change some federal powers, and support more scientific research. It also includes changes for marijuana descheduling and drug sentencing rules.

US-119-HR10924.s: The bill would create a new national health program called Medicare for America and expand health coverage for people in the United States and U.S. territories. It would also set up a temporary public plan option on the health insurance exchanges for 2028 and 2029. The bill includes automatic enrollment steps for some people, including babies born in those years and some current Medicare users, and it changes some tax rules, drug pricing rules, and health plan rules.

US-119-HR10925.s: The bill would require the State Department to assess its technical ability to deal with the use of artificial intelligence and other new technology to help trafficking in people, especially trafficking involving children. It would also ask what staff or training gaps exist and what steps the department would take to fix them if needed. The report would be due within 180 days after the bill becomes law and would go to House and Senate foreign affairs committees.

US-119-HR10926.s: The bill would add new penalties for using force, threats, or violence to interfere with voting, poll watchers, election officials, and people helping run elections. It would also make it a crime to damage or threaten to damage polling places, tabulation centers, or other election equipment. Penalties could include fines up to $2,500 or up to 6 months in jail, and higher penalties up to $5,000 or 1 year if someone is injured or a dangerous weapon, explosive, or fire is used. The Justice Department could bring a federal case only in certain situations, such as when a state lacks jurisdiction or asks the federal government to step in.

US-119-HR10927.s: The bill would amend federal voting law to make it a crime to destroy or damage secure, clearly labeled ballot boxes used to drop off voted ballots in federal elections. It would apply to anyone who does this with the intent to harm voted ballots. A person could be fined up to $20,000 for each box or ballot involved, or face up to 20 years in prison, or both.

US-119-HR10928.s: The bill would let the Agriculture Secretary give block grants to certain states for crop losses from freezes or cold weather in April 2026. It covers losses to crops, trees, bushes, and vines, including crops that were not planted, and it also includes multi-year crops. The states named are Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and West Virginia. It authorizes $3.5 billion for fiscal year 2027.

US-119-HR10929.s: The bill would put a 50% import duty on certain hemp and cannabinoid products from China. It would also set new tariff categories for different kinds of cannabinoids and require testing of imported cannabinoid products for things like heavy metals, pesticides, germs, leftover solvents, and unknown compounds when they are meant for people to consume. The new duty would apply to covered imports entered 90 days after the bill becomes law, and federal agencies would publish yearly import and testing reports.

US-119-HR10930.s: The bill would change federal juvenile crime rules to account for the age of some young offenders, raise certain age cutoffs in transfer to adult court rules, and add factors like trauma and foster care involvement for judges to consider. It would also change murder rules for people under 18 in some cases and require the Justice Department to publish yearly data on children in the federal justice system. In addition, it would let the Health and Human Services Secretary award competitive grants to help state child welfare and juvenile justice agencies work together.

US-119-HR10931.s: The bill would create a grant program for public library construction and upgrades. It would let states, local governments, and their agencies apply for money to build, add to, repair, or modernize library buildings, including work on roofs, plumbing, heating and cooling, and safety updates. The federal share of each project could not be more than 50 percent.

US-119-HR10932.s: The bill would make FEMA share its disaster recommendation report with a state or tribal government when it asks for a major disaster declaration. It would also require the President to give that government a detailed reason when a disaster request is approved or denied. The bill would direct FEMA to set new factors it can use when deciding whether a snowstorm or other snowfall event should get a major disaster declaration.

US-119-HR10933.s: The bill would direct the Health and Human Services Department to give grants to eligible fire departments, EMS groups, and some towns for emergency medical services work. The money could help hire and support EMS staff, pay for training and required certificates, buy gear and supplies, and upgrade equipment, buildings, and vehicles. It authorizes $750 million each year from 2027 through 2031, and the program would end on September 30, 2031.

US-119-HR10934.s: The bill would change rules for certain hardrock minerals and set a royalty on income from minerals taken from covered mining claims. It would send royalty money into a new fund, with shares for states, tribes, and other programs, and it would create a federal aid program to help pay for U.S. facilities and equipment that process critical minerals. The aid program would have rules on who can get help, how the money can be used, and how much one project can receive.

US-119-HR10935.s: The bill would direct the Interior Department to offer about 2,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land in Monterey County, California, for public sale within 2 years after it becomes law. The land would be sold by competitive bidding for at least fair market value, and the sale would follow existing federal land sale rules. Money from the sale would fund grants for wildlife habitat protection, habitat restoration, and related conservation work for state, local, and nonprofit groups, with priority for Stockdale Mountain and southern Monterey County.

US-119-HR10936.s: The bill would make certain color additives unsafe for use in food, drugs, devices, and cosmetics. It would take effect 2 years after enactment and would apply to color additives that need federal certification, including certified color lakes. The Health and Human Services Secretary would also have to send Congress a report within 3 years on industry changes, new rules, and any further action needed.

US-119-HR10937.s: This bill would change rules for the 340B drug discount program so covered health providers and their contract pharmacies must be treated like other providers and pharmacies by health plans, insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers. It would bar lower pay, extra fees, limits on networks, and other different terms based on 340B status, and it would allow penalties of up to $5,000 per violation per day for pharmacy benefit managers. The bill would also extend these rules to some Medicare plans, set up data checks to help stop duplicate Medicaid rebates, and block federal funds from being used to carry out a 2020 order that limited what covered entities charge patients for 340B drugs.

US-119-HR10938.s: The bill would raise the maximum home health service benefit for certain veterans under Department of Veterans Affairs rules from $6,800 to $15,000. It would affect veterans who use this home health service benefit.

US-119-HR10939.s: The bill would bar people from being paid to lobby for the Nigerian government while Nigeria is listed as a country of particular concern for religious freedom. It would affect paid lobbyists and other paid agents working for Nigeria under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, which covers foreign lobbying. Someone who knowingly breaks the rule could face a civil fine of up to $200,000, and in some cases prison for up to 5 years or a fine.

US-119-HR10940.s: The bill would direct the Federal Communications Commission to set rules for wireless emergency alerts, including measures for speed, reliability, and sending alerts to the right area. It would require providers that send these alerts to collect and report data, and would have the FCC publish yearly updates on whether providers meet the goals and minimum rules. It would also require a study of advanced translation tools for multi-language alerts, a possible pilot test, and clearer warnings before a user opts out of certain alerts.

US-119-HR10941.s: The bill would change how courts review antitrust settlements and voluntary dismissals in cases brought by the Justice Department or the Federal Trade Commission. It would add more public notice and comment time, require more details about settlement terms and related communications, and give state attorneys general a chance to step in. It would also spell out how courts decide if a proposed consent judgment is in the public interest and when it can take effect.

US-119-HR10942.s: The bill would bar bankruptcy debtors from paying bonuses to certain highly paid workers and insiders while a bankruptcy case is going on. It covers people paid over $250,000 a year, as well as insiders, and it treats some sales commissions and union contract payments as not being bonuses. It would also let a trustee undo some bonus payments made within 180 days before a bankruptcy filing.

US-119-HR10943.s: The bill would require the Health and Human Services secretary to provide free in-person legal counsel to certain unaccompanied children in immigration cases through an independent third party. It would affect unaccompanied alien children who are or have been in federal custody. It would also remove language that says the government does not have to pay for counsel in some immigration rules.

US-119-HR10944.s: The bill would let some people leave certain retirement plan money out of taxable income if they use it for a down payment or closing costs on a main home. It would apply to some defined contribution plans, annuity plans, and government deferred pay plans, with limits based on the larger of $40,000 or 40% of the vested account balance. The rule would apply to distributions in tax years after December 31, 2025, and would end for distributions in tax years after December 31, 2035.

US-119-HR10945.s: The bill would let certain food and nutrition help be given as part of some health care programs without being treated as an improper payment under the anti-kickback law, which bans certain payment deals in health care. It would cover things like healthy groceries, meals, nutrition counseling, and rides to get food when used to treat or prevent diet-related health problems. The health secretary would set the rules, and the change would start 18 months after the bill became law.

US-119-HR10946.s: The bill would rename the Office of Technology Assessment as the Congressional Office of Technology and update its duties. It would let the office give faster technical help to lawmakers, do more early scanning for new science and tech issues, and make some findings public. It would also change how the board is chosen, require annual reports, and call for the office to work with other congressional and government research offices to avoid overlap.

US-119-HR10947.s: The bill would require the Environmental Protection Agency to add certain nanoplastics and microplastics to a drinking water list of unregulated contaminants. These are tiny plastic pieces smaller than 1,000 nanometers or 5 millimeters, and they would be added to the sixth version of that list. If that list has already been issued, the agency would have to issue it again with these substances included.

US-119-HR10948.s: The bill would expand federal hiring and advancement rules for veterans to include military spouses. It would apply these rules to larger federal contractors, and raise the contract amount threshold from $100,000 to $5,000,000. It would also require certain contractors, colleges, and research groups to report hiring numbers and related efforts, and to post that information on a public website.

US-119-HR10949.s: The bill would tell the Secretary of Defense to update a grant program for public schools on military bases. It would make sure at least 90 schools on the 2018 priority list can apply for competitive grants to build, fix, or expand school buildings. This would affect public schools on military installations and the Defense Department program that serves them.

US-119-HR10950.s: The bill would require sponsors of large data centers to file public disclosure statements with the Secretary of Energy. The reports would cover details like the site, power use, water use, labor, and costs that may affect electric bills, and they would be posted in a public online database. It would apply to new and some existing facilities and could bring civil penalties for failing to file correct reports.

US-119-HR10951.s: The bill would change the Commodity Exchange Act to ban the trading of contracts tied to wildfires. It would apply to registered trading firms and clearing groups, which would not be allowed to list or process these wildfire-related deals.

US-119-HR10952.s: This bill would create fireshed management areas in high-risk wildfire areas and direct the Agriculture Secretary and other federal agencies to carry out hazardous fuels reduction and forest restoration there. It would also require a public Fireshed Registry with information about wildfire exposure, past fuel work, and planned projects. The bill would add tax incentives for certain biomass facilities near these areas and change a federal grant program for community wood facilities to focus more on forest biomass and fireshed projects.

US-119-HR10954.s: This bill would change federal drug law so abortion drugs must carry a "Do Not Flush" warning label and related warning images and text on the package. It would also require abortion providers to give patients a catch kit and instructions, and to receive human fetal remains and solid medical waste back from patients. The bill would require providers to arrange burial or cremation of human fetal remains and disposal of solid medical waste, and it sets penalties for certain violations.

US-119-HR10955.s: This bill would change the age rules for the earned income tax credit. It would replace the current age limit with a rule that a person must have attained age 18 to qualify. The change would apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2026.

US-119-HR10956.s: This bill would amend the Indian Health Care Improvement Act to let some Indian Health Service scholarship and loan recipients meet their service obligations through half-time clinical practice. It would also set rules for how long they must serve and how loan repayment or damages are calculated if they do not complete the obligation. The bill affects Indian Health Service scholarship and loan recipients who serve in Indian health programs, the Service, certain contracts, or qualifying private practice.

US-119-HR10957.s: This bill would direct the Environmental Protection Agency to study anti-microplastic strategies and report its findings to Congress. It would also require the agency to start a pilot program to demonstrate and evaluate these strategies in at least 3 geographic regions. The program would look at effectiveness, cost, scalability, and whether the strategies can work with existing water treatment or stormwater systems.

US-119-HR10958.s: This bill would require companies that sell or offer clothing for sale to disclose the estimated mass of microplastic in the clothing using a stamp, tag, label, or similar mark. It would direct the Federal Trade Commission, with the Environmental Protection Agency, to write rules for how companies measure that amount. The requirement would apply to companies that sell clothing, and violations would be treated as unfair or deceptive acts or practices.

US-119-HR10959.s: This bill would amend the Affordable Care Act to require health insurance exchanges to offer a special enrollment period when a plan’s provider network changes because a provider or facility is dropped. People enrolled in the affected plan could switch to a different qualified health plan during a 60-day period after the change. It also would require notice to enrollees and says certain services during that period must be covered under the same terms, with limits on added cost-sharing in some cases.

US-119-HR10960.s: This bill would let federal agency heads convert certain time-limited employees who do technology, science, engineering, research, and related work into career or career-conditional civil service jobs, or into certain other federal positions. It would also let agencies offer those employees a choice of student loan repayment or job-related training after conversion. Federal agencies would have to report each year on how many people were converted and what positions were filled.

US-119-HR10967.s: This bill would amend federal law to add Diwali Day as a Federal holiday. It says Diwali, also known as Deepavali, is celebrated by many South and Southeast Asian communities and by members of Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh, and Jain communities. The bill also says millions of Americans, both religious and secular, celebrate Diwali.

US-119-HR1114.s: The bill would let the President name a private nonprofit group to run a Haitian American Enterprise Fund for Haiti. The fund would support business growth and development in Haiti, with help from the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and possible coordination with USAID. It would also set up a 9-member oversight panel to monitor the fund.

US-119-HR1266.s: The bill would add xylazine, a drug used in animals, to a federal list of controlled drugs. It would make making, selling, or giving out xylazine for illegal use subject to criminal penalties, and it would require those drug sales to be tracked by the DEA. It would also exempt some lawful veterinary and animal-control use, and it would require the DEA and FDA to report on illegal xylazine use and trafficking. The House passed the bill on September 15, 2026.
US-119-HR1266.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-02-12)

US-119-HR1276.s: The law removes deed limits from about 3.62 acres at 2956 Park Avenue in Paducah, Kentucky, at the Paducah Memorial Army Reserve Center. It affects that parcel of land and clears the easements, exceptions, reservations, terms, conditions, and covenants tied to the 2012 deed.
US-119-HR1276.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-02-13)

US-119-HR1316.s: The law requires the Commerce Department’s export control office to send Congress a yearly report on export licenses, other approval requests, and site checks for certain dual-use and military items. It covers exports, reexports, releases, and transfers to covered entities in countries under U.S. arms embargoes that are also on certain watch lists. The report must include key details about the application and the decision, but public release is limited to overall totals.

US-119-HR1382.s: The bill would change the San Francisco Bay restoration program in the federal water pollution law. It would let the program use agreements, contracts, and other funding methods with more kinds of public and private groups, and it would cap federal money at 75% of a project’s cost. For projects run by non-federal groups, at least 25% would have to come from non-federal sources, and federal funds could not go to certain groups tied to a foreign country of concern.

US-119-HR1483.s: The bill would limit when the Securities and Exchange Commission can require certain stock market groups and their members to give personal information about investors. It would affect exchanges, securities groups, and members that report data used to track market activity. The rule is meant to cover information used in the Consolidated Audit Trail, which is a data system regulators use to follow trades.
US-119-HR1483.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-02-21)

US-119-HR1491.s: The law changes how the IRS handles tax deadlines after a federally declared disaster or some other events. It makes those delayed deadlines count as extensions when figuring if someone can still get a tax refund, and it also changes when the IRS can send certain tax notices. It applies to people filing federal taxes and to IRS tax notice timing.

US-119-HR1501.s: The bill would make certain mining infrastructure projects eligible for faster environmental review under the FAST Act, a federal law for speeding up some project checks. It would affect some mining project developers and the federal agencies that review them. It would also block the Permitting Council from finalizing a proposed rule that would narrow which mining projects can use this faster review, including by limiting it to critical minerals mining projects.
US-119-HR1501.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-02-21)

US-119-HR1512.s: The law changes how often the State Department must review its guidance on U.S. relations with Taiwan and report to Congress. Instead of one review, it must do this every two years while the guidance is in effect. The reports must explain how the guidance handles key Taiwan issues and point out ways to remove U.S.-set limits on ties with Taiwan.
US-119-HR1512.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-02-21)

US-119-HR1640.s: The bill would require the Department of Housing and Urban Development to give grants to help people with the legal steps of inheriting certain real estate. It would send money to states with certain property laws, and to counseling agencies, legal aid clinics at colleges, and qualified nonprofits. The grants could pay for title records, estate work, heir searches, filing fees, notary fees, and legal help for people who inherit property together.
US-119-HR1640.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-02-26)

US-119-HR165.s: The law directs the Interior Department to finish placing about 40 acres in Oglala Lakota County, South Dakota, into a special land status for the Oglala Sioux Tribe and the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe. The land must be kept as a memorial and sacred site under a 2022 agreement. It also bars commercial development and gaming on the land.

US-119-HR1653.s: The bill would change how the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau can use civil investigative demands, which are requests for information before a formal case begins. It would require those demands to be issued and served within six years of the alleged violation and to point to specific facts about it. It would also let a lawyer ask questions for someone called to testify, allow court review if a demand is kept in place, and add more reasons to challenge a demand, such as if it is too broad, too costly, or can be gotten another way.
US-119-HR1653.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-02-27)

US-119-HR1703.s: This bill would change Medicare Part B payment rules for certain ultralightweight manual wheelchairs. It would require separate HCPCS codes for wheelchairs with titanium or carbon fiber bases and for those without those materials. For wheelchairs with titanium or carbon fiber in the base, Medicare payment to the supplier would be made as otherwise allowed, and the supplier could charge the person the difference between that payment and the supplier’s actual charge. The Secretary could also require a notice telling the person about possible financial liability before purchase or rental.

US-119-HR1721.s: The law directs the Commerce Department to study products that are in high demand in critical infrastructure sectors. It must identify products that are being imported because of manufacturing, material, or supply chain limits, and examine the costs, benefits, and feasibility of making them in the United States. Critical infrastructure means the systems and assets vital to national security, the economy, public health, or safety.
US-119-HR1721.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-02-27)

US-119-HR1744.s: This law would extend the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom through 2028. The commission is an independent federal group that watches religious freedom conditions around the world and gives policy advice to the U.S. government.

US-119-HR1815.s: This law changes the VA home loan program so the Department of Veterans Affairs can help avoid foreclosure on some VA-backed home loans. It creates a five-year partial claim program, which lets the VA cover part of a loan balance for some primary homes that are in default or at risk of default. It also requires the VA to report to Congress on access to real estate agents or brokers for veteran home buyers and temporarily raises funding for housing and support services for homeless veterans in fiscal years 2025 and 2026.

US-119-HR1823.s: The law requires the Government Accountability Office to review and report on why the Veterans Benefits Administration had a funding shortfall for fiscal year 2024 and why the Veterans Health Administration is expected to have one in fiscal year 2025. The Department of Veterans Affairs must send that report to Congress. GAO must also do more reviews and reports on VA funding for each of the next five fiscal years after enactment.

US-119-HR1829.s: The bill would require the Forest Service to give certain land in the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest to Apache County and Navajo County, Arizona. The counties would have to use the land as cemeteries. The counties would also have to pay all related costs, including survey and environmental review costs.
US-119-HR1829.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-03-04)

US-119-HR1869.s: The bill would require the Justice Department to set up a task force, program, or similar group in its Criminal Division. That group would investigate and prosecute trade-related crimes. It would affect the Justice Department and people or companies involved in those crimes.
US-119-HR1869.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-03-05)

US-119-HR187.s: The law requires the Forest Service and the Interior Department to set common rules for collecting and sharing data on public access to federal waterways and fishing limits. Within five years, they must put certain waterway access, restriction, and fishing data online, and update some of it on a set schedule or in real time. It also lets the public send questions or comments about some of that data and requires yearly progress reports to Congress.

US-119-HR1912.s: The law changes how the Department of Veterans Affairs reissues benefits that were misused by a fiduciary, or person who manages benefits for someone else. It requires the VA to set rules for when and how it decides whether the misuse happened because of VA negligence, but the VA cannot delay reissuing the payment while that decision is pending. If the beneficiary dies before the payment is reissued, the VA must pay the amount to a surviving beneficiary in the same way it pays certain other VA benefits after death.

US-119-HR1968.s: The law provides full-year funding for most federal agencies for fiscal year 2025 at mostly FY2024 levels. It also extends many expiring programs and rules, including health programs, Medicare payments, and telehealth flexibilities. These changes affect federal agencies, health care providers, hospitals, states, tribes, and Medicare patients.

US-119-HR2004.s: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Department to study how often Medicare hospitals test for fentanyl in overdose cases, how much those tests cost, and how they affect patients. After the study, the department would issue guidance on whether emergency rooms should use fentanyl testing as a routine part of overdose care and how doctors can know which drugs they are testing for. It would also look at how fentanyl testing may affect future overdose risk and other health results.
US-119-HR2004.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-03-10)

US-119-HR204.s: The bill would require the Agriculture and Interior departments to report each year on how many acres of federal land were treated to reduce wildfire risk. It would also require them to use the same ways to track and check the data for these fuel-reduction activities, including how well they work over time and how to count acres inside and outside the wildland-urban interface, the area where homes meet wildland. The Government Accountability Office would study how the bill is carried out and report the results to Congress.
US-119-HR204.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-01-03)

US-119-HR2066.s: This law changes how much financing Small Business Investment Companies, or SBICs, can get from the Small Business Administration. It lowers the main cap from 300% to 200% of an SBIC’s private capital, but raises the cap for some commonly controlled SBICs from $350 million to $475 million. It also changes which investments and funds count in the limit, including some money tied to rural areas, certain technology, small manufacturers, some government-sponsored corporations, and college or university trusts or endowments.

US-119-HR2069.s: The law expands federal spending reports on USAspending.gov to include other transaction agreements, which are special contracts not covered by many normal procurement rules. The Treasury Department must make sure this data is sent to the site automatically and post a yearly report on spending data that has not been posted and why. For 10 years after enactment, certain agency watchdogs must report to Congress and the public on spending data and data standards.
US-119-HR2069.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-03-11)

US-119-HR2140.s: The bill would extend a federal program through fiscal year 2029 that helps cut diesel pollution. Under the program, the Environmental Protection Agency would give grants, rebates, or loans to replace diesel engines or add pollution control equipment. It would affect diesel engine owners and others who take part in the program.
US-119-HR2140.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-03-14)

US-119-HR2170.s: The law names the Department of Veterans Affairs community clinic in Toms River, New Jersey, the Leonard G. “Bud” Lomell VA Clinic. It affects that VA clinic and the people who use it.

US-119-HR2196.s: The law extends the group’s authority to build a memorial in Washington, DC, to honor emergency medical services. That permission ends seven years after the law takes effect. It affects the National Emergency Medical Services Memorial Foundation and the work of building the monument.
US-119-HR2196.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-02-24)

US-119-HR224.s: This law says military disability payments will not count as income when deciding if a veteran can get help from the Community Development Block Grant program. It also requires the Government Accountability Office to report on how the Department of Housing and Urban Development treats these payments in its other programs. The law became Public Law 119-70 on January 20, 2026.

US-119-HR227.s: The law gives clergy members who had opted out of Social Security and Medicare taxes a two-year chance to opt back in. They must file with the IRS by the due date for their federal tax return for the second year after Dec. 31, 2028, and the change can take effect in 2029 or 2030. The IRS must also make a plan to tell affected clergy about this option.

US-119-HR2306.s: The bill would extend the Adams Memorial Commission through 2032 so it can keep working on a permanent memorial in Washington, DC, for John Adams and his legacy. It would place the memorial in the area named by the commission on a February 25, 2025 map, south of the White House near Ellipse Road and Pennsylvania Avenue and 15th Street, Northwest. If that spot is not workable because of space or security issues, the memorial would go in the Reserve, the area from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial and from the White House to the Jefferson Memorial.
US-119-HR2306.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2025-10-31)

US-119-HR2316.s: Became law on Nov. 25, 2025. It extends through fiscal year 2033 a rule that sends interest from certain wildlife funds to state wildlife conservation and restoration programs. It also keeps that money tied to programs funded by taxes on some firearms, ammunition, and archery gear.

US-119-HR2317.s: Passed the House, this bill would change the use and ownership of some federal land in Nevada. It would move certain lands to the state, counties, cities, and a few local agencies for economic development, recreation, or other public uses, and it would set aside some land as wilderness. It would also let Nevada use the Jean Prison site for other purposes, allow a federal office complex on certain federal lands, and take land into trust for the Washoe Tribe of Nevada and California.
US-119-HR2317.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-03-25)

US-119-HR2347.s: This bill would change tax law so that damages received because of a sexual act or sexual contact would be excluded from gross income, except for punitive damages. It would also treat a statement in a decision or agreement as credible evidence that the damages are for a sexual act or sexual contact. The bill would direct the Secretary of the Treasury to run a program to promote public awareness of this tax exclusion.

US-119-HR2388.s: The law takes about 1,082.63 acres of named land in Washington into trust for the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe. Land taken into trust becomes part of the tribe’s reservation. It also bars gaming on that land.
US-119-HR2388.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-03-26)

US-119-HR2478.s: The bill would let certain investment companies and transfer agents delay cashing out some securities if they think an older adult or a person with certain mental or physical limits is being financially exploited. The delay could last up to 15 days at first, with up to 10 more days after a finding of exploitation, and the money would be held in a demand deposit account. It would also require notices and ask the SEC to make recommendations on financial exploitation of these adults.
US-119-HR2478.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-03-27)

US-119-HR2481.s: The law requires online dating apps and websites to warn users if they got a message from a banned user. The warning must include the banned user’s profile name, the time of the last message, a note that the person may have used a fake identity or tried to scam people, and tips and contact help for avoiding fraud. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general can enforce the rule.

US-119-HR2483.s: Became law on December 1, 2025. It reauthorizes and updates federal programs that deal with substance use disorders, overdoses, and mental health, mainly through the CDC and SAMHSA. It affects people and groups tied to prevention, treatment, crisis response, pregnant and postpartum women, youth, and state and local health programs.

US-119-HR2555.s: The bill would give college students the right to form or join social groups, including single-sex groups. It would stop colleges that take federal student aid from punishing those groups or their members just because the group limits membership to one sex. It would also bar colleges from forcing students to give up these protections or from placing special recruitment limits on such groups unless the school and group agree in writing.
US-119-HR2555.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-04-01)

US-119-HR2616.s: Public elementary and middle schools would have to get a parent’s okay before changing a student’s gender marker, pronouns, or preferred name on school forms. They would also need parent consent before changing sex-based school accommodations, such as bathroom or locker room access. The rule would apply when these schools receive certain federal education funds.
US-119-HR2616.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-04-03)

US-119-HR2805.s: The bill would require the National Telecommunications and Information Administration to make a national plan to better coordinate federal broadband programs and help reach the goal of high-speed, affordable internet for everyone in the U.S. It would also require a public draft plan, a report to Congress, and regular updates on progress. The Government Accountability Office would review the plan and give Congress its own report with ways to improve it.
US-119-HR2805.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-04-09)

US-119-HR2808.s: This law limits when credit reporting agencies can give a person's credit report to other companies during a home mortgage deal. It mainly affects credit bureaus, mortgage lenders, loan servicers, and some banks, and it allows these reports only in set cases with the person's consent or a direct loan link. The main rules take effect 180 days after enactment, and the Government Accountability Office must study text message trigger leads.

US-119-HR2815.s: The law changes how Cape Fox Corporation can finish getting land it is owed under federal rules. It lets Cape Fox choose about 180 acres in Alaska's Tongass National Forest if it gives written notice within 90 days, and it requires the federal government to transfer the land. The law also gives the surface land to Cape Fox, the land below it to Sealaska Corporation, and keeps a public access path on the land.

US-119-HR3100.s: This bill would amend the National Child Protection Act of 1993 to expand who can be covered by background checks. It would let businesses and organizations that work with vulnerable populations request background checks for their contractors and for people who work for or volunteer with an entity under contract with them. It would also cover people who are licensed or certified, or who seek to be licensed or certified, by a qualified entity.

US-119-HR3164.s: The bill would make Medicare cover certain pharmacist services on a permanent basis. It would cover testing and treatment for COVID-19, flu, RSV, strep throat, and other public health needs during a declared public health emergency, as long as the services follow state law on what pharmacists can do.
US-119-HR3164.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-05-01)

US-119-HR3194.s: The bill would change the Clean Air Act so states could not set their own rules for emissions from existing locomotives and the engines used in them. It would affect state governments and rail locomotives that are used in commerce, including common carrier railroad service for pay. The bill was introduced in the House and later sent to committee review.

US-119-HR3331.s: The bill would change how the Coast Guard reviews and updates the Merchant Mariner Credentialing Examination, which is the test for merchant mariner credentials. It would expand the review working group, require remote participation when needed, and bar new test questions from use until the group approves them. It would also require a plan to update the exam and a briefing to Congress after enactment.

US-119-HR3342.s: This bill would let the Director of the Bureau of Prisons hire qualified candidates for competitive service jobs at Bureau of Prisons facilities without following some civil service rules. The authority would end when 96 percent of those positions at all such facilities are filled.

US-119-HR3490.s: This law requires the Government Accountability Office to report to Congress on esophageal cancer care costs in the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, which covers federal workers and retirees. It also looks at how often people in that program who are at high risk for esophageal cancer get screenings that follow set guidelines. It became Public Law 119-96.
US-119-HR3490.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-05-19)

US-119-HR3495.s: The bill would keep real estate agents and direct sellers of consumer products out of the Fair Labor Standards Act employee definition. That means those workers would not be covered by that law’s minimum wage and overtime rules. It would affect real estate agents and people who sell consumer products directly to buyers.
US-119-HR3495.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-02-11)

US-119-HR3497.s: The law directs the President to create a medal of sacrifice for eligible law enforcement officers and first responders who are killed in the line of duty. It also creates a commission to help decide the medal’s design and how it will be given out. The medal can cover federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial workers, and the commission must review cases where there is an official finding of wrongdoing before deciding if someone is eligible.

US-119-HR3514.s: The bill would set new rules for prior approval requests in Medicare Advantage plans, which are private plans that cover Medicare benefits. It would require these plans to use an electronic system, send yearly data to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services on approvals and response times, and meet other quality and speed standards set by the agency. The agency and another health tech office would also post a report on these requests, real-time decisions, and how artificial intelligence decisions affect patient access.
US-119-HR3514.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-05-20)

US-119-HR3620.s: The law directs the Department of Health and Human Services to give about 3.4 acres in Anchorage, Alaska, to the Southcentral Foundation for health and social service programs. The land must be transferred by deed with no payment and no added terms, and the United States keeps only any access needed to meet its own remaining duties. It also limits who can be held responsible for certain pollution on the property before and after the transfer.
US-119-HR3620.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2025-12-09)

US-119-HR3657.s: The law tells the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to send Congress a yearly report on the status of each request to renew a hydropower dam license. It affects the federal agency that handles these licenses and Congress. It became Public Law 119-112 on September 25, 2026.
US-119-HR3657.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-05-29)

US-119-HR3857.s: This bill would amend the Snow Water Supply Forecasting Program Authorization Act and continue work on snow monitoring and water supply forecasting. It would direct the program to use technologies for snowpack measurement and modeling, and it would focus on river basins where the data can inform water management decisions, including interstate decisions. It would also change the program’s reporting requirements and set funding at $3,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2031.

US-119-HR3872.s: The bill would let all federally acquired lands be considered for leases to mine hardrock minerals. It defines hardrock minerals to include things like base metals, precious metals, industrial minerals, and some gemstones. It would not cover coal, oil, gas, sulfur, or some other minerals named in the bill.
US-119-HR3872.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2025-10-31)

US-119-HR3937.s: The bill would require the Forest Service to sell about 14 acres of federal land in Wisconsin’s Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest, along with the mineral rights, to Tony’s Wabeno Redi-Mix, LLC, if the company makes an offer at market value. The company would have to pay the land’s market value and related costs, and the offer would have to come within 180 days after the land appraisal is approved. It would also require the Interior Department to publish a review of federal permit rules for stone, sand, and gravel development on federal land.
US-119-HR3937.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-06-11)

US-119-HR3978.s: The bill would tell the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to use a different licensing process for future domestic fuel recycling plants that reprocess spent nuclear fuel without isolating plutonium. These plants could turn used nuclear fuel into material that may be used again to make electricity. The new process would be under rules for special nuclear material, which has fewer steps than the process for production and use facilities.
US-119-HR3978.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-06-12)

US-119-HR4.s: The law cancels some unused federal money that had been set aside for the State Department, USAID, several other agencies, and public broadcasting. It affects funding for foreign aid, global health, peacekeeping, and some program support. It became Public Law 119-28 on July 24, 2025.

US-119-HR4093.s: The bill would require more public reports about Medicare enrollment and spending. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services would have to post yearly data on hospital care, doctor care, prescription drugs, and Medicare Advantage, broken down by county and metro area and by month. Medicare advisers and the Medicare trustees would also have to give yearly reports comparing costs for people with and without Medicare Advantage and for people with different parts of Medicare coverage.
US-119-HR4093.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-06-24)

US-119-HR410.s: This law gives Alaska Native Vietnam-era veterans five more years to apply for a federal land allotment in Alaska. It applies to eligible Alaska Native veterans who served in Vietnam during the covered years, or their heirs. The application deadline moves from December 29, 2025, to December 29, 2030.

US-119-HR42.s: The law changes how some settlement trust payments are counted for Alaska Natives and their descendants who are aged, blind, or disabled. Those payments would not count when checking if someone can get certain need-based federal programs, like food aid. It became Public Law 119-22 on July 7, 2025.

US-119-HR4219.s: The bill would give legal backing to a Fish and Wildlife Service program that runs invasive species strike teams in each region of the National Wildlife Refuge System. These teams would work with public and private groups to deal with invasive species and related conservation issues near refuges. The Fish and Wildlife Service would also have to report to Congress on the program’s work and progress.
US-119-HR4219.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-08-27)

US-119-HR43.s: This law changes rules for Alaska Native village lands. It ends the rule that village corporations must give certain lands to Alaska to hold for future town governments. It also lets village corporations take back title to those lands if the village corporation and the village residents approve dissolving the trust in a formal vote.

US-119-HR4307.s: The law requires the Labor Department to train some of its workers on how to help police detect human trafficking. The training must fit each worker’s job and local setting, and cover current trends, ways to spot suspected victims, and how to refer cases to the Justice Department and other officials. It became Public Law 119-131.

US-119-HR4323.s: This law creates a way for some human trafficking survivors to ask a court to erase certain arrest records and set aside some convictions tied to their trafficking. It also requires new reports from U.S. Attorneys and the Justice Department, and it lets some legal aid grants be used to help with this kind of case. It became law on January 23, 2026.

US-119-HR4348.s: The bill would extend through fiscal year 2030 federal work to track and fight diseases spread by ticks and mosquitoes. It would keep a national plan, grants for regional expert centers, and agreements with state, local, and tribal health departments. These efforts are aimed at helping public health agencies prevent and respond to these diseases.
US-119-HR4348.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-07-02)

US-119-HR4398.s: The bill would require a VA doctor or nurse practitioner who is the main care provider for a veteran who dies of natural causes to certify the death within 48 hours of learning about it. If that cannot be done, a coroner or medical examiner in that area could certify the death instead. It would also require the VA to send Congress a yearly report on how often this deadline is met and why it is not met in some cases.

US-119-HR4405.s: The law requires the Justice Department to publish, in a searchable and downloadable format, unclassified records and other materials it has on the Jeffrey Epstein case. It covers materials tied to Ghislaine Maxwell, flight logs, travel records, and people named in the case, including government officials. The department may keep back victim personal details and items that could hurt an active federal case, and it must report to Congress within 15 days after publishing the records.

US-119-HR4446.s: This law changes when the Department of Veterans Affairs must update a veteran’s job training plan under the Veteran Readiness and Employment program. If the VA decides the original long-term goals are no longer possible because the veteran’s work limits have changed, it must work with the veteran on a new plan. It affects veterans with service-connected disabilities who get job training and employment help from the VA.

US-119-HR4464.s: The bill would require the Congressional Budget Office, when Congress asks, to check whether a proposed law would cut spending beyond the 10-year budget period by using preventive health care. Preventive health care means steps that help protect health, prevent disease, and avoid early death. If CBO finds savings, its cost estimate would have to explain the savings and how it reached that view, and that estimate would be extra information only, not used for budget rules.
US-119-HR4464.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-07-16)

US-119-HR4467.s: The law requires the Interior Department to give about 7 acres of land in two parcels from Vicksburg National Military Park to Mississippi for an interpretive center. The land must help people get to the park and cannot be used in a way that harms park resources or the visitor experience. The transfer must be by quitclaim deed, with no payment, and the park boundary must be changed to leave out the land.
US-119-HR4467.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-01-14)

US-119-HR452.s: The law gives Congressional Gold Medals to the members of the 1980 U.S. Olympic men's ice hockey team. It honors the team's achievement at the 1980 Winter Olympic Games. The bill became Public Law 119-53 on December 12, 2025.

US-119-HR4586.s: Would set up a U.S. plan to support African and Caribbean diaspora investment and development. It would seek to cut remittance costs, create tax breaks for some remittances and diaspora investments, and give federal agencies new tools to back investment funds, bonds, and remittance providers. It would also ask for yearly reports on remittance costs and diaspora investment.

US-119-HR4598.s: The bill would allow unpaid interest to be deposited into three water settlement funds: the Navajo Nation Water Resources Development Trust Fund, the Taos Pueblo Water Development Fund, and the Aamodt Settlement Pueblos’ Fund. These funds are tied to water rights settlement deals for Native communities in New Mexico. It would make technical fixes to those older laws.
US-119-HR4598.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-07-22)

US-119-HR4615.s: The bill would change the Small Business Act to let small business construction contractors get an interim partial payment when a government contract change raises their costs and they ask for an equitable adjustment. The payment would be at least 50% of the estimated added cost, and the contractor would have to pass along the related share to lower-level subcontractors. The Small Business Administration would have to write rules within 90 days after the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR4646.s: The bill would expand whistleblower protections for people who work for HUD contractors or grant recipients. It would cover HUD contracts and grants no matter when they were signed. The House passed the bill and sent it to the Senate.
US-119-HR4646.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-09-01)

US-119-HR4795.s: Colleges and universities that take part in federal student aid programs would be barred from joining boycotts against Israel. Schools that get or apply for Title VI foreign-language and international education funds would also have to certify each year that students and faculty can take part in academic programs in Israel on the same terms as in other countries, and that people from schools in Israel can join their programs on the same terms.
US-119-HR4795.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-08-27)

US-119-HR4931.s: The bill would let the National Park Service extend some long-term leases for federal property in national parks without opening them to competitive bidding. The lessee would need to have had the lease for at least five years, be following its terms, and the agency would have to find the extension is best for the park unit. It passed the House and was sent to the Senate.
US-119-HR4931.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-08-08)

US-119-HR5063.s: The bill would require enough lifeguards at certain swimming areas and beaches run by federal land agencies, like the National Park Service and others. If there is a staffing shortage, the Interior Department could make an agreement with a local government to provide lifeguards and must pay back all reasonable costs. It would not apply to short, temporary absences like sick or annual leave.
US-119-HR5063.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-08-27)

US-119-HR5109.s: The bill would direct the Transportation Security Administration to make guidance for helping people in prison get ready to apply for a TWIC card before release. It would cover people in federal, state, and local prisons and help them pre-apply or prepare an application. It would also help them ask for an appeal or waiver if they are first found not eligible for the card.
US-119-HR5109.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-09-03)

US-119-HR517.s: The law lets the IRS delay federal tax deadlines for people hit by certain state-declared disasters if the governor or D.C. mayor asks for it. It also raises the automatic deadline extension for certain relief workers, people killed or hurt in a federally declared disaster, and people whose home, business, or tax records are in the disaster area to 120 days from 60 days. It applies to taxes and other related filing and payment deadlines.

US-119-HR5254.s: This bill would let the Secretary of the Interior make a one-time agreement with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation to host private events in Gateway Arch National Park buildings for up to five years. The agreement would have to set terms to protect the park, limit when and where events can happen, require insurance, and allow the government to recover costs from the events. It would also require a report on how the agreement is working and would end the authority after seven years.

US-119-HR5267.s: The bill would change labor law rules for franchise businesses by saying a franchisor can be treated as a joint employer of a franchisee’s workers only if it has substantial direct and immediate control over key job terms, like pay, hours, hiring, firing, discipline, supervision, and direction. It also applies the same rule under the Fair Labor Standards Act, which is the federal wage law. The change would affect franchisors and franchisees, and it would not apply to proceedings started before enactment.

US-119-HR5334.s: The law adds sanctions, trade limits, and other penalties tied to Russia and extends an Iran sanctions law through 2031. It also bars some U.S. exports and investment in Russia, and can raise import duties on goods from some countries that keep buying Russian oil or gas. The law also lets early childhood educators claim the teacher expense tax deduction if they provide care or education to children under age 6.

US-119-HR5345.s: The law requires the Social Security Administration to give people one main contact when their Social Security number is misused or their card is lost in transit. That contact must track the case to the end and work with other offices to fix the problem as quickly as possible. It also requires specially trained staff and steps to keep records moving and tell affected people when needed.

US-119-HR5349.s: The bill would give the U.S. Tax Court more power to issue subpoenas for papers and other items from a party or witness, even outside a set hearing. It would also let the court extend some deadlines for filing a petition over an IRS deficiency notice if fairness calls for it. In addition, it would change some court procedures, including the use of special trial judges and rules on when judges must step aside.
US-119-HR5349.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-09-15)

US-119-HR5366.s: The law extends a federal tax break for certain disaster losses in areas hit by major disasters with incident periods starting on or after December 28, 2019, and before January 1, 2027. It also extends a rule that lets people leave certain wildfire relief payments out of taxable income for fires declared federal disasters after 2014 and before 2027, no matter when the payments are received. It became Public Law 119-108 on September 11, 2026.

US-119-HR5371.s: Became law on November 12, 2025. It provides short-term funding for most federal agencies through January 30, 2026, and full-year funding for agriculture, military construction and veterans affairs, and the legislative branch for fiscal year 2026. It also extends some expiring programs and rules, and it helps cover back pay for federal workers affected by the shutdown.

US-119-HR5402.s: The bill would let rent, utility, and phone payment history be sent to consumer reporting agencies, including on-time payments. It would also stop energy utilities from reporting a bill as late if the customer is on a payment plan and is meeting it. The Government Accountability Office would have to study how this reporting affects consumers and credit data.
US-119-HR5402.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-09-16)

US-119-HR5439.s: The bill would create a temporary Medicare program for some people with diet-related illnesses, such as kidney disease, so they can get medically tailored meals delivered to their homes. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services would choose at least 40 hospitals to run the six-year pilot program. People would have to meet certain health and care needs, and hospitals would need to check patients when they leave the hospital and every 12 weeks after that.
US-119-HR5439.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-09-17)

US-119-HR5549.s: The bill would speed up review of some uncontested permits and licenses for nuclear power plants by removing the need for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to hold a public hearing at the end if no affected person asks for one. If a hearing is held, the commission would use a simpler hearing process. It would also require a hearing on a uranium enrichment facility only if an affected person requests one.
US-119-HR5549.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-09-23)

US-119-HR5576.s: The bill would exempt certain geothermal projects on federal land from environmental review under NEPA, the main federal law for checking environmental effects. It would cover some low-impact geothermal exploration work, like drilling test wells. It would also exempt some related work such as geotechnical studies, off-road travel in certain existing rights-of-way, and building or fixing access roads in those rights-of-way.
US-119-HR5576.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-08-27)

US-119-HR5634.s: The bill would put a lifetime cap on the amount of Post-9/11 education aid that veterans can use for flight training and some other education programs at public colleges. For people who first use this benefit in the school year starting August 1, 2026, the cap would be $119,684, and it would change in later years with inflation. The limit would apply to school years starting on or after August 1, 2026.

US-119-HR5723.s: This bill would require the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to take steps to identify fraudulent activity in disability benefit questionnaire forms submitted to the department, no matter where the forms came from. It would also require claims processors to report suspected fraud to the Office of Inspector General, direct routine audits of these forms, and inform claimants when information is not enough to assign a rating or make a decision. The bill also gives the Inspector General special authority for certain undercover investigations and requires reports to Congress about those investigations.

US-119-HR5745.s: The bill would let certain inactive offshore oil and gas platforms and pipelines be turned into artificial reefs to help fish habitat. It sets a process for checking if a structure can be kept in place, reviewed by federal officials, and then approved if it meets safety and reef rules. It would affect offshore operators, the Interior Department, NOAA, and state reef programs.

US-119-HR5929.s: The bill would let certain Defense Department actions to secure strategic and critical materials for energy infrastructure, including critical minerals, get faster environmental review. It would add those actions to the list of covered projects under the FAST Act, which is a law that speeds up some project reviews.
US-119-HR5929.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-06-09)

US-119-HR5967.s: The bill would have the Federal Trade Commission and the Justice Department set up a federal task force to fight scams. The group would include several other agencies and would make a national plan, use public education, work with industry, and use existing law enforcement tools. It would report to Congress and the public within 1 year after enactment, and the task force would end 10 years after enactment.

US-119-HR6021.s: The bill would let Alaska Native handicrafts, clothing, and art include nonedible parts of migratory birds if the birds were not taken in a wasteful or illegal way. It would also direct the State Department and the Interior Department to work with other treaty countries to clarify how these items are treated, and it would require Interior to update its rules. The House passed the bill and sent it to the Senate.
US-119-HR6021.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-11-12)

US-119-HR6130.s: The bill would make Medicare cover certain blood tests used to screen for early Alzheimer’s disease or related dementias. It would cover genomic sequencing blood tests, blood product tests, or similar tests that the Food and Drug Administration has approved. The change would affect people with Medicare who may need these screenings.
US-119-HR6130.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-11-19)

US-119-HR6152.s: The bill would change and expand FCC efforts against illegal robocalls and create a task force to advise the federal government on robocalls from outside the United States. It would let the FCC require some phone companies to post a bond before filing certain robocall compliance papers, and it would set exemptions for some legitimate providers. It would also change how the FCC traceback group can share information and publish lists tied to suspected illegal robocalls.
US-119-HR6152.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-11-19)

US-119-HR618.s: This law directs the Interior Department to grant certain land-use rights for the Apex Project industrial park in Nevada to Clark County, the city of North Las Vegas, and the Apex Industrial Park Owners Association. It covers rights for roads, utilities, and other needed access to help expand the park's infrastructure. The law also keeps federal limits on the land in place and eases rules for some sales of mineral materials from surface work on the site.

US-119-HR6207.s: The bill would bar some companies that get certain federal funds from buying specified chip-making equipment from foreign-owned or foreign-controlled companies for the funded project. It would affect companies receiving CHIPS money and would require the Commerce Department to put this rule into those funding deals for 10 years. Commerce could waive the rule in some cases, such as when the needed equipment is not available in the United States or in allied or partner countries in enough quantity or with acceptable quality.
US-119-HR6207.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-11-20)

US-119-HR6213.s: The bill would block OSHA from making, using, or enforcing a new workplace heat safety rule. It would stop OSHA from finalizing a proposed rule that would require some employers to make plans to find and control heat risks for workers in outdoor and indoor jobs. The affected workers are those in general industry, construction, maritime, and agriculture jobs covered by OSHA.
US-119-HR6213.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-11-20)

US-119-HR625.s: The bill would add College Station as a place where federal court must be held in the Galveston Division of the Southern District of Texas. It would also add El Centro as a court site in the Southern District of California.
US-119-HR625.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-01-22)

US-119-HR6365.s: This bill would require the Secretary of the Interior to issue a right-of-way for an emergency exit on certain National Park Service land in Virginia. It says the right-of-way must be the one shown on the Blue Ridge Parkway map if the Secretary reports on other route options, fire ecology behavior, and required reviews.

US-119-HR6380.s: The law redesignates Chiricahua National Monument in Arizona as Chiricahua National Park. It tells the National Park Service to protect traditional cultural and religious sites and to give Indian tribes access to those sites for customary uses. If a tribe asks, the park can temporarily close small areas for the least time needed for those uses.
US-119-HR6380.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-12-03)
