US-119-HR6470.s: The bill would require the Congressional Budget Office to send Congress at least two updates each year to its budget forecast, unless the House and Senate budget committee chairs direct otherwise. One of those updates would have to include the economic data used to make the forecast. It would also ask the President to send technical budget data to Congress by February 1 each year, if that is practical.
US-119-HR6470.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-12-04)

US-119-HR6500.s: Became Public Law 119-103. It provides short-term funding for federal agencies through December 11, 2026, and helps avoid a government shutdown. It also extends or changes a range of programs and rules, including food aid, farm standards, cyber programs, trade preferences, and some Medicaid and Medicare funds.

US-119-HR6610.s: This bill would set rules for Federal employee health plans on how pharmacy benefit managers handle prescription drug payments and rebates. It would require these managers to pay in-network pharmacies based on drug cost rules, pass rebate savings to patients at the point of sale, and stop steering people to certain pharmacies or adding hidden fees. If the Office of Personnel Management finds violations, it could fine the manager and, after repeated violations, bar it from handling drug benefits for these plans.

US-119-HR6633.s: The bill would require public electric utilities to use the best available transmission conductor on certain interstate power lines when they seek to recover those costs through electric bills. It would tell the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to treat that choice as a proper one, and to treat a less capable conductor as not proper, when deciding if the costs can be charged to customers. The rules would apply to new transmission lines and to lines that are being changed, upgraded, or replaced.
US-119-HR6633.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-12-11)

US-119-HR6644.s: The law changes many federal housing programs. It directs HUD to review housing counseling groups, support local rules for certain small apartment buildings, and make some rural housing projects and some housing aid easier to process under environmental rules. It also creates or expands programs for home repairs, low-cost mortgages, housing plans, mixed-income housing designs, and turning empty buildings into homes. The law makes the Rental Assistance Demonstration program permanent and became Public Law 119-101.

US-119-HR677.s: The bill would let a person appealing a Department of the Interior decision to the Interior Board of Land Appeals ask for faster review in writing. If the board gets that request, it would have to make a final decision within six months, but not sooner than 18 months after the appeal was first filed. If it misses that deadline, the Interior decision would count as final and could be reviewed by a court from scratch.
US-119-HR677.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-01-23)

US-119-HR6832.s: The bill would set rules for claims that consumer product packaging is recyclable, compostable, or reusable. It would bar false claims, require clear labels in some cases, and require third-party certification for those claims. It would direct the Federal Trade Commission to issue guidance and enforce the rules, and it would affect companies that make these packaging claims.

US-119-HR6938.s: The law provides money for several federal agencies and programs in 2026, including commerce, law enforcement, science, energy, water projects, public lands, and environmental work. It covers agencies such as the Commerce and Justice departments, NASA, the National Science Foundation, the Army Corps of Engineers, Energy, Interior, the Environmental Protection Agency, the Forest Service, and the Indian Health Service. It also sets rules and limits for how the funded money can be used.
US-119-HR6938.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-01-06)

US-119-HR695.s: The law raises the monthly special pension for living Medal of Honor recipients. It also blocks the Veterans Affairs Department from adding an inflation increase in a year when the pension was already raised. The law extends a $90-a-month cap on some veterans in Medicaid nursing homes who have no spouse or child through January 31, 2033.

US-119-HR7022.s: The law lets wireless emergency alerts be sent to mobile phones by satellite as well as through regular cell networks. Phone companies that take part in the alert system must tell the Federal Communications Commission whether they will send satellite alerts, and the FCC must set the rules for how those alerts work. Companies that do not send satellite alerts must tell new and current customers, and users may opt out of satellite alerts.
US-119-HR7022.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-01-12)

US-119-HR7030.s: The bill would change the hospital mortgage insurance program in the National Housing Act so licensed hospitals have equal access to it. It would take effect 9 months after the bill becomes law. The Housing and Urban Development secretary would also have to send Congress a report within 2 years on how the expanded program is working.

US-119-HR7147.s: The bill became law and gives 2026 funding for most Department of Homeland Security offices and programs, but not ICE or the Border Patrol. It also covers pay and approved costs tied to the partial DHS shutdown that began on February 14, 2026. The law sets limits and reporting rules for some DHS spending, overtime, fees, and certain intelligence and border-related actions.

US-119-HR7148.s: Becoming law, this measure funds several federal departments and agencies for the rest of fiscal year 2026. It also keeps Homeland Security funded through February 13, 2026, at fiscal year 2025 levels unless a Homeland Security spending law is enacted sooner. The law also extends a number of programs and powers that were set to expire, including flood insurance, farm and trade programs, and some health care and immigration programs.
US-119-HR7148.src: Congressional Research Service summary (House agreed to Senate amendment, 2026-02-03)

US-119-HR7187.s: The bill would let some people who work for registered brokers be paid through their own personal business without having to register as a broker with the SEC. It applies to certain personal services entities that are tied to the worker, if the broker approves the payments, keeps records, and supervises the worker. These entities would also have to keep records and share them with the SEC or the self-regulatory group when asked.
US-119-HR7187.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-01-21)

US-119-HR7211.s: The law lets the President give John W. Ripley the Medal of Honor for brave actions on April 2, 1972, during the Vietnam War. Ripley served in the Marine Corps and had already received the Navy Cross for the same actions. It became Public Law 119-81 on March 26, 2026.

US-119-HR7250.s: The law renews funding authority through fiscal year 2028 for planning, design, and construction of two rural water systems in Montana: the Assiniboine and Sioux Rural Water System and the Dry Prairie Rural Water System. It affects the water projects tied to the Fort Peck Reservation area. It was signed into law on September 25, 2026.
US-119-HR7250.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-01-27)

US-119-HR7254.s: The bill would direct the Secretary of the Interior to study whether the Bay Area Ridge Trail could be named a national scenic trail. The trail is about 550 miles long and runs along the hills and mountains around the San Francisco Bay Area in Northern California, linking more than 75 parks and open spaces. The study would be due within 3 years after the law takes effect and would be done with other agencies and interested groups.

US-119-HR726.s: The bill would update a water rights deal between the Crow Tribe of Montana and Montana. It would change how some water project funds are handled, including new accounts for Crow irrigation and other water supply projects. It would also extend, through 2030, the tribe’s exclusive right to build hydropower facilities on the Yellowtail Afterbay Dam in Montana.
US-119-HR726.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-01-24)

US-119-HR741.s: The bill would raise the head of the Indian Health Service in the Department of Health and Human Services from a director to an assistant secretary. That would change the job title and rank for the person in charge of Indian Health Service work, which affects Native American health programs. The House passed the bill and it was sent to the Senate.
US-119-HR741.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-01-28)

US-119-HR7436.s: The bill would require the Department of Homeland Security’s intelligence office to give new employees training on privacy rights, civil rights, civil liberties, and how information is handled. It would also add extra training for people in analysis and open-source intelligence jobs, and require special training options and a way to track who completes training. The Government Accountability Office would report to Congress on how these training programs are carried out.
US-119-HR7436.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-02-09)

US-119-HR7487.s: The bill would change a 1939 water law to make it easier for non-federal groups to develop hydropower at Bureau of Reclamation projects. It would broaden the kinds of Reclamation facilities that can be used for hydropower and update how power rights and project control are handled. The changes would affect people and groups involved with Reclamation water and power projects.

US-119-HR7618.s: The bill would extend three National Park Service grant programs that help preserve U.S. battlefields through fiscal year 2036. These grants cover buying land, updating how sites are explained to visitors, and restoring battlefield areas. It would also require the Park Service to study or confirm studies of places tied to major events in the French and Indian War and the Mexican-American War for possible protection.
US-119-HR7618.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-05-20)

US-119-HR7651.s: The bill would let a child, or the child’s parents or guardians, sue health care workers, hospitals, or clinics in federal court for damages tied to certain medical interventions. It defines those interventions as the use of puberty blockers, sex hormones, or some surgeries done to delay puberty or change a person’s body to match a sex different from their own. The bill also says claims could seek money for medical costs, emotional harm, and, in some cases, extra damages.

US-119-HR7661.s: The bill would bar federal elementary and secondary education funds from being used for sexually oriented material. That includes material with sexual acts or material involving gender dysphoria or transgenderism, when it is used in programs or materials for children under 18. It also says the funds could still be used for standard science classes, major world religion texts, classic literature or art, and safety lessons about sex trafficking and grooming.
US-119-HR7661.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-07-02)

US-119-HR7683.s: The bill would change how the Department of Veterans Affairs handles planning, budget, and financial work. It would rename and expand the role of the top budget and finance official, add two deputy positions, and create a small office to give Congress budget and finance details. It would also require some changes within 180 days, end several parts of the new setup after five years, and extend a pension payment limit to December 31, 2033.

US-119-HR7730.s: The bill would raise the debt limits for two kinds of bankruptcy cases used by small businesses and wage earners. It would increase the Subchapter V limit from about $3.4 million to $7.5 million and the Chapter 13 limit from about $2.1 million to $2.75 million. It would also count both secured debt and unsecured debt toward the Chapter 13 limit. It passed the Senate without change.
US-119-HR7730.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-02-26)

US-119-HR7831.s: The License to Drill Act extends through fiscal year 2037 the federal land agency’s power to collect fees for processing new oil and gas permit applications. Those fees go to a fund used to improve permit processing. It became law on October 20, 2026.

US-119-HR7834.s: This bill would give legal protection to vendors that work with law enforcement to store and process child sexual abuse material for online exploitation investigations. It would cover federal, state, and local agencies, as long as the vendor does not act with intent, neglect, malice, or reckless disregard. The bill would also require those vendors to follow cybersecurity and storage rules for that material. It passed the House and was sent to the Senate.
US-119-HR7834.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-09-08)

US-119-HR7945.s: The bill would make consumer products that contain nitrous oxide a banned hazardous product 180 days after the law takes effect. It would not apply to nitrous oxide used for medical or dental care, food production in a commercial setting, or research and development. It also would not apply when nitrous oxide is used as part of food in a pressurized container to push the food out.

US-119-HR7954.s: The bill would help Tribal governments manage buffalo and buffalo habitat on Indian land and bring buffalo back to Tribal lands. It would let the Interior Department work with Tribes and Tribal groups, give grants and contracts, provide help, and keep certain Tribe-shared information private. It would also allow surplus buffalo from federal land to be moved to Indian land, and the authority would end 7 years after the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR7970.s: This bill would permanently place 2-benzylbenzimidazole opioids, commonly called nitazenes, in Schedule I under the Controlled Substances Act. It would cover materials, compounds, mixtures, and preparations that contain these substances, along with their salts, isomers, and salts of isomers. It would also require the Attorney General to issue rules to carry out the changes, including a public comment process.

US-119-HR7972.s: The bill would require the Internal Revenue Service to set up a fellowship program to recruit qualified data scientists. It would also create a task force, including those fellows, to help with audit case selection, offshore tax evasion, and the use of artificial intelligence and data analytics in tax work. The task force would also support training and education efforts.
US-119-HR7972.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-03-18)

US-119-HR8141.s: The bill would require consumer credit data resellers to use reasonable steps to make the credit information they share as accurate as possible. It would also say a reseller is not liable under the Fair Credit Reporting Act if it correctly passes along information it got from another credit reporting agency.
US-119-HR8141.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-03-27)

US-119-HR8163.s: The bill would change how Medicare pays doctors by allowing bigger yearly updates to the physician fee schedule. It would also require the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to correct payment amounts when spending on certain services goes over set limits or when expected use does not match actual use. The bill would make some payment-related price updates happen at least every five years and would limit how much one adjustment factor can change each year.
US-119-HR8163.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-03-30)

US-119-HR8183.s: The bill would create a test program run by the Labor Department to give grants to state agencies or groups of state agencies. The grants would help build workforce data systems, talent marketplaces, and public websites that show job, training, and skill information, with privacy and security rules. It would also support voluntary skills assessment tools and require reports to Congress on the program.

US-119-HR8195.s: The bill would require the Interior Secretary to create regional plans for managing double-crested cormorants, working with flyway councils, states, and tribes. The plans would set rules for when and how the birds may be taken, require public yearly reports, and call for nonlethal steps and habitat fixes. It would also require bird population surveys every 5 years, updates to the plans every 5 years, and would end on January 1, 2034.

US-119-HR8205.s: The law reauthorizes federal programs through fiscal year 2031 that support research and development of drugs and other therapies for ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease, and other brain and nerve diseases. It continues NIH and FDA grants and a public-private partnership that help study and review possible treatments. It also requires NIH and FDA to review safety information, report serious side effects, and publish plans and reports on how they will support these drugs.

US-119-HR8313.s: This bill would make the Trump accounts contribution pilot program permanent. It would also add an inflation adjustment to the $1,000 amount for taxable years beginning after 2028. The changes would apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2026.

US-119-HR8322.s: The law extends certain surveillance powers under title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act through April 30, 2026. It also changes the timing rules for the transition to those changes. The law takes effect on the earlier of the date it was enacted or April 19, 2026.

US-119-HR8347.s: The bill would treat certain temporary doctors and advanced care workers as independent contractors, not employees, under two federal labor laws. It would apply to qualified locum tenens professionals and advanced care practitioners who work on a temporary basis under a written contract, for up to one year at one site. The laws covered are the Fair Labor Standards Act and the National Labor Relations Act.

US-119-HR837.s: This law directs the Secretary of Agriculture to convey about 232.9 acres of National Forest System land in the Tonto National Forest in Arizona to Gila County if the county asks for it in writing on time. The county must use the land only to serve and support veterans of the Armed Forces. The county must pay the costs of the conveyance, and if the land is later used for another purpose, it reverts to the United States.

US-119-HR8437.s: The bill would create a milestone-based program to give federal financing support to geothermal demonstration projects in low-permeability and impermeable rock formations. It would focus on projects in new regions, including places with little or no geothermal power now, and on or near Indian land. The program would be aimed at project sponsors, and the Energy Department would have 180 days after enactment to set it up.

US-119-HR8483.s: The bill would transfer certain federal land in California into trust for the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians. It covers about 847 acres total, made up of one 164-acre parcel and two parcels of about 168 acres and 515 acres. The land would become part of the tribe’s reservation, and the bill keeps some public access, Forest Service access, and existing water rights in place.

US-119-HR8552.s: This bill would increase the pay rates for veterans with service-connected disabilities and for certain survivors who receive dependency and indemnity compensation. It would also raise related amounts for dependents, clothing allowance, and some other disability compensation payments. The Secretary of Veterans Affairs would have to publish the updated rates in the Federal Register.

US-119-HR8658.s: The bill would give people using the Indian Health Service emergency care program at least 15 days to tell the program about emergency care they got from a non-IHS doctor or hospital. Right now, that notice is due within 72 hours. People who are elderly or disabled would still have a 30-day notice rule for emergency services.
US-119-HR8658.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-05-04)

US-119-HR8660.s: The bill would change overtime pay rules so employer stock units, called restricted stock units, can be treated like other types of employee stock plans. It would affect workers and employers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act. The change would take effect 90 days after the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR8705.s: The bill would block federal money for the American History and Civics Education program from being used for certain ideas tied to race, sex, gender identity, or national origin. It would also stop the Education Department from giving grant priority based on race, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, or immigration status. The bill would affect groups seeking these grants.
US-119-HR8705.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-05-07)

US-119-HR8781.s: The bill would define “sex,” “female,” and “male” for Title IX, the law that bars sex discrimination in education programs that get federal money. It would say sex means a person’s biological sex, male or female. It would affect how Title IX is applied in schools and other education programs covered by that law.
US-119-HR8781.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-05-13)

US-119-HR8800.s: This bill would set rules and spending authority for Defense Department programs, military building projects, and some national security work at the Energy Department for fiscal year 2027. It would cover military purchases, troop levels, health care and pay, contracting rules, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and some ties with foreign nations. It would also direct some planning for defense sales, new sources of key materials, and certain military construction projects.
US-119-HR8800.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-06-15)

US-119-HR8876.s: This bill would update federal law on aquatic invasive species to expand prevention, management, control, and eradication efforts. It would create a grant program for research and development of technologies and methods to control and eradicate these species, and it would involve federal, state, tribal, regional, and local officials and nongovernmental organizations. The bill would also require new planning and study work on watercraft inspections and decontaminations, rapid response activities, and monitoring of waterways for aquatic invasive species.

US-119-HR8893.s: The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to create task forces to help develop technical standards and guidance for spotting content made with artificial intelligence. The work would focus on labeling audio, video, and text that was made or heavily changed by AI, and on tools like metadata, watermarks, and digital fingerprints. The task forces would also look at how online platforms store and show this origin data while protecting privacy, and they would report their findings to NIST and Congress.
US-119-HR8893.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-05-19)

US-119-HR8945.s: This bill would rename the U.S. Postal Service facility at 86-014 Farrington Highway in Wai'anae, Hawai'i as the "U.S. Representative Colleen Hanabusa Post Office Building." It would also make any reference to that facility in U.S. records mean the new name.

US-119-HR8979.s: The bill would direct the Department of Education to give grants to states, which would pass money on as subgrants to local school districts. The money would be used to increase access to school-based mental health providers in high-need public elementary and secondary schools.
US-119-HR8979.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-05-21)

US-119-HR8981.s: The bill would expand the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s work on biometrology, which is the science of measuring living systems. It would create a new lab program, support research and data work, and help set common terms and technical standards for engineering biology, biomanufacturing, and biotechnology. It would also back the development of specialized engineering biology facilities with industry and other partners.
US-119-HR8981.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-05-21)

US-119-HR8985.s: The bill would create a rental aid program for low-income veteran families through the federal housing voucher system. It would let eligible veteran families get help paying rent and would require housing agencies to help verify veteran status and share information on local veteran services. The bill also sets service fees for housing agencies of up to $4,000 per eligible household, adjusted for inflation, and the change would take effect at the start of the next fiscal year after enactment.

US-119-HR9012.s: The bill would let people and businesses carrying the low-income housing tax credit move it back up to 5 prior years to help use the credit. It would change the tax code for the low-income housing tax credit. The change would apply to tax years that begin after the law is enacted.

US-119-HR9034.s: The bill would add new standards for offshore oil and gas operators on the outer continental shelf, including checks on past rule compliance, financial strength, and decommissioning duties. It would also create decommissioning escrow accounts, which are accounts set aside for cleanup costs, and require annual reviews and reports to Congress. The bill would authorize $30 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2031 to carry out these rules.

US-119-HR9035.s: This bill would change bankruptcy rules for oil, gas, and coal companies so cleanup and land restoration costs come first in payment order. It would also block these costs from being wiped out in bankruptcy, stop some fossil fuel assets from being abandoned, and let courts look back up to 10 years for certain transfers or debts tied to these companies. New federal fossil fuel leases would have to bar transfer if the leaseholder files for bankruptcy, and the changes would apply to bankruptcy cases started on or after the date the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR9039.s: The bill would create a Venezuela Restoration Fund in the U.S. Treasury. The fund would be used by the Secretary of State to support democracy, human rights, independent media, and anti-corruption work in Venezuela, using certain forfeited funds tied to people or groups acting for the Chavez or Maduro regimes. It would also require yearly reports to Congress on money deposited and spent from the fund.

US-119-HR9043.s: This bill would change how the U.S. judges foreign countries under the anti-trafficking law. It would add steps for countries to show serious efforts to stop buying commercial sex, teach buyers how traffickers exploit people in prostitution, and cut demand for sex tourism. The change would take effect on the date the bill becomes law and would apply to later country checks.

US-119-HR9048.s: The bill would add gluten-containing grains, such as wheat, rye, and barley, to the federal list of major food allergens. That would affect food makers and labels under the food safety law. The change would apply to food introduced into interstate commerce 18 months after the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR9084.s: This bill would require the Secretary of Energy to post public announcements on a Department of Energy website within 72 hours after changing certain directives or safety standards for covered DOE nuclear facilities. It would also require public notices after issuing certain safety analyses or entering into agreements to authorize those facilities, and it would require an annual report to Congress on actions taken during the previous calendar year. The bill applies to covered DOE nuclear facilities and to the Department of Energy.

US-119-HR9086.s: The bill would change how the State Department manages and trains U.S. Foreign Service members. It would create new programs for expeditionary diplomacy, veteran and military hiring, and a reserve corps pilot program, and it would add training and job rules for some Foreign Service staff. It would also give some workers protections while they take approved outside training, education, or work details.
US-119-HR9086.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-02)

US-119-HR9090.s: The bill would direct federal health agencies to expand research on menopause and mid-life women’s health, including symptoms, related conditions, and care methods. It would also create public health education and outreach efforts, along with grants and training to improve care and treatment for women going through perimenopause, menopause, and postmenopause. It authorizes $25 million each year from fiscal years 2027 through 2031 for research, and $10 million each year from fiscal years 2027 through 2031 for public health activities.

US-119-HR9098.s: The bill would limit when the government can use a search warrant, subpoena, court order, or other legal order to get congressional records. Those records include work emails and other messages tied to members of Congress and their staff. It would mainly affect the government, members of Congress, and congressional employees, and it includes some exceptions for criminal investigations.
US-119-HR9098.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-09-08)

US-119-HR9112.s: The bill would give visual artists a federal right to control the sale or public sharing of a style copy that imitates their work in commerce. It also sets rules for online services and AI tools, with notice-and-takedown steps and some uses like criticism, parody, research, news, and independent art left out. Courts could award damages and orders to stop violations, and the bill also limits some state claims that overlap with this new right.

US-119-HR9150.s: The bill would require the Department of Veterans Affairs to provide boxing-based exercise classes to enrolled veterans who have Parkinson’s disease or a similar movement disorder and choose to join. It would apply to veterans in the VA health care system. The classes would be for treatment of that condition.
US-119-HR9150.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-04)

US-119-HR9177.s: The bill would direct the National Science Foundation to run a grant program for projects that improve mentoring in STEM higher education. It would give special attention to minority-serving schools, historically Black colleges and universities, Tribal colleges, rural schools, emerging research institutions, and groups that include them. It also would add a new reporting item on how schools and agencies handle reports of harassment, discrimination, and other professional or scientific misconduct, and it authorizes $5 million for fiscal years 2027 through 2031.

US-119-HR9191.s: The bill would name the American mastodon fossil as the national fossil mammal and the Tyrannosaurus rex fossil as the national fossil dinosaur. It would affect how the United States recognizes these fossils.
US-119-HR9191.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-09-08)

US-119-HR9192.s: The bill would require certain health plans and insurers to cover drugs used to treat autoimmune diseases, hemophilia, and Von Willebrand disease. It would also limit how often a plan can require prior approval for those drugs to once in any 12-month period, with some exceptions. The changes would apply to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2027.

US-119-HR9194.s: The bill would let the Housing and Urban Development secretary treat certain paperwork made under a named process standard as enough proof that a project meets domestic content rules under the Build America, Buy America Act. It applies to HUD financial aid and to funding recipients who must show their materials meet U.S. content requirements. It would also let HUD accept similar standards if they provide a checkable and verifiable process.

US-119-HR9203.s: The bill would require colleges and other schools that take federal student aid to set up clear steps for handling civil rights complaints under Title VI, including naming a coordinator and keeping complaint records. It would also require the Education Department to give Congress regular updates on complaints and investigations. Schools that do not follow the rules for two straight years could lose access to federal student aid for at least two more years, unless they later show they are in compliance.
US-119-HR9203.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-09-08)

US-119-HR9204.s: The bill would let the Attorney General award grants to colleges and firearm makers to research and develop safer gun storage devices, including ones that use biometric data, like fingerprint or other body-based ID, to block unauthorized access. It would also fund work on how to get more people to buy these devices and lower their cost. The bill authorizes $10 million a year from fiscal years 2027 through 2030, and it would require grant recipients to file yearly reports.

US-119-HR9211.s: This bill would direct the Department of Education to carry out training, public awareness, and written guidance on Title VI rights and responsibilities related to antisemitism. It would also require the department to name an antisemitism coordinator to oversee this work and review complaints and strategies. Schools and other recipients of Federal education funds would have to designate a Title VI coordinator, and campus crime data would be reported in a more detailed way.

US-119-HR9216.s: The bill would change federal overtime pay rules so employers would have to pay two times a worker’s regular rate for overtime hours, instead of one and one-half times. It would affect workers who get overtime pay and the employers who pay it. The change would take effect 180 days after the bill became law.

US-119-HR9224.s: The bill would update and reauthorize the federal child care grant law for fiscal years 2027 through 2031. It would change definitions and planning rules, including who can qualify for help, and would require states to consult parents, child care providers, employers, local governments, and tribal groups when making plans. It would also expand language on child care quality, training, safety checks, and mixed delivery systems, which use a mix of child care settings and programs.

US-119-HR9231.s: The bill would make certain chemicals unsafe for use in food packaging that touches food, including some PFAS, phthalates, bisphenol A, and other listed substances. It would also tell the FDA to consider risks to vulnerable groups, like children, pregnant women, and workers, when reviewing other substances used as alternatives. The changes would take effect 2 years after enactment, and states could keep or add stricter rules.

US-119-HR9248.s: The bill would change the FAST Act so some recreation projects count as covered projects for faster federal permit review. It would affect certain recreation activities that need federal permits. The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the House Natural Resources Committee.

US-119-HR9253.s: The bill would let certain independent music creators and owners work together to negotiate music licensing terms with large online music platforms and with companies that make generative AI, which is AI that can create new text, images, audio, or video. It would give them protection from antitrust laws, the rules against certain anti-competitive deals, if the talks meet set limits. The bill says the group talks cannot be only about price and must be limited to eligible independent creators and the platform or AI company.

US-119-HR9255.s: The bill would set new rules for timeshare sales so buyers get a single document with all costs, ongoing fees, any fees the company can change, and ways to end ownership. It would also give buyers a 14-day right to cancel without penalty and a chance to review all papers on their own before signing. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, and they would apply to agreements made 90 days after the law takes effect.

US-119-HR9259.s: The bill would require legal counsel for unaccompanied children in immigration cases, paid for by the government unless the child already has a lawyer. It would also give detained noncitizens access to counsel in federal and contract detention sites, and require the government to give them their immigration file and time to review it before a removal case moves forward. The bill would direct the Health and Human Services Department to make rules, train and organize counsel, and send Congress a yearly report on how often children got counsel. It would also change some rules for motions to reopen cases if counsel was not provided.

US-119-HR9269.s: The bill would extend the authorization for the African American Civil Rights Network, a federal program that recognizes and helps preserve Black civil rights history. It would change the end date for that authority so it runs 7 years after this bill becomes law. The measure affects the network and the federal law that governs it.

US-119-HR9289.s: The bill would end a federal tax break for people who give money to scholarship-granting groups. It would also end a related rule that lets some scholarship amounts be left out of taxable income. These changes would apply to taxable years ending after December 31, 2026, and to amounts received after that date.

US-119-HR9297.s: The bill would direct the Transportation Secretary to set new safety standards for motor vehicles to help reduce crashes with pedestrians, bicyclists, and other vulnerable road users. It would look at features like hood, bumper, and windshield design, as well as vehicle height and weight, and would also set minimum visibility standards. It would also require public information and ratings on how well vehicles let drivers see pedestrians and other road users.

US-119-HR9298.s: The bill would change the federal law that limits lawsuits against firearms makers and sellers. It would expand the law’s definitions, require some cases to be dismissed faster, and let defendants move certain state cases to federal court. It would also bar foreign governments from bringing these kinds of claims and say the federal rules override matching state and local laws.

US-119-HR9325.s: The bill would create the Lone Star Coastal National Recreation Area in the Upper and Middle Texas Gulf Coast as part of the National Park System. It would aim to protect natural, cultural, and recreational resources and support outdoor recreation, tourism, and the local economy. The Interior Secretary could add land only in set ways, and only with landowner consent for network sites.

US-119-HR9326.s: The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST, to help U.S. groups take part in making standards for artificial intelligence and other new technologies. It would require NIST to brief Congress, set up a website with information on standard-making efforts, and run a five-year pilot program with grants for stakeholder meetings in the United States. It would also push for open, fair, and agreed-upon rules in international standards work and better coordination among federal agencies.
US-119-HR9326.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-15)

US-119-HR9327.s: The bill would require U.S. Customs and Border Protection to start a pilot program that takes dogs from local animal shelters and trains them for its support dog program. These dogs would be used to help with grief, trauma, and morale for CBP staff. The House passed the bill on September 16, 2026.
US-119-HR9327.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-18)

US-119-HR9329.s: The bill would change how the Securities and Exchange Commission writes and reviews its rules. It would require the SEC to weigh costs and benefits, explain how a rule affects people and markets, and hold public comment periods that fit the size of the rule. It would also require SEC leaders to testify to Congress twice a year, direct a GAO audit of the SEC’s tech and data systems, and move the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board under the SEC.

US-119-HR9330.s: The bill would set rules for earned wage access services, which let people get wages they have already earned before payday. It would exempt these services from the Truth in Lending Act, a law that covers loan cost disclosures, and would require providers to give a free option, show fees clearly, and tell users how to avoid paying a fee or tip. It would also bar most collection suits, require repayment of certain bank fees caused by provider errors, and stop providers from sharing fees or tips with an employer.
US-119-HR9330.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-09-01)

US-119-HR9331.s: The bill would let banks delay checks and wire transfers they reasonably suspect are fraudulent. It sets a first hold of up to 10 days and a longer hold of up to 45 days, and it limits some fraud safeguards to 60 days at a time. It also says no overdraft fees may be charged in some cases when a wire transfer hold causes an account to go below zero without written notice. The changes would start 60 days after the required rules are issued, and those rules must be issued within one year after enactment.
US-119-HR9331.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-09-01)

US-119-HR9339.s: Passed by the House, this bill would direct the Department of Energy to study and report on using artificial intelligence and high-performance computing to help the bulk power system work better, stay reliable, and handle more electricity. It would affect the Department of Energy and people who rely on the electric grid.
US-119-HR9339.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-18)

US-119-HR9340.s: The bill would require state utility regulators and some utilities to consider a rule that makes certain large electric users pay the full extra cost of upgrades needed to serve them. It applies to large nonresidential users like data centers with peak use of 100 megawatts or more at one site or campus. The rule would also require those customers to give financial backing before the utility makes the upgrades.
US-119-HR9340.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-09-10)

US-119-HR9342.s: The bill would update how the Government Publishing Office handles federal publications, including digital ones, and would change rules for the Federal Depository Library Program. It would also change some GPO operations, such as publishing services, gifts, purchase limits, and employee leave rules. The bill would also switch the Library of Congress from printed to digital versions of the Constitution Annotated and related supplements, and the House passed it.
US-119-HR9342.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-18)

US-119-HR9350.s: The bill would change a victims compensation law to add a one-time catch-up payment for certain eligible claimants, including some spouses and dependents tied to covered claims. It would set that payment at 5.8573% of certain court judgments and require the special master to notify eligible people and make payments within 90 days after receiving the needed information. It would also provide whatever federal money is needed to make these extra payments.

US-119-HR9367.s: This bill would bar members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from making or offering deals tied to prediction markets, such as bets based on government action or political outcomes. It would also let ethics offices give guidance and assess a fee if the rule is broken, with the money paid to the Treasury. The changes would take effect 180 days after the bill becomes law.

US-119-HR9374.s: The bill would require Homeland Security to run a public online tool to help people find certain people held by Customs and Border Protection or Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It would also require faster updates, more language access, and a way for family members or legal representatives to report wrong or missing information. The bill would add notice rules for medical transfers and would require public reports on some Customs and Border Protection arrests and operations.

US-119-HR9375.s: The bill would let the Department of Veterans Affairs give grants to public or nonprofit groups that provide immigration legal help to noncitizen veterans. The help could cover removal cases, naturalization, parole, lawful reentry or repatriation, and some discharge upgrades. It would authorize $20 million for fiscal years 2027 through 2030, and the VA would have to set and publish grant rules within 180 days after enactment.

US-119-HR9381.s: This bill would direct the Bureau of Labor Statistics to include statistics on the use of artificial intelligence in workplace conditions, products, and distribution. It would also require the bureau to begin collecting those statistics not later than 18 months after enactment. The measure would affect the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the workplaces, employers, workers, and occupations that its data covers.

US-119-HR9382.s: The bill would make U.S. Customs and Border Protection link family members’ NEXUS applications during the application process. A family member could schedule interviews for linked family members, and CBP could let them do a joint interview. It could also skip the interview for a child under 14 who is linked to an eligible family member.
US-119-HR9382.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-22)

US-119-HR9385.s: The bill would bar certain U.S. businesses and other entities that are seen as tied to the national interests of the United States from following foreign sustainability due diligence rules, including the European Union’s corporate sustainability rule. It would also let them ask the President for an exemption if compliance would cause hardship. The bill would protect them from adverse action over that compliance and set a civil penalty of up to $1,000,000 for violations.

US-119-HR9394.s: The bill would require the Department of Homeland Security to hold an exercise within four years to improve how the United States prevents, responds to, and recovers from agroterrorism, which means attacks on agriculture and food systems. The exercise would use a case where attackers bring and spread a harmful biological agent in the U.S. and would look at how public and private groups can work together. DHS would then have to send Congress a report on the results and any lessons learned. The House passed the bill.
US-119-HR9394.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-23)

US-119-HR9398.s: The bill would let certain partnerships make a one-time election to settle open federal tax disputes tied to donations of conservation easements. If they use it, the partnership and related partners would give up the right to challenge certain settlement amounts, and the election would be available during a 180-day period after the law takes effect. It would apply to eligible contributions made on or before December 31, 2024, that still have unresolved tax matters.

US-119-HR9401.s: The bill would bar government agencies and insurance companies from denying community-based services to people with disabilities who need long-term support to live in the community. It would ban things like unfair eligibility rules, service caps, waiting lists, or refusing a needed service, and it would require people to be offered community-based services before being placed in an institution. It would also require federal rules, self-checks by agencies and insurers, housing planning, regular notice of community options for people in institutions, and the right for affected people to sue.
US-119-HR9401.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-23)

US-119-HR9404.s: The bill would require the Department of Veterans Affairs to create a free, optional support program for veterans and other eligible borrowers using VA housing loan benefits. It would give help with loan eligibility papers, buying or refinancing a home, appraisal rules, loan service issues, and avoiding foreclosure. The VA could use approved nonprofit housing counselors, set training and certification rules, and must report on the program starting two years after enactment.

US-119-HR9407.s: The bill would create a new tax credit for small distillers who use mostly U.S.-grown materials. It would cut the federal tax on distilled spirits made in the United States by $2.35 per proof gallon for distillers that make no more than 100,000 proof gallons a year and meet the material rule. The change would apply to spirits produced after December 31, 2025.

US-119-HR9414.s: The bill would change the Federal Pell Grant program by raising the maximum grant amount over several award years and then tying future increases to inflation. It would also let some students get larger grants based on low income, make students who get certain public benefits count as having a lower aid score, and add aid access for Dreamer students. In addition, it would restore Pell Grant eligibility from 12 semesters to 18 semesters.

US-119-HR9417.s: The bill would award a Congressional Gold Medal to each member of the Artemis II crew, a group of four astronauts. It would have the Treasury Department make the medals and allow bronze copies to be sold at a price that covers the cost of making them. Money from those sales would go into the U.S. Mint Public Enterprise Fund.

US-119-HR9420.s: The bill would create a grant program for training people who provide abortion care. The Health Resources and Services Administration would give grants to health schools, academic health centers, and other nonprofit safety net providers in states where that training is allowed. The money could help train students, residents, and advanced practice clinicians and connect them with places to provide that care.
US-119-HR9420.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-24)

US-119-HR9421.s: The bill would require a certified health care provider to see a patient in person before prescribing mifepristone or another abortion drug. It would also require the provider to have a medical license in the state where the patient lives. A federal health official would send Congress a yearly list of providers who lose this certification for breaking these rules or for unsafe prescribing.

US-119-HR9423.s: The bill would require the Agriculture Secretary to report to Congress on residue testing for imported organic feedstuffs shipped in bulk and covered by an organic import certificate. It would also require yearly testing for certain imported organic feedstuffs and would set rules for how the testing is done. If testing finds a banned substance above the allowed level, that shipment could not be sold as organic.

US-119-HR9428.s: The bill would let employees take one one-time withdrawal of unused money from certain commuter benefit accounts, which are used for things like transit passes and parking. It would affect workers who have these pay set-aside accounts from an employer. The withdrawn amount would count as taxable income, and the money could be used for any purpose.
US-119-HR9428.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-24)

US-119-HR9434.s: The bill would change federal securities laws so agencies must look at the combined effect of a new rule with certain other recent rules and proposed rules. It would apply to rulemaking under the Securities Act, the Securities Exchange Act, the Investment Company Act, and the Investment Advisers Act. These changes would affect federal regulators that write securities rules.

US-119-HR9436.s: The bill would give the National Marine Fisheries Service until 2035, instead of 2028, to issue new rules to protect the endangered Atlantic large whale from some lobster and crab fishing gear. The new rules would apply to the American lobster and Jonah crab fisheries. They would require use of current and new fishing gear technologies as needed to lower the risk of whales getting tangled in gear.
US-119-HR9436.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-08-27)

US-119-HR9442.s: The bill would halt the building or upgrading of new artificial intelligence data centers after it becomes law until new laws are passed that set safety rules for AI. It would also require the Energy Secretary to report each quarter on these data centers and let the department check information about them. The Commerce Secretary would have to block exports and transfers of certain computing hardware to countries without similar laws, when the hardware is meant for AI data centers or large-scale AI use.

US-119-HR9458.s: The bill would change federal wage laws to help workers recover unpaid wages and stop wage theft. It would require employers to give new workers clear pay and job info, regular paystubs, and final pay on time, and it would give Labor the power to run grants that support efforts to prevent wage and hour violations. It would also give workers better tools to bring wage claims in court and seek more pay from employers who break the rules.

US-119-HR9467.s: The bill would expand the Education Department’s Green Ribbon Schools program, which recognizes schools and other learning centers for reducing environmental harm, supporting health and wellness, and teaching sustainability. It would also set up grants for state education agencies, provide a cash award to winners if money is available, and set aside funds for Bureau of Indian Education schools. It would create a similar award program for libraries, museums, and zoos, and set up an Office of School Infrastructure and Sustainability in the Education Department.
US-119-HR9467.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-25)

US-119-HR9468.s: The bill would change Medicare payment rules for long-term care hospitals. It would extend some site-neutral payment cuts from 2026 to 2032 and add a new high-acuity rule for some hospital stays. The changes would affect long-term care hospitals and Medicare payments for certain patients, starting with discharges on or after October 1, 2026.

US-119-HR9474.s: The bill would direct the Agriculture Secretary to create a program that helps state or local government agencies buy local foods and send them to schools. It would use federal funds for food purchases, limited training and oversight, and require reports on how the money and food are used. The program would apply to schools in the school lunch and breakfast programs, and it would start with funding for fiscal year 2026 and each year after.

US-119-HR9489.s: This bill would give military survivors more time to put death benefits into Roth IRAs and Coverdell education savings accounts. It would change the deadline from 1 year to 3 years. The new rule would apply to benefits received on or after the date the bill becomes law, and it would also cover some earlier payments from October 7, 2001, if the contribution is made within the time limits in the bill.

US-119-HR9490.s: The bill would require large financial institutions and their subsidiaries to hold back part of pay for certain senior employees. The held-back money would be used first to pay civil or criminal fines, and for some banks or credit unions that fail, to help make depositors whole. It would apply to financial firms with more than $1 billion in assets, with different rules based on firm size and employee pay.

US-119-HR9496.s: The bill would give U.S. nationals who are wrongly detained or held hostage abroad, and their spouses, more time to meet certain federal tax deadlines. It would also let the IRS cancel and refund some added taxes, interest, and penalties tied to missed deadlines during that time. The bill would require the State Department and the Justice Department to send the IRS yearly lists of people who qualify, and it would set up a way to claim refunds for certain years starting in 2021.
US-119-HR9496.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-09-08)

US-119-HR9498.s: The bill would let the National Taxpayer Advocate take part in federal tax court cases by filing a short outside brief, called an amicus brief. Federal courts would have to allow those filings in cases that may affect taxpayers' rights. The House passed the bill, and it was sent to the Senate Finance Committee.
US-119-HR9498.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-29)

US-119-HR9499.s: This bill would limit when the IRS can take more time to assess taxes on false or fraudulent federal tax returns. It would make that longer time apply only when the taxpayer meant to evade taxes. The bill passed the House on September 15, 2026, and then went to the Senate.

US-119-HR9501.s: The bill would require the Internal Revenue Service to start a pilot program that uses artificial intelligence to find inaccurate federal tax returns. After the pilot ends, the Government Accountability Office would have to send Congress a report on how much improper tax money was caught or recovered and how accurate the AI tools were. It affects federal tax returns and tax refunds.
US-119-HR9501.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-29)

US-119-HR9509.s: This bill would expand Medicare coverage for kidney disease education services and add those services as a preventive service under private health insurance. It would make more people eligible, including people with hypertension, diabetes, any stage of chronic kidney disease, or other risk factors for kidney disease progression or kidney failure. It would also allow group services, caregiver support, telehealth, and screening for chronic kidney disease and kidney failure, and it would create a working group and assessment process to measure how well the services work.

US-119-HR9514.s: The bill would limit certain home loan help to U.S. citizens. It would change rules for Federal Housing Administration mortgage insurance and for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac when they buy and package home loans. It would affect people applying for these mortgage programs on one- to four-family homes.

US-119-HR9519.s: This bill would change Social Security benefits and tax rules, and it would also change how the program is run. It would affect current and future Social Security recipients, workers who pay Social Security taxes, and people who work with the Social Security system. The parts shown would raise some benefits, change the cost-of-living formula, and update some service and data rules.

US-119-HR952.s: The law directs the Bureau of Land Management to offer to sell the United States’ reversionary interest in about 8.43 acres of land in Sacramento, California. If the land owner asks, the agency must make the offer within two years and sell the interest for at least fair market value. The buyer must also pay the costs of the sale, such as surveys, appraisals, and other admin costs, and the money goes into a federal land disposal account.
US-119-HR952.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2025-02-04)

US-119-HR9521.s: The bill would give more time to use certain federal funds for broadband infrastructure projects. It would let state and local fiscal recovery funds be spent through September 30, 2027, for those projects. It would also let Capital Projects Fund money for broadband projects be spent before January 1, 2028.

US-119-HR9530.s: The bill would require the Transportation Secretary to write rules that ban certain cell phone voice calls on scheduled passenger flights within or between states. If enacted, those rules would have to be finished within 180 days. It would affect airlines and passengers on those flights.

US-119-HR9535.s: The bill would expand the H-2A farm worker visa program so it could cover year-round farm work, not just seasonal or temporary work. It would also widen the kinds of work covered, including reforestation, aquaculture, and livestock work, and it would create a visa path for some current unauthorized farm workers who meet the rules. The bill would also set up online tools for employers, workers, and agencies, and it would lock in the current method for figuring H-2A wage rates.
US-119-HR9535.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-06-30)

US-119-HR9548.s: The bill would set up a federal license for people who buy or keep certain firearms, including handguns and some semiautomatic rifles. It would also require a record of sale or transfer for those firearms and add rules for reporting loss, theft, and changes of address. It would affect buyers, owners, and people who transfer these firearms, with some exemptions for law enforcement, the military, and a few other cases.

US-119-HR9550.s: The bill would create a U.S.-Ukraine defense innovation working group to look at ways to co-develop, co-produce, buy, and share certain unmanned systems and related technology. It would include U.S. defense leaders and seek input from Ukraine’s defense ministry, military forces, and other groups. The group would report to Congress, meet at least every 120 days, and end five years after enactment unless extended for one more year for national security reasons.

US-119-HR9558.s: The bill would create a grant program at the National Endowment for the Arts to help document the history, culture, customs, folklore, and daily life of people in the United States. It would let eligible nonprofit groups, state arts agencies, and some state or territorial groups apply for grants to hire writers, photographers, audio makers, and other documentary workers. If enacted, the agency would have to set up the program within 180 days, and appoint a five-member advisory panel within 90 days.

US-119-HR9561.s: The bill would direct the Health and Human Services Secretary to study whether a standard test can be made to detect tuberculosis in tissue from a human body after death. The study would look at donor screening, transplant safety, and other issues tied to organ and tissue donation. The secretary would also have to report the findings to Congress, and the work would involve health agencies and groups that handle organ and tissue donations.

US-119-HR9567.s: This bill would bar the United States, its territories, and federal courts and agencies from recognizing or enforcing any foreign law, religious law, custom, or practice that conflicts with the Constitution or federal law. It would also stop courts and agencies from enforcing contract terms, foreign forum choices, or foreign decisions that apply those incompatible laws. The bill says it would not create a new cause of action for injunctive relief or damages.

US-119-HR9576.s: The bill would give formal legal authority to the National Fraud Enforcement Division in the Department of Justice. That division investigates and prosecutes fraud involving taxpayer dollars and programs paid for by taxpayers.
US-119-HR9576.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-02)

US-119-HR9578.s: The bill would require AI-made content, like video, images, audio, or text, to be labeled as AI-generated in its metadata or by another technical method. It would direct the Federal Trade Commission to issue rules on how the label must be shown, with help from the National Institute of Standards and Technology. The FTC would also enforce these rules for people or groups that control AI-generated content.

US-119-HR9594.s: The bill would ban cosmetics that contain PFAS, which are certain fluorinated chemicals added on purpose. It would apply to makers and suppliers of cosmetics, ingredients, raw materials, and packaging. The ban would start on January 1, 2027.

US-119-HR9600.s: The bill would approve the location of a commemorative work for Thomas Paine in Area I, a designated area in Washington, D.C. and nearby areas. It would require that the memorial be placed in that area.

US-119-HR9604.s: The bill would move certain tribal education and job training duties from the Education Department to the Interior Department. It would also move the related staff and money, and end two specific programs: one for STEM education and one archives program. The change would take effect one year after the Education Department sends and publishes its response to tribes on how it will be carried out.
US-119-HR9604.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-09)

US-119-HR9605.s: This bill would move the Department of Education’s functions for the National Committee on Foreign Medical Education and Accreditation to the Department of Health and Human Services. It would also transfer related personnel, records, funds, and other resources tied to those functions. References to the Secretary or Department of Education for these functions would be treated as references to the Secretary or Department of Health and Human Services.

US-119-HR9609.s: The bill would move several federal student aid tasks from the Education Department to the Treasury Department. These tasks include handling defaulted and non-defaulted student loans, plus some aid programs such as Pell Grants and Direct Loans. It would also move the staff and money tied to those tasks, require no net increase in full-time jobs at either department, and end a rule that lets delinquent or defaulted student loans be exempt from the debt collection law.
US-119-HR9609.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-09)

US-119-HR9612.s: This bill would change the licensing rules for uranium enrichment facilities. It would allow construction before a license is issued, under the same terms and conditions that apply to other fuel cycle facilities. It would also require the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to issue or revise regulations within 180 days, and it would not change environmental review, hearing rights, or inspection authority.

US-119-HR9613.s: This bill would update the role of the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards in licensing and oversight of nuclear reactor facilities. It would set the committee at a maximum of 15 members, limit most members to two 4-year terms, and require the committee to focus on certain safety and design issues. It would also let the committee decline to review some license applications if they do not raise unique, novel, or noteworthy issues or other issues that warrant review.

US-119-HR9614.s: This bill would let the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission set the pay of certain career appointees at up to 110% of the top basic pay for Senior Executive Service positions. It would apply no matter when the career appointee was appointed. The bill would also update reporting and other related rules in the Atomic Energy Act and the ADVANCE Act of 2024.

US-119-HR9616.s: Creates an EPA program to study and help recover critical materials from contaminated sites. It lets the EPA give aid to people, nonprofit groups, and state, local, and tribal governments, with limits of $10 million total in a year and $3 million to any one recipient. The House passed the bill, and the program would end after 10 years.
US-119-HR9616.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-09)

US-119-HR9619.s: The bill would set privacy and safety rules for AI chatbot providers. It would limit how they can use, keep, sell, or train on chat logs and personal data, and it would give users access to their chat logs and let them ask for deletion. It would also require clear notice that a user is talking to an AI, regular risk checks, special protections for minors, and disclosure when a business uses a chatbot for customer service.

US-119-HR9638.s: This bill would make standard time permanent by repealing daylight saving time under federal law. A state could still choose to observe daylight saving time if it passes a law to do so. For states in more than one time zone, the law lets the state choose for the whole state or for the part of the state in one time zone.

US-119-HR9640.s: The bill would renew the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and update how it can use mapping data, including newer sensing tools and the USGS 3D Hydrography Program. It would extend funding for the initiative with $84 million for fiscal years 2027 through 2031. It would also require the U.S. Geological Survey to favor U.S.-owned and U.S.-controlled contractors when possible and to collect ownership details for contractors and subcontractors.

US-119-HR9641.s: The bill would require certain nursing and long-term care facilities to let each resident choose two essential caregivers and give them in-person access even when visits are limited. It applies to certain Medicare and Medicaid care facilities, and the caregivers would have to follow the facility’s safety rules.
US-119-HR9641.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-13)

US-119-HR9643.s: This bill would change how federal agencies handle mass comments and computer-generated comments in the regulatory review process. It would require agencies to try to verify whether electronic comments were submitted by a human being, identify mass comments, and mark them as such. Agencies could post one sample or one version of a mass comment instead of every identical comment, and they would have to set policies for posting and considering these comments.

US-119-HR9656.s: This bill would require hospitals that take part in federal health care programs to ask patients about immigration status on admission and intake forms. It would also require hospitals to send quarterly reports to the Secretary of Health and Human Services and the Secretary of Homeland Security about patient responses and related immigration status information. Hospitals that do not meet these requirements could be excluded from federal health care programs. The bill would also require the Secretary to report to Congress each year on the reported information and on uncompensated care for people who are not lawfully present in the United States.

US-119-HR9658.s: This bill would change how the Nuclear Regulatory Commission handles certain hearings and judicial review for construction permits, operating licenses, and license amendments. It would let the Commission issue some approvals without a hearing when no one requests one, and it would allow informal hearing procedures. The bill would also allow construction of uranium enrichment facilities to begin before a license is issued, while saying this should not change the right to a hearing or the ban on imports of uranium from the Russian Federation.

US-119-HR9666.s: The bill would direct the Department of Veterans Affairs to start a pilot program that uses approved lung imaging software to help find breathing disorders and lung disease in veterans getting care at VA facilities. The VA would try to lease the software from a company that makes it, and the authority to do that would end five years after the bill becomes law. It would authorize $5 million each year from fiscal years 2027 through 2031, and the VA would have to send Congress a report on how well the program worked.

US-119-HR9668.s: The bill would let financial institutions pause or refuse a payment or transfer if they reasonably think it may be part of fraud or financial abuse against an older adult or other vulnerable person. It would also require notice to account holders or a trusted contact, reporting to agencies, and employee training on spotting this kind of abuse. The new rules would take effect 180 days after enactment.

US-119-HR9671.s: The bill would require certain employers and other covered workplaces to provide reasonable changes for workers whose menopause symptoms affect their job, unless doing so would be too hard on the business. It would also bar employers from forcing leave, denying opportunities, or treating requesters badly because they asked for an accommodation, and it would keep medical details confidential. The bill includes a $4.5 million appropriation to carry it out.

US-119-HR9675.s: The bill would require a federal treatment agency to give grants to states to expand access to care for opioid abuse or addiction. States would use the money to provide up to 60 straight days of services for people who otherwise would not have access to substance abuse care.
US-119-HR9675.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-14)

US-119-HR9681.s: The bill would limit federal intellectual property protection for plants, plant varieties, and plant material that can be used to grow more plants, except under two existing plant law systems. It would also make contracts that block research, breeding, experimentation, seed saving, or propagation of that material unenforceable. The change would apply to patent applications already pending or filed after the bill becomes law, and to new agreements made after that date.

US-119-HR9684.s: This bill would direct the Secretary of Labor to make competitive grants to eligible nonprofit partnerships to support pre-apprenticeship programs in the building and construction trades. The programs would serve underrepresented populations, including people from low-income and rural census tracts. Grant funds could be used for training, curriculum development, participant assessments, enrollment, evaluations, and some stipends during work-based training.

US-119-HR9685.s: The bill would bar federal, state, foreign, or private money from being used to install permanent fencing around the White House complex. It would affect anyone planning or funding that kind of fencing around that federal area in Washington, D.C. It would still allow repair or replacement of fencing that already exists when the law takes effect.

US-119-HR9693.s: The bill would change how Medicare pays doctors and other health providers. It would create a short-term monthly payment model for some primary care services, including care management, behavioral health care, office visits, telehealth, and phone calls, for providers who choose to join and meet the rules. It would also change the Medicare performance reward program, including new measures tied to care efficiency, and allow larger yearly fee updates based on inflation.
US-119-HR9693.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-15)

US-119-HR970.s: This law requires the Department of Veterans Affairs to review and report on the top coverage amount for Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance and Veterans' Group Life Insurance every five years. The review must use the average rise in the Consumer Price Index for the five years before each review. It affects servicemembers, veterans, and their families.

US-119-HR9701.s: This bill would amend the federal charter of the National Society of the Daughters of the American Revolution. It would limit membership to a woman who also meets the organization’s genealogical and membership rules. It defines “woman” as an adult human female and gives a definition of “female” for this section.

US-119-HR9712.s: The bill would require state Medicaid programs to cover care from doulas, midwives, and lactation support providers. That coverage would include care before birth, during delivery, and after birth, in different care settings. It would affect people who use Medicaid for pregnancy and newborn care.
US-119-HR9712.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-15)

US-119-HR9716.s: The bill would require federal law enforcement to get a federal warrant before using certain state or local surveillance tools or data, unless an emergency or written consent applies. It would also create a list of covered surveillance technologies, set limits on how long the data can be kept, and require regular reports and records. The rules would affect federal law enforcement agencies and the use of federal funds for some surveillance equipment.

US-119-HR9718.s: The bill would require the Small Business Administration’s manufacturing and trade office to create and keep a webpage with help and information about moving some or all of a small business’s manufacturing to the United States. The page would include contact details for SBA offices and partner groups, plus a free tool to help small businesses find groups that may assist them. It would also include other information the office thinks is useful.
US-119-HR9718.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to House, 2026-10-09)

US-119-HR9719.s: The bill would let people possess a firearm in certain federal lands and facilities that are open to visitors and invitees, if they are not otherwise barred from having one and follow state law. It applies to areas run or leased by agencies like the Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, National Wildlife Refuge System, and others named in the bill.

US-119-HR972.s: The law expands the Sloan Canyon National Conservation Area in Clark County, Nevada, by about 9,290 acres. It also requires the Bureau of Land Management to grant rights-of-way for a water pipeline and related facilities, and to allow site checks and tunneling work for that pipeline. The pipeline route cannot go through or under wilderness areas, and the expansion must still allow existing rights and future utility rights-of-way.

US-119-HR9720.s: The bill would require Congress to approve certain District of Columbia laws before they can take effect. It covers laws tied to title 47 of the D.C. code and laws that would add or raise a tax or fee. The rule would apply to D.C. laws sent to Congress after this bill becomes law.

US-119-HR9721.s: The bill would require certain charitable groups to report details about fiscal sponsorship deals to the IRS. It would also add excise taxes, which are extra taxes, if a group lets money be used without keeping real control over it. Donations made under those improper deals would not get a federal tax deduction.
US-119-HR9721.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-16)

US-119-HR9722.s: The bill would say that a religious group’s views or practices about marriage, sexuality, or gender identity cannot be treated as against public law or policy when deciding if it has a charitable purpose and can get federal income tax exemption. It would also say a belief does not have to be forced by, or central to, a religion to count as a religious belief. It would affect religious organizations seeking tax-exempt status.
US-119-HR9722.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-16)

US-119-HR9736.s: The bill would give the IRS extra money for fiscal years 2026 through 2031 for tax enforcement, taxpayer help, technology, and system upgrades.
