It would also require the IRS to report to Congress every two years on its plan to focus more audits on high-income people and large companies, hire and keep skilled auditors, and improve tax compliance. A separate watchdog office would also have to report on the IRS plan and its progress.
US-119-HR9736.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-16)

US-119-HR9739.s: The bill would bar federal funds from being used for eminent domain, or forced government taking of land, tied to Mount Cristo Rey in Sunland Park, New Mexico. It would also block federal money for lawsuits and for building or running roads, fences, lights, cameras, sensors, or similar structures on or near the site. The measure affects federal actions related to this land.

US-119-HR9771.s: The bill would tax certain tax-exempt groups, like charities, social welfare groups, labor groups, and business or civic leagues, if they give to a political group within two years of getting money or gifts from a foreign national. It would charge taxes equal to 100% of the first such donation and 200% of later ones, and on a third or later case it would also take away tax-exempt status for two years. Some larger tax-exempt groups would also owe a penalty equal to twice the amount of the donation.
US-119-HR9771.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-18)

US-119-HR9772.s: The bill would require certain tax-exempt groups, like charities and labor groups, to report to the IRS how much money they get from foreign donors. It would apply to groups with at least $200,000 in yearly receipts or $500,000 in assets. These groups would also have to report how much of that money came from donors from China, Iran, Korea, or Russia.
US-119-HR9772.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-18)

US-119-HR9785.s: The bill would direct the Interior Department to study whether three water supply projects could be built for towns, rural areas, and industry in parts of the Missouri River basin. The studies would cover the Western Dakota Regional Water System, an expansion of the Lewis and Clark Regional Water System, and the Dakota Mainstem Water Supply Project. For two of the studies, the federal share of study costs could not be more than $10 million or more than 50% of the total, and the authority would end 7 years after enactment.

US-119-HR9790.s: The bill would let certain qualified doctors and other prescribers write methadone for opioid use disorder so it can be filled at a pharmacy. It would use electronic prescriptions, require informed consent, and allow telemedicine for some treatment, while still keeping other care through opioid treatment programs. States could ask the Attorney General to stop this registration in that state, and pharmacies would not need a separate registration to dispense the medicine. The changes would take effect 180 days after enactment.

US-119-HR9797.s: This bill would create a one-year pilot program to train certain State, local, Tribal, and territorial officials to do security vulnerability or terrorism risk assessments of critical infrastructure facilities. It would also let the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency maintain clearinghouses for critical infrastructure owners and operators and other stakeholders to access security guidance and best practices. The bill also would require annual public reports on outreach to critical infrastructure owners and operators.

US-119-HR9800.s: The bill would bar federal agencies from buying or using automated surveillance systems that identify, track, or record people, including license plate readers, facial recognition, and some biometric tools. It would also stop state, local, and Tribal governments from using federal money for those systems. If a federal agency gets data in violation of the bill, it would have to delete it within 30 days, and that data could not be used in court or other official proceedings.

US-119-HR9807.s: The bill would change pesticide law so state court claims tied to false or missing pesticide warning labels would not be blocked if they match federal misbranding rules. It would also let a pesticide maker update a label when new health or environment data points to a possible labeling problem, and the federal agency could still reject that change. The change would apply to pending and new civil cases once the bill became law.

US-119-HR9809.s: The bill would change the disabled access tax credit for eligible small businesses. It would let the credit cover more kinds of costs, including changes to remove barriers, interpreters, readers, equipment changes, and similar help for people with disabilities. The new rules would apply to costs paid or incurred after December 31, 2026, and the Treasury Department would have to issue guidance and do outreach to small businesses.

US-119-HR9810.s: The bill would change rules for the Small Business Development Center Program and related small business programs at the Small Business Administration. It would add reporting, data collection, marketing, privacy, and grant rules, and it would let some centers use part of their grant money for advertising and collect fees from certain private partnerships. It would also set funding limits and grant amounts, including $175 million for formula grants each fiscal year from 2026 through 2029.

US-119-HR9815.s: The bill would require the Bureau of Prisons to give voting information to inmates from places that allow people in custody to vote. Before federal, state, or local elections, the bureau would have to send details on how to register and how to ask for an absentee ballot, which is a ballot sent by mail. It would also have to give this information in English and Spanish to reentry staff at each federal prison.
US-119-HR9815.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-21)

US-119-HR9816.s: The bill would change Medicaid and CHIP rules for maternal health. It would extend coverage for some mothers from 60 days to one year after pregnancy ends, and that coverage would include dental care. It would also create state grants for maternity care homes and require a federal report on coverage gaps and telehealth use in state Medicaid programs.
US-119-HR9816.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-21)

US-119-HR9817.s: This bill would reduce certain federal justice grants to states that do not have laws restricting restraints on pregnant people in prison that match federal standards. It would also direct the Bureau of Prisons to set up programs in at least 6 facilities for pregnant and postpartum incarcerated people, and it would create grant programs for states to start or expand similar programs in state and local prisons and jails. The programs may include health workers, nutrition help, staff training, counseling, parenting support, reentry help, and ways to keep contact with newborn children.

US-119-HR9821.s: This bill would make changes to farmers’ markets and local food grants, nursing workforce development funding, student loan contract disclosures, the CDC’s Climate and Health program, House conduct rules, a commemorative silver coin program, and critical infrastructure outreach. It also states support for Black Midwives Day and authorizes the Secretary of State to provide assistance internationally to prevent and respond to criminalization, discrimination, and violence against LGBTQI+ people. The bill would require reports from the Agriculture Department and the Homeland Security Agency, and it would appropriate or authorize funding for several programs.

US-119-HR9823.s: This bill would require group health plans and group and individual health insurance coverage to cover Alzheimer’s biomarker testing. It would also add biomarker testing to Medicaid coverage and require it to be covered in the same manner as under private health coverage. The bill also directs the National Institutes of Health to study and report to Congress on the value of biomarker testing in detecting and treating Alzheimer’s disease.

US-119-HR983.s: The law requires the Department of Veterans Affairs to reject certain classes if a school charges more than in-state tuition to people using Montgomery GI Bill-Selected Reserve benefits while they live in that state. It affects veterans and other eligible service members who use those education benefits and attend school where they live. It became law on December 12, 2025.

US-119-HR9846.s: This bill would change the Social Security Act so some people who receive child’s insurance benefits are treated as receiving supplemental security income for Medicaid eligibility. It would apply when states make or review Medicaid eligibility decisions under a state plan or a waiver. It affects the people covered by those child’s insurance benefits and the Medicaid programs that use those rules.

US-119-HR9847.s: The bill would stop state Medicaid programs from denying payment for primary care, substance use disorder, and mental health care when those services are given on the same day at the same office, clinic, or other outpatient site, including by telehealth. It would affect people who use Medicaid and the providers who treat them.
US-119-HR9847.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-22)

US-119-HR9849.s: The bill would let Tuskegee Airmen, Inc. build a memorial on federal land in Washington, D.C., and nearby areas to honor the original Tuskegee Airmen from World War II. It would require the project to follow federal rules for memorials and would bar the use of federal money for it. Tuskegee Airmen, Inc. would be responsible for raising and paying for the memorial.

US-119-HR9866.s: The bill would create a grant program to help states use interstate licensure compacts for mental health workers. These compacts are agreements between states that let them recognize each other’s licenses for counselors, psychiatrists, psychologists, and pediatric mental health professionals. The Health Resources and Services Administration would give grants to compact groups or licensing boards to help bring workers into compact states and to support the groups that run these agreements.
US-119-HR9866.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-22)

US-119-HR9874.s: This bill would expand the ban on foreign nationals making contributions and expenditures in elections to cover certain foreign-controlled, foreign-influenced, and foreign-owned domestic business entities. It would require some business entities to file a certification after making certain election-related payments, and it would bar others from using those funds unless the certification rules are followed. It would also apply the foreign money ban to state and local ballot initiatives and to certain political committees that accept noncompliant donations or contributions. The bill would add rules for separate corporate funds, including limits on foreign nationals taking part in their decisionmaking.

US-119-HR9877.s: The bill would create a wide set of health changes aimed at improving care for minority people, people with limited English, rural and tribal communities, and people in U.S. territories. It would expand data collection, language access, health worker training, and grants, and it would change some Medicare and Medicaid rules to make coverage and care easier to get. It also includes steps on health equity, anti-discrimination, dental care, telehealth, and women’s and family health.

US-119-HR9901.s: The bill would block a federal rule that changed the meaning of "harm" under the Endangered Species Act. It would affect the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, along with how the law is carried out. The rule would have no force or effect.

US-119-HR9902.s: The bill would stop federal buildings, facilities, and programs from being named after living elected officials or political appointees for a set time after they leave office. If a person makes more than $1 million a year from selling or licensing their name, image, or likeness, the limit would last longer until they drop below that amount. It would also require agency inspectors general to look into complaints and report findings to Congress within 90 days.

US-119-HR9911.s: The bill would let certain maritime industry areas be picked as opportunity zones, which are tax break areas, under the tax code. It would limit these special zones to 100 tracts and tie them to work on shipyards, ports, harbor facilities, and vessels. The changes would start after December 31, 2026, and the Commerce Secretary would have to begin the nomination process by July 1, 2027.

US-119-HR9914.s: The bill would let non-federal groups share information or help each other on certain AI security risks without breaking antitrust laws, if they act in good faith for that purpose. It would also let them agree to delay or limit some AI release, use, development, training, testing, or evaluation if they first give written notice to the Justice Department’s antitrust chief. The bill would let the Attorney General ask a court to stop conduct that still breaks antitrust laws or could raise those AI security risks.

US-119-HR9915.s: The bill would ban “stealth bots,” meaning software that accesses websites or online services without clearly saying who it is or why it is there. It would also bar bots from hiding that they are bots when used with generative AI tools, and it would let the Federal Trade Commission and state officials take civil action. Violations could bring civil penalties of up to $53,000 per violation, and the rule would take effect 180 days after enactment.

US-119-HR9917.s: The bill would require certain large AI companies and other entities to keep a technical way to stop, limit, suspend, or shut down certain AI systems. It would also require reports on covered incidents, let the Homeland Security Department set rules and issue emergency orders, and allow audits and penalties for violations. The rules would apply only to certain entities that meet the bill’s size and revenue tests, with an exception for personal, academic, or non-commercial use.

US-119-HR9921.s: The bill would create a new tax credit for building shipyard facilities in the United States, including territories and possessions. The credit would cover 25% of qualified investment, or 35% for facilities in certain areas, for shipyards that build or repair commercial or military vessels or make key parts or equipment for them. The change would apply to property put in service after the bill is introduced, and the credit would end for property put in service after December 31, 2033.

US-119-HR9936.s: The bill would limit bonuses and other performance pay for the Postmaster General if the Postal Service lost money, missed nationwide service goals, got a serious audit finding, or did not file a required report to Congress. It would also require the Postmaster General to send Congress a yearly report on senior executive pay, the reasons for those payments, the Postal Service’s finances, and service data. The Postal Service inspector general would review the report and check if the rules were followed.

US-119-HR9937.s: The bill would lower the fentanyl amounts that can trigger a required prison term for people who make, sell, import, export, or have fentanyl with the intent to sell it. It would also lower the amounts for fentanyl-like drugs, called fentanyl analogues. The U.S. Postal Service would be told to make more chemical screening devices available and assign enough staff to help stop fentanyl and other illegal imports.
US-119-HR9937.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in House, 2026-07-23)

US-119-HR9938.s: The bill would create a tax credit for spending to fix up movie theaters in the United States. The credit would cover 30% of certain building and property costs, with caps based on the number of screens, and it could be sold or transferred. The credit would apply to amounts paid after the bill becomes law and would end for amounts paid after December 31, 2030.

US-119-HR9966.s: The bill would change the Department of Homeland Security's nonprofit security grant program. It would say grant money can be used for onsite security staff, help with grant applications and administration, and hiring off-duty police officers. It would also let groups use up to 5% of a grant to pay people to apply for this funding.

US-119-HR997.s: This bill would amend the tax code to let the National Taxpayer Advocate appoint counsel in the Office of the Taxpayer Advocate. That counsel would report directly to the National Taxpayer Advocate, or to someone the advocate delegates. It also makes a conforming change to the rule covering employees of the Office of the Taxpayer Advocate.

US-119-HR9970.s: The bill would change how Medicare pays for ambulance services, including both ground and air ambulance care. It would require the health secretary to review and update payment rates using newer cost and service data, with new rules starting in 2028 and yearly updates in some years after that. It would also require air ambulance providers to report certain data and would call for a stakeholder meeting by the end of 2028, with recommendations due by July 1, 2029.

US-119-HR998.s: The law changes how the IRS tells people about math or clerical errors on tax returns. It requires clearer notices, a way to ask for tax relief in writing, online, by phone, or in person, and a pilot program to send some notices by certified or registered mail.

US-119-HR9988.s: The bill would add barley, rye, and oats to the list of major food allergens under federal food law. It would affect food makers and others who sell food in interstate commerce, starting one year after it becomes law. It would also require a federal health report on celiac disease within one year after enactment.

US-119-S1003.s: The law requires the Federal Communications Commission to issue an order that clearly allows wireless emergency alerts to be sent to mobile phones during a shark attack. These alerts are used for public safety warnings. It became Public Law 119-100 on June 26, 2026.

US-119-S1020.s: This law lets the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission give more time for some hydropower projects to start construction. It applies to projects licensed before March 13, 2020, and can add up to six more years, in no more than three two-year steps. It also lets the agency bring back some expired licenses for projects that get these extra time extensions.

US-119-S1055.s: The bill would give patients, or someone acting for them, 15 days instead of 72 hours to tell the Indian Health Service's Purchased/Referred Care program about emergency care from a non-IHS provider or facility. It would apply to American Indian and Alaska Native patients who use that program. People who are elderly or disabled would still have a 30-day notice rule for emergency care.
US-119-S1055.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-03-13)

US-119-S1071.s: Sets rules and powers for the 2026 defense budget and programs at the Defense Department, Energy Department security programs, State Department, Coast Guard, and intelligence agencies. It covers buying military gear, troop levels, military pay and health care, cyber and AI policy, military construction, and some policies for foreign ties, including Israel, Ukraine, and the Indo-Pacific. It became Public Law 119-60 on December 18, 2025.

US-119-S1157.s: The bill would require the Department of Health and Human Services to review ways to speed up lung cancer research, prevention, and awareness for women and underserved groups. The review would look at current research, find gaps in knowledge, and point to new chances for shared research on causes, screening, diagnosis, and treatment. It would also make recommendations for a national lung cancer screening plan and a public education campaign.
US-119-S1157.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-03-26)

US-119-S146.s: The TAKE IT DOWN Act became law on May 19, 2025. It bans the online posting of intimate images or deepfakes shared without consent when meant to harm, abuse, or harass someone, and it also covers threats to post such images. It requires covered websites and apps to remove reported images within 48 hours after notice.

US-119-S1513.s: The bill would place about 1,082.63 acres of land in Washington into trust for the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe. That land would become part of the tribe’s reservation. It would also bar gaming, or casino-style gambling, on that land.
US-119-S1513.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-04-29)

US-119-S1582.s: The law sets rules for payment stablecoins, which are digital tokens meant to be redeemable for a fixed value. It limits who may issue them in the United States, sets reserve and disclosure rules for issuers, and gives federal and some state regulators oversight. It also affects foreign issuers and digital asset service providers, and it treats permitted stablecoins as neither securities nor commodities under law.

US-119-S1596.s: The law renames the Anahuac National Wildlife Refuge in Anahuac, Texas, as the Jocelyn Nungaray National Wildlife Refuge. It also gives legal backing to the earlier executive order that used the same new name.

US-119-S160.s: Lawmakers passed this bill, which lets the Defense Department sell extra aircraft and parts that can be used for wildfire suppression. It also allows those aircraft to drop water from the air, not just fire retardant, and removes a limit on using them to help fight fires in other countries. The authority runs from June 12, 2025, through October 1, 2035.

US-119-S164.s: This bill would change the rules for congressional resolutions of disapproval for certain "midnight rules." It would let one resolution cover more than one rule if each rule was submitted during the final year of a President's term. It affects Congress's review of those rules and the rules themselves.

US-119-S1884.s: The law permanently extends and expands the rules for court cases over art and other property taken from people during Nazi persecution between 1933 and 1945. It removes the filing deadline for these claims, while still requiring them to be filed within six years after the person learns where the property is. It also lets courts hear more of these cases against foreign states, allows nationwide service of process, and limits some time-based and other dismissal defenses.

US-119-S195.s: The law directs the Commerce Department’s National Travel and Tourism Office to promote travel to U.S. music festivals, concert venues, and other music-related places. It also expands the office’s work on sports and recreation to include promoting international travel to those activities in the United States. The office must report to Congress within one year after enactment and then every two years.
US-119-S195.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-01-22)

US-119-S1981.s: The bill would require the Agriculture and Interior departments to make a plan for using livestock grazing to reduce wildfire risk on national forest lands and other public lands. The plan would be due within 18 months after the bill becomes law and would look at targeted grazing, temporary permits, postfire recovery, and tools like virtual fencing. It would involve working with states, local governments, Indian Tribes, fire agencies, and other groups.

US-119-S2.s: The law provides $70 billion through fiscal year 2029 for the Department of Homeland Security, Customs and Border Protection, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It gives money for border security, immigration enforcement, technology, staffing, and related work, including some funds for child exploitation investigators and forensics staff. It also limits some spending, such as on certain surveillance towers and on processing coordinator hiring after October 31, 2028.

US-119-S201.s: The law requires the Department of Veterans Affairs to work with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine on a study about cancer rates and deaths among veterans who served as aircrew members and flew fixed-wing aircraft. It affects veterans who did this kind of active-duty flying. The bill became Public Law 119-32 on August 14, 2025.

US-119-S2098.s: The bill would have the Department of Health and Human Services give about 3.4 acres in Anchorage, Alaska, to Southcentral Foundation. The land would be used for health and social services programs, and the group would not have to pay for it or accept extra conditions on the property. It also sets rules about access for HHS and limits who can be held responsible for certain environmental contamination on the land.
US-119-S2098.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-06-17)

US-119-S216.s: The law renews and changes the Marine Debris Program and the Marine Debris Foundation, which work on ocean trash and its effects on the economy, sea life, and safe travel by water. It extends NOAA’s program through fiscal year 2029 and lets NOAA use in-kind support and other types of project agreements. It also updates how the foundation is run, requires outreach to tribes and tribal governments, sets where its main office must be, and lets it match outside contributions.

US-119-S222.s: Lawmakers changed school milk rules in the National School Lunch Program so schools may offer whole, reduced-fat, low-fat, and fat-free milk, including flavored and unflavored kinds, and some dairy-free drinks that meet USDA nutrition rules. It also lets a parent or guardian, not just a doctor, give the note needed for a milk substitute for some students, and it adds food allergy training and yearly certification for school food service staff. The law took effect when it was signed on January 14, 2026.

US-119-S2283.s: The bill would rename the U.S. Postal Service building at 201 West Oklahoma Avenue in Guthrie, Oklahoma, as the "Oscar J. Upham Post Office." It applies to that one post office facility. The bill became Public Law 119-59.
US-119-S2283.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-07-15)

US-119-S2378.s: This bill would create two funds in the Department of Homeland Security for aviation security. It would direct part of the 9/11 Security Fee to the Aviation Security Capital Fund and the Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund. The money would be used for aviation security grants and for the procurement, deployment, and sustainment of checkpoint and exit lane technology.

US-119-S2392.s: Became law on November 25, 2025. It requires the Department of Veterans Affairs to raise several payments for veterans, surviving spouses, and children by the same amount as the Social Security cost-of-living increase that starts on December 1, 2025. It also lets the VA make a similar change to some disability payments for people who did not get compensation before.

US-119-S2393.s: The law lets the Department of Veterans Affairs build a major medical facility project in St. Louis, Missouri, in fiscal year 2026. It sets a top spending amount for the project. The project includes a new bed tower, expanded clinic space, a new administrative and warehouse building, utility plant work, and parking garages.

US-119-S2398.s: The law renews CDC programs through fiscal year 2030 to help prevent and respond to diseases spread by ticks, mosquitoes, and other pests. It includes a national plan, grants for regional centers of excellence, and agreements with state, local, and tribal health departments. It became Public Law 119-118 on September 30, 2026.

US-119-S240.s: This law updates a 2010 water rights settlement between the Crow Tribe of Montana and Montana. It changes how money is handled for the Crow Irrigation Project and for other water system projects tied to water supply, treatment, and delivery. It also extends the tribe’s exclusive right to build hydropower facilities on the Yellowtail Afterbay Dam to 2030.
US-119-S240.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-01-24)

US-119-S2403.s: The law lets the person who manages an employee stock ownership plan use a value set by an outside expert or business appraiser for certain plan assets, if those assets are not traded on a regular market. The expert or appraiser must use the method set out in IRS Rule 59-60, which lists factors for valuing a closely held business. It affects employee stock ownership plans and the workers who have shares in them.

US-119-S254.s: The law bars states from banning certain marine mammal products made by Alaska Natives, including ivory, bone, and baleen. It covers their sale, trade, transport, possession, and other business across state lines when the items are legal Alaska Native handicrafts or clothing. It became Public Law 119-99 on June 12, 2026.

US-119-S2554.s: The bill would let Alaska Native residents in Haines, Ketchikan, Petersburg, Tenakee, and Wrangell form urban corporations and get certain settlement land. The Department of the Interior would have to transfer specified land to each corporation, and the subsurface rights would go to the Southeast Alaska regional corporation. Each corporation could also set up a settlement trust to support health, education, welfare, and Native heritage and culture.
US-119-S2554.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-07-30)

US-119-S260.s: The law directs the Transportation Security Administration to update its rules so breast milk, baby formula, purified water for infants, juice, and related cooling items are less likely to be contaminated during extra screening. It also tells the Homeland Security inspector general to check whether those rules are being followed and report to Congress. It became Public Law 119-41 on November 25, 2025.
US-119-S260.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-01-27)

US-119-S2658.s: The bill would require companies seeking approval of a drug or license for a biological product to give certain patent information to both the FDA and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. It would also require them to certify that the patent-related information they send to each agency matches. If a patent owner negligently or intentionally fails to make the required disclosures, the bill would create a defense in a patent infringement case.
US-119-S2658.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to Senate, 2026-07-28)

US-119-S269.s: The law gives the Treasury Department permanent access to certain death records from the Social Security Administration to help stop and recover payments made to people who have died. It also makes the Social Security Administration use a higher proof standard before marking someone as dead in its file. If someone is wrongly listed as dead and shows proof, the agency may tell Treasury and other agencies that use the file.

US-119-S2754.s: The bill would direct the Agriculture Secretary to transfer Crystal Reservoir and nearby Forest Service land in Ouray County, Colorado, to the City of Ouray, along with related water rights. The city would have to keep the land as open space for public recreation, take on dam and maintenance costs, and follow limits on development and reservoir changes. The federal government would pay most transfer costs, but the city would pay survey costs. It passed the Senate.

US-119-S2787.s: The bill would change a federal land law so ranchers with grazing agreements on national grasslands are treated the same as people who have grazing permits on other federal land. It would affect ranchers who graze livestock on national grasslands and the agencies that manage those lands. The measure was reported in the Senate with an amendment.

US-119-S283.s: This law tells NOAA and NIST to work together on a standard way to find where seafood comes from, to help stop illegal fishing and seafood fraud. They must use chemical testing, work with Customs and Border Protection and the Coast Guard, and make a portable field kit that can also be used on some prepared seafood like sushi when possible. They must test the method on red snapper and tuna, and NIST must report to Congress within two years on the method and how it could be used in practice.

US-119-S284.s: This law reauthorizes the Congressional Award Board through fiscal year 2028 and lets the Congressional Award Program keep operating. It also changes the rules for the program medals by removing the rule that they must be made of gold-plate over bronze, rhodium over bronze, or bronze. The change is treated as if it took effect on October 1, 2023.

US-119-S2878.s: This law reauthorizes U.S. Geological Survey research and monitoring for Great Lakes fisheries through fiscal year 2030. The work is done through the Great Lakes Science Center and may include invasive species studies, fish population research, and tools that help guide fishery management. It affects Great Lakes basin fisheries and became law on December 26, 2025.

US-119-S3004.s: The bill would direct the Interior Department to transfer about 124.23 acres of Bureau of Land Management land to the city of Price, Utah. The city would use the land for public purposes, including a reservoir and related roads and other infrastructure for public safety, transportation, and access. If the land is used for a purpose not allowed under the bill, the land could go back to the United States.

US-119-S3023.s: The bill would give civil and criminal liability protection to vendors that work with law enforcement to store, keep, and process child sexual abuse material for online exploitation cases. It would apply to federal, state, and local law enforcement, as long as the vendor did not act with bad intent, reckless disregard, or outside its contract. The bill would also require these vendors to follow cybersecurity and storage rules for this material when it is kept as evidence.

US-119-S307.s: The law requires the Justice Department to set national rules to prevent, reduce, and punish sexual harassment and sexual assault by prisoners against Bureau of Prisons staff. It also requires the Bureau of Prisons to carry out the Justice Department inspector general’s recommendations on this issue.

US-119-S3131.s: The bill would require the Department of Defense to allow the names of the 74 USS Frank E. Evans crew members killed on June 3, 1969, to be added to the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Wall in Washington, D.C. It would affect the memorial and the families of those crew members.
US-119-S3131.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-11-06)

US-119-S3135.s: The bill would require the Environmental Protection Agency to change its rules so certain diesel vehicle makers can suspend engine power cuts or shutdowns in cold weather, when temperatures are at or below 20 degrees Fahrenheit. It would let those systems return to normal when temperatures rise above 20 degrees Fahrenheit. It would also allow permanent suspension of those functions on agricultural equipment and on vehicles mainly used north of 59 degrees north latitude.

US-119-S32.s: The law adds College Station as a place where court must be held in the Galveston Division of the Southern District of Texas. It also adds El Centro as a place where court must be held in the Southern District of California.

US-119-S3226.s: This bill would create a records collection at the National Archives for missing Armed Forces and civilian personnel records. It would require government offices to search for, preserve, and send those records to the Archivist, and it would direct public disclosure of them with narrow exceptions. It also sets up review and reporting steps for records that are withheld or heavily redacted.

US-119-S331.s: The law permanently puts fentanyl-related substances into the most restricted drug category under federal law. It sets the same quantity triggers and penalties for those substances as for fentanyl analogues, including a 10-year minimum prison term for offenses involving 100 grams or more. It also creates a new way to register some schedule I research and changes some research rules, including single-site registration in some cases, skipping a new inspection in some cases, and limited small-scale manufacturing by registered researchers.

US-119-S3331.s: This bill would rename the U.S. Postal Service facility at 50 East 100 North in Moab, Utah, as the "2nd Lieutenant Mitch Williams Post Office." Any U.S. law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record that refers to that facility would be treated as a reference to the new name.

US-119-S3371.s: The bill would give the Museum of the Blind People’s Movement in Baltimore, Maryland, the name "National Museum of the Blind People’s Movement." It would apply to that museum at 200 East Wells Street. The measure is about a museum that holds items and records about the blind people’s movement.

US-119-S3404.s: The bill would require a federal study and report on how the government supports cybersecurity for commercial satellite systems. It would also direct the Commerce Department to create a public online clearinghouse with cybersecurity resources and voluntary guidance, including help for small businesses. The bill would also call for a strategy on sharing information and setting roles among federal agencies and private companies.

US-119-S3424.s: This law changes how bankruptcy cases are run. It raises some payments to trustees in Chapter 7 cases, keeps Chapter 11 quarterly trustee fees in place for five more years, and raises the fee rate for some large Chapter 11 cases within set limits. It also extends certain temporary bankruptcy judge jobs for five more years.

US-119-S3493.s: The bill would direct the transfer of certain federal land in Carson City, Nevada, to the city and would also allow some other federal land in the area to be sold. It would require the land to be used for public purposes such as recreation, flood control, a roadway expansion, and other public uses named in the bill. Money from the land sales would go into a special Carson City account for land-sale costs and other listed local projects.

US-119-S3518.s: The bill would change federal hydropower rules so license holders would not need agency approval for small project changes, routine repairs, or seasonal or temporary operation changes, while keeping safety oversight in place. It would also set a faster license path for small micro hydrokinetic energy projects, which use waves, tides, currents, or free-flowing water to make power. The measure would affect hydropower license holders and people seeking licenses for these small water-energy projects.

US-119-S3524.s: The bill would change some grant rules in the American Battlefield Protection Program. It would raise the required local share for two grant programs from 50% to 75%, extend one grant program through 2035, and set aside $2 million each year through fiscal year 2035 for certain grants. It would also direct the Interior Department to study U.S. sites linked to the French and Indian War and the Mexican-American War and report the results to Congress.

US-119-S356.s: This law extends the Secure Rural Schools program, which sends money to states and counties with certain federal land for schools, roads, and other local services. It also provides missed payments for fiscal years 2024 and 2025. Counties and local resource advisory committees can keep starting projects with these funds through fiscal year 2028.

US-119-S3589.s: This bill would amend the Higher Education Act to give students with disabilities and their families more information to choose a college and to succeed after enrolling. It would require colleges to accept certain disability documents, explain how students can qualify for reasonable accommodations or modifications, and share that information with students, parents, and faculty in accessible form and on a public website. It would also require colleges to report data on students with disabilities in federal postsecondary data systems, unless doing so would reveal a student’s identity. The bill also authorizes funding for the National Center for Information and Technical Support for Postsecondary Students with Disabilities.

US-119-S3618.s: The bill would require the Federal Trade Commission, working with federal health and drug agencies, to report to Congress on how minors can access fentanyl through social media platforms. The report would cover how sellers use these platforms, the risks to minors, how platform design may affect access, and what steps platforms and others have taken. It would also include recommendations for Congress and would be made public within 1 year after enactment.

US-119-S3700.s: The bill would create an independent expert panel to review the FAA’s safety management system, which is the agency’s way of managing safety risks, and to make recommendations for a more complete, agency-wide system. The panel would study FAA rules, policies, training, audits, reporting programs, and how well the system works across different parts of the agency. It would send its findings and recommendations to the FAA and Congress, and the FAA would have to post the report online.

US-119-S3705.s: Lawmakers made a time capsule for the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence and directed it to be placed in the Capitol Visitor Center by July 4, 2026. The capsule must include a joint letter from House and Senate leaders and other items they choose, and a plaque about it must also be put up with approval from the House and Senate committees named in the bill. It will stay sealed until July 4, 2276, when House and Senate leaders are to present it to the 244th Congress.

US-119-S3715.s: The bill would rename Chiricahua National Monument in Arizona as Chiricahua National Park. It would also direct the National Park Service to protect traditional cultural and religious sites there and to let members of Indian tribes access those sites for traditional uses. If a tribe asks, the park service could temporarily close small areas of the park to the public to support those uses.
US-119-S3715.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-01-28)

US-119-S3720.s: The bill would direct the Secretary of the Interior to study whether the Bay Area Ridge Trail can be designated as a national scenic trail. The study would be done with state, Tribal, and local agencies, and with other interested organizations, including the Bay Area Ridge Trail Council. The trail is described as a multi-use trail of about 550 miles that connects over 75 parks and open spaces.

US-119-S3723.s: The bill would require the Secretary of the Interior to study whether a project could bring water from the Missouri River to the Western Dakota Regional Water System for homes, farms, and industry. The study would be done with the local water group, and the Secretary would later report on whether the project is technically and financially workable and whether it should be built. It would cap federal spending on the study at $10 million, with the federal share limited to no more than half.

US-119-S3725.s: The bill would require the Secretary of the Interior to study whether a water project could expand the Lewis & Clark Regional Water System in Iowa, Minnesota, and South Dakota. The study would look at whether the project is technically and financially workable and whether it should be built. Federal costs for the study could not exceed $10 million, and the authority would end 5 years after the bill becomes law.

US-119-S3736.s: The bill would direct the Secretary of the Interior to study whether a water project could be built to serve municipal, rural, and industrial water needs in parts of South Dakota, Iowa, Nebraska, and Minnesota. It would require a report on whether the project is technically and financially workable and what share of construction costs the non-Federal side should pay. Up to $10 million in federal funds could be used for the study, and the authority would end 5 years after enactment.

US-119-S3791.s: The bill would extend Regional Ocean Partnerships and update the rules for how they work. It would set funding levels for fiscal years 2028 through 2031 and change reporting and wording in the law. It would also bar these partnerships from using funds to develop regulatory proposals, model regulations, or compliance programs.

US-119-S3798.s: The bill would create new federal crimes for robbing or trying to rob someone at an ATM, including stand-alone ATMs. It would also make it a crime to tamper with, damage, steal, or handle money or property taken from an ATM. These rules would apply to ATMs tied to banks, credit unions, and savings and loan groups, and the bill would set higher prison terms for cases with a weapon, forced movement, or a killing.

US-119-S3885.s: The bill would require the FAA to update how it handles type certification, which is the approval process for aircraft and related parts. It would set out plans for clearer issue papers, standard time ranges for some steps, and updated guidance on when the FAA can delegate work. It would also require FAA reports to Congress and ask the agency to consult with industry, airport and vertiport groups, and FAA staff groups.

US-119-S3897.s: The bill would change how claims are handled under the Public Safety Officers' Benefits program, which gives death, disability, and education benefits to public safety officers and their survivors. It would require the Justice Department to flag missing claim information within 90 days and usually decide on a completed claim within 270 days. It would also expand claims help, public outreach, reporting, and yearly audits for claims that have been pending more than one year.

US-119-S3923.s: The bill would update and extend NOAA weather research programs and support better weather forecasts, warnings, and prediction tools. It also would expand private business opportunities for providing weather data. The bill includes new spending plans for weather research programs for fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

US-119-S3929.s: The bill would require the Federal Aviation Administration to buy and install certified airborne position reference tools at certain contract air traffic control towers within 1 year after enactment. It would also require the agency to buy or maintain other air traffic awareness systems at towers that do not already have them, and to set up training for tower workers. The bill would also allow reimbursement for some systems that were bought and installed before these new rules took effect.

US-119-S3971.s: The law reauthorizes and changes the Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer programs through fiscal year 2031. It adds more checks on security risks for small businesses that apply, requires agencies to give a reason if they deny an award for security reasons, and sets limits on how many proposals a business may submit each year. It also expands training for federal staff and creates extra Phase II awards in key technology areas for small businesses that meet the matching-funds rules.

US-119-S3984.s: This bill would extend the authorization for the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom for 2 years. It would also change the funding authorization period to 2026 through 2028 and extend the commission’s authorization date to December 31, 2028. It affects the commission and the law that governs it.

US-119-S4116.s: The bill would create a new program to help fund geothermal power demo projects in places that do not yet have much geothermal electricity. It would direct the Energy Secretary to set up a competitive program within 180 days to support projects in low-permeability and impermeable rock, with a focus on new regions, public data, and projects that could reach at least 30 megawatts. It also would authorize whatever money is needed to carry out the program.

US-119-S4138.s: The law lets Captain Cody Khork of the Army be given an honorary promotion after death to major without the usual 60-day notice to Congress. It affects this one Army promotion and became Public Law 119-80 on March 20, 2026.

US-119-S423.s: The law requires the Department of Veterans Affairs to give Congress quarterly budget briefings and explain any budget shortfalls and plans to fix them. It also limits certain pay bonuses for some senior VA employees and requires yearly reports to Congress on those bonuses. In addition, it creates a Veterans Experience Office through FY2028 to help improve how veterans and beneficiaries use VA services, and it directs the Government Accountability Office to study that work.

US-119-S4239.s: The bill would require the Secretary of the Interior to send Congress and post online a yearly report on how offshore oil and gas wells, platforms, and pipelines are being taken out of service. The report would cover how many decommissioning applications were filed and received, how many sites missed the required deadline, how much pipeline was left in place or removed, and the status of related enforcement actions. It would affect the Interior Department and offshore oil and gas operators.

US-119-S4406.s: The bill would update federal geothermal energy rules to support research, testing, and commercial use of next-generation geothermal systems, including enhanced and closed-loop systems. It would add new definitions, expand data sharing and mapping for geothermal projects, and call for deeper drilling data and public data updates. It would also create grant programs, a center of excellence, and a report on water use, and it would require at least one FORGE site to be able to test next-generation geothermal systems in supercritical conditions within 1 year after enactment.

US-119-S4429.s: This bill would prohibit the importation, manufacture, sale, resale, or interstate sale of connected vehicles and related software and hardware tied to foreign adversaries. It would apply to connected vehicles from covered countries, vehicles designed in a covered country, and vehicles made by certain companies with significant ownership or control from covered countries. It would also ban covered software and, later, connected vehicle hardware from covered countries, with limited exceptions for repair, warranty, and testing and evaluation.

US-119-S4448.s: The bill would require the Commerce Department to make public tracking tools for broadband grant progress and for permit steps tied to those grants. It would also require help for federal agencies to track and report delays in processing communications use applications, with new data controls and alerts set within 90 days after enactment. The bill would also change a broadband project cost rule so a project with broadband infrastructure and a likely total investment of more than $5 million can count as a minimum-cost project under the FAST Act.

US-119-S4465.s: This law extends certain foreign surveillance powers in Title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act until June 12, 2026. Those powers cover electronic spying and other ways to collect foreign intelligence about targets outside the United States, including Section 702. It may also affect U.S. persons if their communications are collected by chance and later searched under certain rules.

US-119-S4530.s: This law lets the Capitol Police Board raise the mandatory retirement age for a Capitol Police member to as high as 62, if the board says it is in the public interest. It also lets the board set a waiver retirement age anywhere from 57 to 62. It affects members of the Capitol Police and became law on May 29, 2026.

US-119-S4570.s: The bill would be about encouraging foreign government partners to buy United States-origin cyber and digital technologies. It says the goal is to streamline and sustain those purchases, but the detailed program sections in the bill text are struck out.

US-119-S4573.s: The bill would name the Great Lakes Commission as a Regional Great Lakes Partnership. It would affect the commission and the eight states it includes: Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin, New York, Ohio, and Pennsylvania.

US-119-S4605.s: This bill would change the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970 to let the Department of the Interior require applicants for, or holders of, geothermal leases to pay back certain reasonable costs. Those costs include processing lease-related applications and inspecting and monitoring geothermal exploration, wells, and related sites and facilities. The Secretary of the Interior could reduce the amount if full reimbursement would cause hardship or if a lower amount would help promote the greatest use of geothermal resources. The bill would also require a report on the changes and their effects on the Bureau of Land Management's geothermal program.

US-119-S4618.s: The bill would direct the Education Department to give grants to states, which would then pass money to local school districts. The money would help high-need public elementary and secondary schools add more school-based mental health staff. It would affect states, local school agencies, and students in those schools.
US-119-S4618.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-05-21)

US-119-S4632.s: The bill would provide temporary funding to keep federal programs, projects, and activities going if a new budget is not in place at the start of the fiscal year. It would use the prior year's funding rate and would also limit official travel, recesses or adjournments, and work on bills not tied to spending after the fiscal year begins if the budget process is not finished. It affects federal agencies and Congress.
US-119-S4632.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-05-21)

US-119-S4659.s: The bill would give the Election Assistance Commission $20 million more for election security grants. States could get this money if they got a 2026 election security grant and sign an agreement to share their full voter registration list with the Department of Homeland Security at least every three months after September 30, 2026. The extra payment to each state could not be more than 10% of what it got from the 2026 grant program.

US-119-S4660.s: The bill would give the Agriculture Secretary $5 billion for fiscal year 2027 to make payments to specialty crop producers. Specialty crops are crops covered under the existing federal definition for specialty crops. The payments would follow the terms in an Agriculture Department notice from January 8, 2025, and could also be made through a similar later aid program.

US-119-S4661.s: This bill would create a permanent aid program for growers of specialty crops, like fruits, vegetables, and nuts, when their crops are hurt by an adverse event, including an economic crisis or market disruption. The U.S. Agriculture Secretary would set the program rules and calculate payments based on past specialty crop sales and a payment factor for losses. It would also set payment limits, and some farming-based businesses could receive at least $500,000 as a maximum amount.

US-119-S4662.s: The bill would change tax rules for very high-income and high-asset people, trusts, and some estates. For people who meet the bill’s tests, certain loans and long leases would be treated like a sale, which could trigger tax on gains. It sets income and asset thresholds, including more than $100 million in yearly income or more than $1 billion in covered assets, with lower amounts for some married filers.

US-119-S4671.s: The bill would change the penalties for stealing a firearm from a licensed gun importer, maker, or dealer, or from their business place. It would raise the top prison term from 10 years to 20 years. If the theft happens during a burglary or robbery, it would set a required prison term of 3 or 5 years, and attempts would face the same penalties.
US-119-S4671.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-06-03)

US-119-S4691.s: This bill would direct the Federal Communications Commission to review how it notifies people when DIRS is activated or deactivated. It would also have the Commission study ways to improve its public safety liaison functions during disasters and emergencies. In addition, it would require the Commission to create plain-language materials for State, local, Tribal, and territorial emergency management and public safety authorities about Federal communications and emergency coordination mechanisms.

US-119-S4715.s: The bill would set fitness-to-operate rules for offshore oil and gas operators on the outer continental shelf. Before a lease, easement, or right-of-way could be issued, extended, or transferred, the company would have to meet standards tied to past law compliance, financial strength, safety, and cleanup duties. It would also require decommissioning escrow accounts and direct the Interior Department to review compliance each year and report to Congress.

US-119-S4767.s: This bill would extend the federal authorization for the African American Civil Rights Network. It would change the current 7-year time limit to 10 years after this bill becomes law. The change would affect the network itself and the programs or groups connected to it.

US-119-S4784.s: This bill would set defense and national security policy and funding rules for fiscal year 2027. It would cover Defense Department programs, military construction, and some Energy Department security programs. It would also set troop levels, authorize some weapons and ship buys, and address military pay, health care, cyber work, and some defense industry materials.
US-119-S4784.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to Senate, 2026-06-15)

US-119-S4830.s: This bill would rename the U.S. Postal Service facility at 86-014 Farrington Highway in Waianae, Hawaii, as the "United States Representative Colleen Hanabusa Post Office Building." It would also make any reference in U.S. laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records to that facility mean the new name.

US-119-S4845.s: The bill would require Congress to approve, before any deployment, the use of troops or armed men, including federal law enforcement officers, at polling places when they are sent to repel armed enemies of the United States. It would also set up a fast notice and review process for Congress and limit federal money for using troops or armed men to access certain election records. The changes to the Civil Rights Act of 1960 would end on January 20, 2029.

US-119-S4846.s: This bill would amend the United States-Mexico Transboundary Aquifer Assessment Act to reauthorize the transboundary aquifer assessment program. It would update which transboundary aquifers can be given priority, including aquifers in New Mexico, Texas, and Arizona, with one Arizona-Sonora aquifer excluded. It would also change the authorization of appropriations to cover fiscal years 2026 through 2036 and update the law’s sunset language.

US-119-S4865.s: The bill would stop government agencies and insurance providers from denying community-based services to people with disabilities who need long-term support to live on their own in the community. It would bar rules like strict eligibility limits, service caps, and waiting lists, and it would require people to be told about community options before being placed in an institution. The Department of Justice would have to write rules, and people could sue if these rights are violated.
US-119-S4865.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-06-23)

US-119-S4900.s: This bill would reauthorize the North Korean Human Rights Act of 2004 and extend several related programs and reporting requirements through 2030. It would also change some references to the United States Agency for Global Media, require a report on appointing a Special Envoy if the office is vacant, and direct the State Department to share resettlement information for eligible North Korean refugees. The bill would add sanctions authority for people who knowingly force the repatriation of North Korean refugees to North Korea and would require a report on humanitarian exemptions to North Korea sanctions.

US-119-S4901.s: The bill would make it a federal crime to knowingly carry out, or try to carry out, a plan to cheat someone out of veterans' benefits, or to do so when getting benefits for a veteran. A person who breaks this rule could face a fine, up to five years in prison, or both.
US-119-S4901.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-06-24)

US-119-S4908.s: The bill would tell the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to review fuel economy rules if gas prices rise much faster than overall inflation over a 180-day period. It would also raise the fuel economy penalty amounts in federal law from $0 to $25 and $50. This would affect the agency and car makers that must meet those standards.

US-119-S4914.s: The bill would expand the Green Ribbon Schools program at the Education Department, which recognizes schools and other learning centers for cutting environmental impact, improving health and wellness, and teaching about sustainability. It would set aside money for the Interior Department to work with schools run by the Bureau of Indian Education, give grants to state education agencies to support green schools, and provide a cash award to winners if money is approved. It would also create a similar award program for libraries, museums, zoos, and other non-school learning places, and set up a new office in the Education Department focused on school buildings and sustainability.
US-119-S4914.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-06-24)

US-119-S4919.s: This bill would amend federal wage laws to prevent wage theft and help workers recover stolen wages. It would require certain employers to give new workers written or digital disclosures, regular paystubs, and final payments, and to update workers when pay information changes. It would also create tools and grants to help enforce wage and hour laws and address violations.

US-119-S4928.s: The bill would let an employee take one one-time withdrawal of unused money from a commuter benefit account, if the account was set up through a pay cut agreement. The money could be taken out without rules on how it is used, but only within a set time and only up to the highest balance the account had from March 13, 2020, through December 31, 2023. The withdrawn amount would count as income for federal tax purposes.
US-119-S4928.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-06-24)

US-119-S4950.s:
The bill would codify the Institute for Telecommunication Sciences as a test center under the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information. ITS would study radio frequency emissions, spectrum propagation, and ways to share spectrum between federal and non-federal users, and it could enter into certain agreements to do that work.

The bill would also require an initiative to support emergency communication and tracking technologies for locating trapped individuals in confined spaces and other shielded environments. The Assistant Secretary would work with private sector entities and federal agencies, do a needs assessment, and submit a report to Congress.

US-119-S4961.s: This bill would direct the Secretary of Labor to award competitive grants for pre-apprenticeship programs in the building and construction trades. The programs would serve underrepresented populations, including people from low-income and rural census tracts. Eligible groups would be nonprofit partnerships with industry and labor participation, and the grants could pay for training, curriculum development, participant assessments, enrollment, and related evaluations.

US-119-S4975.s: This bill would change geothermal law so a Federal drilling permit would not be required for certain geothermal exploration and production activities on non-Federal surface land when the United States owns less than half of the subsurface geothermal estate and the operator submits a State permit. Those activities would not be treated as a major Federal action under the National Environmental Policy Act, would not need additional Federal action, and could begin 30 days after the State permit is submitted. The bill would also block application to Indian lands or resources managed in trust for Indian Tribes, while leaving royalties to the United States unchanged.

US-119-S4979.s: The bill would set up a process to help keep the Social Security trust funds financially stable over the long term. It would have the Social Security Advisory Board gather public input, hold listening sessions, and send Congress a report with recommendations and draft bill language. It would also set deadlines for Congress to take up that language and for committees in both chambers to review it.

US-119-S4984.s: This bill would amend the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 on the use of subminimum wage for people with disabilities. It would change the rules so certain adults with disabilities can choose to accept employment with an entity, and it changes some counseling and documentation requirements. The changes would apply to employment on or after the date the bill becomes law.

US-119-S5.s: Public Law 119-1 requires Homeland Security to hold certain non-U.S. citizens who are in the U.S. without legal status and who have been arrested, charged, convicted, or admit to certain crimes like burglary, theft, assault on an officer, or crimes causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue the federal government over some immigration enforcement decisions or failures that harm the state or its people, including financial harm over $100. The law took effect when it was signed on January 29, 2025.

US-119-S5012.s: This bill would let the Secretary of Health and Human Services award grants for career support for internationally educated health care professionals. The grants would help eligible groups provide training, mentoring, licensing help, counseling, and other support to help these workers enter and stay in the health care workforce. The bill gives priority to projects that support recruitment and retention in communities with workforce gaps or in rural communities.

US-119-S5022.s: This bill would decriminalize and deschedule cannabis and direct the Attorney General to remove marihuana and tetrahydrocannabinols in cannabis from the controlled substances schedules. It would also require a review of some other tetrahydrocannabinols and cannabimimetic agents, and it includes provisions for expungement and reinvestment related to certain cannabis offenses. The bill would affect people with cannabis offenses, cannabis businesses, and federal agencies that regulate cannabis.

US-119-S5033.s: This bill would apply the Freedom of Information Act and the Privacy Act to the courts of the United States, with some limits. It would let people request certain court records, including attorney discipline records, complaints or investigations about judges or court personnel, meeting calendars and minutes, jury selection forms, performance reports, PACER audit or update plans, and annual reports to Congress. It would not apply to matters in ongoing cases or to information not held by the courts, and published information would have to be machine-readable.

US-119-S5039.s: The bill would extend until fiscal year 2037 the Bureau of Land Management’s power to collect fees for processing new oil and gas permit applications. Those fees go into the BLM Permit Processing Improvement Fund. It would affect people and companies that apply for new oil and gas permits on federal land.
US-119-S5039.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-07-21)

US-119-S5047.s: The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to set up a working group on the risks from artificial intelligence systems that interact with sensors, robots, and other physical systems. The group would include 12 to 20 members from industry, schools, research groups, and public-interest groups, and would study safety and security concerns and possible best practices. The agency would publish a public report within 540 days after the bill becomes law, with later updates allowed every 2 years.

US-119-S5074.s: This bill would amend the Federal Power Act to let certain interstate and offshore electric power transmission lines have their costs allocated through tariffs filed with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. It covers new transmission lines of national significance and upgrades or expansions that meet the bill’s capacity rules. The costs would be assigned to customers in the related transmission planning region or regions based on expected benefits.

US-119-S5075.s: This bill would expand the ban on foreign nationals’ contributions and spending on elections to cover certain foreign-controlled, foreign-influenced, and foreign-owned domestic business entities. It would require some business entities to file a certification after making election-related spending and give that certification to recipients. The bill would also apply the foreign money ban to state and local ballot initiatives and to disbursements to certain political committees, and it would set certification rules for corporate PACs.

US-119-S5098.s: This bill would direct the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to set up a way to share cyber safety tips, training, and other resources with elementary and secondary schools. It would also create a voluntary registry to track cyber incidents at school computer systems. The bill would require the agency to create a program to address cyber threats to school information systems.
US-119-S5098.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-07-23)

US-119-S5107.s: The bill would block people convicted of certain corruption-related crimes from being appointed to jobs in the federal executive branch. It covers crimes tied to work as a CEO of a public or private non-federal entity, including bribery, fraud, cybercrime, embezzlement, insider trading, wage theft, tax evasion, and similar state crimes. People already serving in the executive branch who would not qualify under this rule would have to be removed.

US-119-S5118.s: This bill would require the Secretary of the Interior to involve the public and State, Tribal, and local government officials before deciding whether to offer certain land for oil or gas leasing. It would require public disclosure of the leasing proposal, an analysis of expected effects on the land and other uses, and an opportunity for public comment. The Secretary would also have to consider input from the public, State and local governments, and government-to-government consultation with federally recognized Indian Tribes. Based on that process, the Secretary could decide not to offer the parcel for leasing.

US-119-S5159.s: The bill would change federal energy law to support microgrids, which are small power systems that can connect to or run apart from the main grid. It would ask states to consider rules for linking microgrids to the grid and for measuring the benefits of grid resilience, and it would set deadlines for states and some utilities to review those standards. It would also create a state-run grant program for microgrids, with $500 million set aside for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, and would let states use up to 10% of their share for admin costs.

US-119-S5167.s: This bill would require the Comptroller General to report to Congress on program areas and administrative practices that pose the greatest risk to the integrity of federal funds run by state and local governments. The report would look at vulnerabilities, waste, fraud, abuse, and improper payments, and it would cover federal, state, and local practices. It would also review best practices, available federal tools and assistance, and give recommendations to federal agencies and Congress.

US-119-S5175.s: The bill would change U.S. arms export rules for certain defense items sent to Ukraine. It would let some NATO and other partner governments buy and transfer specific weapons and munitions to Ukraine more quickly, if Ukraine agrees in writing not to pass them on without U.S. consent and takes delivery by December 31, 2030. The State Department could extend that deadline each year until December 31, 2035 if Russia is still invading Ukraine, and Congress would get notice before each transfer.

US-119-S5188.s: The bill would change federal boxing safety rules and add standards for unified boxing organizations, which are private groups that run boxing matches under one set of rules. It would require more medical checks, more ringside medical help, anti-doping testing, and support services for boxers under contract. It would also set contract rules, including at least $200 per round, limits on contract length, and rules for how often a boxer must be offered matches or paid.

US-119-S5202.s: This bill would prohibit the use of federal funds for research or publications about gender transition in people under 18. It would also block federally funded observational studies on hormonal treatments or surgical procedures on minors when the purpose is to affirm a minor's perception of sex or asserted identity if it is not the same as the minor's sex. The bill says sex is based only on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.

US-119-S5224.s: The bill would create an FAA task force to study and improve training for airport drivers who work in airport movement areas, like runways and taxiways, at commercial service airports. It would ask the group to look at better training methods, new technology, and barriers such as cost and workforce limits, and to send a report with its recommendations. It would also allow airport sponsors to get grants from fiscal years 2027 through 2031 for training systems and technology that help vehicle safety and awareness in these areas.

US-119-S5238.s: The bill would make a wide set of changes to federal government rules, including limits on how agencies can be reorganized and rules for independent inspectors general and civil service layoffs. It would also bar Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection from using biometric surveillance tools, and would add new limits and protections for noncitizen children in custody. Other parts would address election media made by AI, federal spending, ethics rules, and law enforcement at polls.

US-119-S5268.s: The bill would change federal overtime pay rules so covered workers would get two times their regular pay instead of one and one-half times for overtime hours. It would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act, the main federal wage law. The change would take effect 180 days after the bill became law.

US-119-S5279.s: The bill would designate November as National American History and Founders Month. It would ask the President and state, local, and territorial leaders to issue yearly proclamations calling for programs, ceremonies, and other activities that support civics education and history learning. It affects the public, schools, communities, and organizations that may take part in those observances.

US-119-S5289.s: This bill would make it unlawful to knowingly disrupt or impede a scheduled religious service within 100 feet of a house of worship during the hour before and after the service. It applies to conduct that substantially affects interstate commerce and does not turn on the content of speech. People harmed by a violation, as well as the Attorney General and a State attorney general, could bring civil actions, and the bill sets civil fines for violations.

US-119-S5304.s: The bill would change federal wage rules for farm workers. It would add overtime pay for agricultural workers after set weekly hour limits, starting at 55 hours and moving down to 40 hours over time, with slower timing for employers with 25 or fewer workers. It would also remove some farm-work pay exemptions and update related farm labor rules.

US-119-S5308.s: This bill would designate Afghanistan for temporary protected status under immigration law. It would let nationals of Afghanistan apply for temporary protected status and related work authorization, and the Secretary of Homeland Security would have to process those applications. It also allows some recipients to get permission for brief travel abroad and to apply for a fee waiver.

US-119-S5323.s: The bill would give the U.S. Chancery building in Pristina, Kosovo, a new name: the "Eliot L. Engel Building." It would also treat any U.S. law, map, rule, or record that names that building as referring to the new name. This affects U.S. government references to that building.

US-119-S5335.s: This bill would add new rules for Federal financial institutions regulatory agencies when they examine financial institutions. It would set deadlines for finishing examinations, sending final reports, and holding exit interviews, and it would let a financial institution ask for an appendix listing the information used for a material supervisory determination. It would also require agencies to create a process for written advice on certain actions, and it would establish an Office of Independent Examination Review to handle complaints, review examination practices, and carry out supervisory appeals.

US-119-S5360.s: This bill would reauthorize a program for rural and municipal utility cybersecurity. It would require the Secretary to keep a program that gives technical assistance and funding to eligible electric utilities and related entities to help them protect against, detect, respond to, and recover from cybersecurity threats. The bill also says information shared under the program is exempt from public disclosure laws. It would authorize $250,000,000 for fiscal years 2027 through 2031.

US-119-S5384.s: The bill would change federal wage law so the standard workweek drops from 40 hours to 32 hours. It would also require overtime pay for hours worked above 32 in a week, with a step-down period that moves from 38 hours to 36, then 34, then 32 hours over three years after the law takes effect. It would also limit pay or benefit cuts for workers covered by the change and add rules for workdays over 8 hours.

US-119-S5390.s: The bill would end certain import duties tied to forced-labor import cases, a balance-of-payments rule, and a rule for duties used against discrimination by foreign countries. It would also require U.S. Customs and Border Protection to automatically refund those duties, with interest, to importers within 30 days after enactment. Small businesses would be given priority for refunds when possible.

US-119-S5399.s: The bill would bar federal, state, foreign, or private money from being used to install permanent fencing around the White House complex after it becomes law. It would still allow repair or replacement of fencing that was already there when the law took effect.

US-119-S5400.s: The bill would direct the State Department to work with other countries to stop China, North Korea, Russia, Iran, and other foreign adversaries from getting key semiconductor technology.
