It would push partner countries to line up export controls on chip-making tools and to add limits on design tools, tech transfers, equipment service, and technical help. The State Department would also review how well partner countries follow these steps, take certain follow-up actions if they do not, and report to Congress every 90 days.
US-119-S5400.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-09-15)

US-119-S5403.s: This bill would create grants to help cover the part of college costs that students still owe at certain schools. It would affect students at in-state public colleges, as well as students at historically Black colleges and universities and other minority-serving schools. It would also make some Dreamer students, who came to the U.S. before age 16 and meet other school rules, eligible for federal student aid.
US-119-S5403.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-09-15)

US-119-S5420.s: The bill would raise the tax credit limit for qualified elementary and secondary education scholarships for married couples who file a joint return. It would change the rule to allow 200% of the current amount for those joint returns. The change would apply to tax years starting after December 31, 2025.

US-119-S5441.s: The bill would make many changes to how the IRS handles taxes, help, and disputes. It would expand online filing, require the IRS to digitize paper returns and letters, and add new tools for taxpayers, including call wait time updates and more notice rules. It would also expand Tax Court powers, set rules for paid tax return preparers, and add new steps for people facing tax problems, including some U.S. nationals held abroad and taxpayers with money hardship.
US-119-S5441.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Reported to Senate, 2026-09-17)

US-119-S5460.s: The bill would raise the federal payment rate for school lunches and breakfasts. Starting October 1, 2026, it would add 45 cents for each lunch served in the National School Lunch Program and 28 cents for each breakfast served in the School Breakfast Program. Those amounts would be adjusted each year for inflation starting July 1, 2027, affecting schools that serve these meals.
US-119-S5460.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-09-23)

US-119-S5462.s: The bill would extend the Frontier Community Health Integration Project Demonstration from a 5-year period to a 10-year period. It affects this Medicare-related health care demo program for frontier communities. The change would take effect on December 31, 2026.

US-119-S5463.s: The bill would ask the President to name one month each year as National American History and Founders Month. It would also ask state, local, and territorial leaders to issue their own proclamations and encourage people to mark the month with programs, ceremonies, and other activities that support civics education and history learning.

US-119-S5470.s: This bill would prohibit corporal punishment of students in schools that receive federal financial assistance. It would let a student or parent sue if corporal punishment is used, and it would let the Attorney General and the Department of Education enforce the ban. State education agencies would have to notify schools and parents about the requirements and provide a school climate report.

US-119-S5475.s: The bill would set deadlines for Medicare contractors to review requests for local coverage decisions and reconsideration requests. It would require them to say within 60 days whether a request is complete, and to act on complete requests within 1 year. It would also add public posting, comment, and meeting steps for some coverage decisions, and let interested parties ask the Secretary of Health and Human Services to review a contractor’s final decision.

US-119-S5476.s: The bill would require sanctions on some foreign people and groups linked to Israeli settlement construction in the E1 area of the West Bank. It covers people who help plan, fund, build, or move civilians to those settlements, and it lets the President also sanction others who support them. The sanctions would start 30 days after the bill becomes law and would end 7 years later.

US-119-S5481.s: The bill would expand voting access for young people in federal elections. It would address voter registration at public colleges, allow minors to pre-register, support on-campus polling places, and set rules on residency proof, voter ID, absentee voting, and ballot use. It would also let states get grants for youth voting outreach and require studies and data collection.

US-119-S5485.s: The bill would change immigration law to add new rules for employers who seek to hire certain immigrants. It would require employers to show they tried to hire U.S. workers first, did not lay off U.S. workers, and would pay the promised wage for 3 years. It would also let the Labor Secretary investigate complaints and impose fines, job-related remedies, and, for repeated patterns of noncompliance, criminal penalties.

US-119-S5487.s: This bill would require the Transportation Security Administration to develop guidelines for the Transportation Worker Identification Credential program. The guidelines would focus on improving access for returning citizens, helping incarcerated people pre-apply or prepare applications, and helping people request an appeal or waiver of preliminary ineligibility decisions. The Administrator would also brief two congressional committees on how the guidelines are being put into effect.

US-119-S5497.s: This bill would change veterans law to let the Secretary of Veterans Affairs reimburse certain State homes for costly medications, or provide those medications directly to the homes. It would apply to State homes that give nursing home care to veterans. The bill defines a costly medication based on its average wholesale price and a transaction fee compared with the payment the Secretary makes for that veteran's care.

US-119-S5498.s: The bill would add alpha-gal, a molecule tied to a tick-bite allergy, to the list of major food allergens. Food labels would then have to identify it when it is in a food product.
US-119-S5498.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-09-24)

US-119-S550.s: The law lets the U.S. Court of Federal Claims hear one land claim by the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma about land in Illinois under the Treaty of Grouseland. The court must decide the claim without using time-limit or delay defenses, and the claim must be filed within one year. It also ends other present and future land claims by the tribe in Illinois.
US-119-S550.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-02-12)

US-119-S5508.s: The bill would create a public-private working group within the National Telecommunications and Information Administration to develop cybersecurity best practices for telecommunications carriers and related supply chain companies. It would also set up a process for third-party assessors to certify use of those practices and require the group to share guidance and other materials. The best practices would be voluntary and focused on finding, stopping, reducing, and fixing cyber risks in the telecom sector.

US-119-S5512.s: The bill would make some private investment funds responsible for certain debts and liabilities of companies they buy and control. It would also add rules on worker pay, bankruptcy priorities, taxes, investor disclosures, and risky debt deals for the funds and the companies they affect.

US-119-S5514.s: The bill would require the Interior Secretary to make rules for regional plans to manage double-crested cormorants, a kind of bird. The plans would guide when and how the birds can be taken, who may do it, and steps to protect other wildlife, water quality, and human safety. The department would also have to survey the bird population every 5 years, update the plans every 5 years, and report on hunting licenses within 90 days after enactment. The act would end on January 1, 2034.

US-119-S5515.s: The bill would expand federal health programs for pregnant and postpartum women, with a focus on underserved communities. It would require Medicaid and CHIP to cover women for 12 months after birth and to cover dental care during pregnancy and after birth, and it would allow two years of postpartum WIC coverage. It would also create grants for state groups, mobile obstetric care units, doula training, and centers that teach bias-aware and culturally aware care, while raising federal tobacco taxes.
US-119-S5515.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-09-24)

US-119-S5520.s: The bill would require a national, computer-readable framework for cancer screening recommendations, based on age, sex, and other risk factors. It would also require health information technology certified by the federal government to use that framework so it can help show a patient's cancer screening status. The Health and Human Services Department would issue guidance to encourage some health plans to use this technology, and a federal research institute could support related research and pilot projects.

US-119-S5522.s: The bill would direct the Department of Homeland Security’s cybersecurity agency to protect genetic data and other sensitive biometric data. It would treat some genetic data systems as critical infrastructure and require training, planning, and coordination for federal workers who handle them. It would also call for work with biotechnology industry groups and other stakeholders on security rules and incident reporting.

US-119-S5526.s: This bill would update and continue many Agriculture Department programs through fiscal year 2031. It covers farm support, conservation, trade, nutrition aid, rural development, farm credit, and research programs. It would affect farmers, ranchers, rural communities, food aid programs, and people who use nutrition assistance.

US-119-S5531.s: The bill would add a federal tax on certain digital ad revenue from social media platforms that use personalized recommendations. It would also create a Social Capital Fund in the Treasury and use the tax money for grants through the Housing and Urban Development Department. Some of those grants would go to local governments, nonprofits, religious or civic groups, and Indian tribes.

US-119-S5533.s: The bill would change federal tax rules so AmeriCorps education awards would not count as taxable income. It would affect people who receive these national service education awards, including payments tied to student loan debt under the program. The change would apply to tax years ending after the date the bill becomes law.

US-119-S5540.s: The bill would make permanent and revise several grant programs that help prepare teachers and school leaders for elementary and secondary schools. It would expand support for recruiting well-prepared people, including people from underrepresented groups, and for training school leaders, with added focus on shortages in rural areas and in areas like special education and English language instruction. It would also keep grant support for teacher preparation at minority-serving schools and for science and engineering education at predominantly minority colleges and universities.
US-119-S5540.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-09-24)

US-119-S5541.s: The bill would create the Cybersecurity and AI Board of Investigations, an independent group to review major cyber incidents, near-misses, and broad security risks. It would also set up a voluntary, private reporting system for people and groups to report close calls in critical infrastructure sectors, such as communications, commerce, and public data systems. The board would start 90 days after the law is enacted and would include 5 members chosen for cybersecurity knowledge.

US-119-S5544.s: The bill would bar federal agencies and federal workers from using biometric surveillance, which includes facial recognition and similar tools, unless Congress clearly allows it in a later law. It would also block certain federal public safety grants to state and local governments that use those systems, starting with the first fiscal year after the bill becomes law. It would affect federal agencies, federal workers, and state and local governments that receive Byrne grants.

US-119-S5547.s: This bill would let the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children share information with the Department of State and the Department of Homeland Security. The information could be used for screening and vetting. It would change the list of agencies allowed to receive these disclosures.

US-119-S5551.s: The bill would require certain Foreign Service officers to take training on critical minerals, energy supply chains, and related security risks. It would apply to officers in economic roles, especially those sent to posts where these issues are a main part of the job or where mineral supply chains matter a lot. It also says there should be a Special Advisor to the President for Critical Minerals and Supply Chains to help coordinate work across agencies and serve as a link to Congress and industry.

US-119-S5552.s: The bill would create a federal business tax credit for part of the pay for services tied to certain film and TV productions made in the United States. It would apply to qualified feature films, TV pilots, and TV seasons that meet set cost and filming rules, and it would not cover some shows like news, live sports, or content made mainly for social media. The credit would start at 20% and could rise to 30% if certain added conditions are met. The credit could also be sold to an unrelated buyer for cash.
US-119-S5552.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-09-24)

US-119-S5554.s: The bill would expand federal work on ovarian cancer awareness, genetic risk checks, genetic counseling and testing, and access to specialty care. It would require many health plans to cover certain genetic testing, early detection, and risk-reducing care for people with ovarian cancer, endometrial cancer, or a strong family history of hereditary cancer. It would also create grant programs for outreach and rural care, and it sets aside $20 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2031 for some of these efforts.

US-119-S5556.s: The bill would require U.S.-funded construction and renovation projects in Ukraine to meet accessibility standards for people with disabilities, similar to U.S. rules under the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Architectural Barriers Act. It would cover projects funded through U.S. agencies and funds named in the bill, with some exceptions for normal upkeep and temporary emergency work. The Secretary of State could waive the rule in the national interest, and the bill would also create an accessibility working group and require yearly reports to Congress.

US-119-S5557.s: The bill would create a National Institute of Standards and Technology program for measurement research in engineering biology, biomanufacturing, and biotechnology. It would also direct NIST to support technical standards, data tools, training, partnerships, and research facilities in these fields. The bill would require plans and reports on the program after it is enacted.

US-119-S5572.s: The bill would give the Federal Aviation Administration and the Transportation Department new money for airport and air traffic control projects in fiscal year 2027. It would create a grant program for up to 3 older medium hub airports to update or rebuild main terminal buildings, with up to 90% of project costs covered by federal funds, and it sets aside $10 billion for that program. It also provides money for air traffic control upgrades, airport terminal work, and other airport grants, including $7.2 billion for a common automation system and $5 billion for terminal development projects.

US-119-S5575.s: The bill would add criminal penalties for giving or taking gratuities, meaning gifts or favors, tied to state, local, or Indian tribal public officials. It would cover conduct linked to a business or transaction worth $5,000 or more. A person found guilty could be fined, jailed for up to 2 years, or both.

US-119-S5576.s: The bill would create the Artificial Intelligence Safety Board within the Commerce Department to address risks from artificial intelligence. It would include federal officials and outside experts, and it would set rules for meetings, member terms, classified information, and conflict-of-interest checks. It also says the board could work with foreign partners on testing, guidance, information sharing, and common evaluation methods for advanced AI systems.

US-119-S5577.s: The bill would let the EPA give grants to Hawaii or a local wastewater group to help households upgrade or convert small cesspools. The money could pay for septic systems, hookups to a treatment plant, larger community systems, and some training and education on wastewater management. It would cover 75% of costs, with up to $20 million a year authorized for fiscal years 2028 through 2032.

US-119-S5579.s: The bill would create a grant program for colleges and other eligible schools to analyze, digitize, and map old records about housing discrimination in at least one local area. It would also direct the Department of Housing and Urban Development to set data rules and build a free public national database from the project data. The bill authorizes $5 million each year from fiscal years 2027 through 2036 for grants, plus $750,000 each year for other program costs.

US-119-S5580.s: The bill would create a competitive grant program for public housing agencies to install automatic sprinkler systems in certain public housing projects. It would also require the Housing and Urban Development Secretary to report on whether public housing has sprinkler systems and to give Congress a report within 3 years after enactment. The bill authorizes $25 million each year from fiscal years 2027 through 2036 for this program.

US-119-S5582.s: The bill would extend and revise a Education Department grant program for student veteran centers through fiscal year 2034. It would require grants to colleges and college groups to start, run, improve, or keep these centers open. The centers would give veterans and service members a campus space and a single office for help with student services.
US-119-S5582.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-09-29)

US-119-S5586.s: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Secretary to survey drug prices at non-retail pharmacies, such as mail-order and specialty pharmacies, for Medicaid pricing. It would also require states to have those pharmacies respond to the surveys, make the pricing data public, and let the government use civil money penalties for noncompliance. The bill sets aside $5 million for the HHS Inspector General in fiscal year 2027 and says the changes would take effect 18 months after enactment, on the first day of the next quarter.

US-119-S5587.s: The bill would create a National Critical Minerals Council in the White House to help develop and carry out a U.S. plan for critical minerals and materials. It would bring together federal agencies to coordinate policy, track supply chain risks, support domestic sourcing, and improve sharing of project and funding data. It would also require a report to Congress within 1 year and later briefings on progress.

US-119-S5588.s: The bill would require the Secretary of the Army to issue a general permit for ecological restoration projects under the federal water pollution law within 1 year. It would set rules for when these projects can use the permit, including some limits on roads, trails, and certain chemicals. The bill would affect people and groups planning ecological restoration work in waters of the United States.

US-119-S5589.s: The bill would bar U.S. foreign aid, loan guarantees, and debt relief to the Palestinian Authority, Hamas, and other Palestinian governing bodies in the West Bank and Gaza unless the President certifies certain conditions to Congress. It would also require the State Department to send Congress a report on human rights practices and on U.S. aid tied to these entities. The rules would also cover international groups that give aid to them.

US-119-S5590.s: This bill would require the Secretary of Defense to make a plan for finding and fixing certain equipment and computer facilities in the U.S. electric grid that are owned or controlled by a foreign adversary. The plan would look at risks to military bases, defense missions, and grid reliability, and it would be sent to congressional defense committees within 180 days after enactment. It would also require yearly budget estimates starting with the fiscal year 2028 budget cycle.

US-119-S5592.s: The bill would set up a federal loan program for first-time homebuyers. The Housing and Urban Development secretary could make loans for people buying a one-family home, some manufactured homes, and certain lots tied to those homes. To qualify, a buyer would need to be a first-time homebuyer, have a Homeownership Promise Account, finish housing counseling, and have a credit score of at least 500.

US-119-S5594.s: This bill would create the Data Protection Agency to enforce federal privacy law and oversee data protection rules. It would set limits on certain data practices by data aggregators, including some uses of automated decision systems, biometric information, and precise geolocation. It would affect people and organizations that collect, use, or share personal data in interstate commerce.

US-119-S5595.s: The bill would let the President send certain old or extra U.S. defense and aid items to Taiwan for use as reserve stock. The items include humanitarian and medical supplies, armor, artillery, ammunition, missiles, and other munitions kept in a Taiwan stockpile. It would also require advance notice to Congress and later reports on what was sent, what was received in return, and when items will be delivered.

US-119-S5601.s: The bill would require the Defense Secretary to set reporting rules for large artificial intelligence contractors that do work for the Defense Department. These contractors would have to report security practices, known or suspected AI security incidents, and certain high-risk events, with some updates every 90 days and urgent notice within 72 hours. It would also direct the Defense Secretary to issue voluntary guidance to help these contractors reduce insider threat and other people-related security risks, with an update to that guidance within 1 year.

US-119-S5603.s: The bill would bar the demolition of memorials to honor a U.S. president if Congress had named them by law, unless Congress later gives approval. It would affect federal presidential memorials and any group or agency that wants to tear one down. It defines demolition as intentionally destroying all or a large part of a building or structure.

US-119-S5604.s: The bill would change the Endangered Species Act by setting clearer standards for how the Fish and Wildlife Service considers conservation steps before listing a species as threatened or endangered. It would also require more detail on species status and recovery plans, add rules for how voluntary conservation actions are considered when removing a species from the list, and expand online tools to speed up agency consultations. The measure would affect the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, other agencies that work under the act, and states, landowners, and others involved in species conservation.

US-119-S5607.s: The bill would change the Secure Rural Schools law to restore the full 75% payment to counties from the Oregon and California land-grant fund. It would also update the law’s wording and payment names for forest and Bureau of Land Management land. The bill would spell out more election options for counties and states on which payments to receive.

US-119-S5608.s: The bill would extend parts of the Secure Rural Schools law, which helps states and counties that contain federal land. It would push out the dates for secure payments, special projects on federal land, and the use of county funds, and it would also extend a pilot program for resource advisory committees. The bill also makes a few small wording fixes in that law.

US-119-S5610.s: The bill would bar patents, and the use of a fast-track patent review, for people or groups named on certain U.S. lists tied to Chinese military or security risks, and it would make any patent they already have unenforceable while they remain on those lists. It would also let the President waive the ban for up to 180 days at a time with a report to Congress. The bill would still let those people file patent applications, and it would not change who owns a patent or how long it lasts.

US-119-S5613.s: The bill would raise U.S. import duties on shrimp from Ecuador in stages from 2027 through 2029. It would also add a separate $0.10 per kilogram duty on shrimp imports, with that money used for shrimp and catfish inspections. In addition, it would change labeling rules so some cooked shrimp and cooked crawfish are not treated as processed foods under those rules.

US-119-S5615.s: This bill would change labor rules to say that certain employee stock awards called restricted stock units can be treated like other employer equity for overtime pay calculations. It would affect workers and employers that use these stock programs. The change would take effect 90 days after enactment, and some older stock grants would get limited protection from liability.

US-119-S5621.s: The bill would change rules for the Department of Homeland Security’s grant program for nonprofits. It would make clear that grant money could be used for onsite security staff, help with applying for and managing the grant, and hiring off-duty police officers, with the help for grant applications capped at 5% of the grant amount.

US-119-S5622.s: The bill would change the federal drug law so a person could face criminal liability if a controlled substance was a major cause of someone’s death or serious injury. It says a drug would count if it substantially contributed, even if other substances also played a major role. It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee.

US-119-S5623.s: The bill would state that Congress supports the U.S. policy of extended nuclear deterrence, which means using U.S. nuclear forces and other military power to help protect allies. It says this commitment helps deter attacks and support U.S. security interests, including for allies like South Korea, Japan, Australia, and NATO members. It also says the U.S. should keep its deterrent credible while also working on arms control and nuclear risk reduction talks.

US-119-S5624.s: The bill would give a one-time death payment to federal wildland firefighters who die from injuries tied to their job and in the line of duty. It would cover certain firefighters and some contractors who do fire suppression work for agencies like the Forest Service, Interior agencies, and state or local fire groups. The payment would go to eligible survivors and would apply to deaths on or after January 1, 2026.

US-119-S5627.s: The bill would require the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation to test a payment model that looks at social factors that affect health and health gaps. It would focus on minorities, underserved areas, and people at high risk. It would also tell the agency to take these factors into account when choosing, running, and reviewing other payment models.
US-119-S5627.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-09-30)

US-119-S5628.s: The bill would add new steps the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau must follow when it proposes a rule. It would require the bureau to explain why the rule is needed, review costs and benefits, look at other options, and say how the rule might affect small businesses, consumers, and state, local, and tribal governments. It would also require the bureau to include the assumptions, studies, and data behind its analysis.

US-119-S5632.s: The bill would bar the Archivist from closing certain federal records centers and archive facilities, and from putting unreasonable limits on public access to them. It would also stop rebuilding or changing those facilities if records would need to be moved for more than 180 days. The rule would apply to record centers and archive facilities that were already in place before the law takes effect.

US-119-S5633.s: The bill would reauthorize the Small Business Administration’s State Trade Expansion Program, which helps states support small businesses that want to sell abroad. It would change the grant process, including application timing, simpler forms, more public program information, and an annual survey of states that got grants. It would also set new rules for how grant money is divided among states, territories, and commonwealths, and limit how much a grant can drop from year to year.

US-119-S5637.s: The bill would create a State Department program to help the United States work with chosen countries and groups on new critical minerals technology. Critical minerals are materials used in things like energy systems, semiconductors, and defense. It would set rules for who can join, block work with countries of concern and their entities, and require notice to Congress before new partnerships start.

US-119-S5638.s: The bill would change the wage rule for certain exempt H-1B workers in the Immigration and Nationality Act. It would replace the current $60,000 minimum with a wage set at two times the national average wage index for the most recent year. This would affect H-1B workers and the employers who use that visa category.

US-119-S5639.s: The bill would create a cloud-based portal for appraisers and appraisal management companies to submit license, certification, and registration applications and renewals in one place. It would link state agencies to application details, fees, education records, and some background check information, while letting states still make their own licensing decisions. The Appraisal Subcommittee could charge a reasonable fee to cover the portal and related background checks, and it could give grants to states to connect their systems.

US-119-S5640.s: The bill would require federal agencies to report on how large data centers affect air and water quality, water use, and greenhouse gas emissions. It would also require reports on how much electricity data centers use, by state, and how that use may affect household energy bills and average home energy costs. These reports would be sent to Congress and posted online, and they would focus on data centers that use at least 50 megawatts a day.

US-119-S5641.s: The bill would change tax rules to make more places count as energy communities for some clean electricity tax credits when they have nuclear-related jobs. It would also let makers of distribution transformers and large power transformers get a production tax credit worth 10% of production costs. The transformer change would apply to components produced and sold 90 days after the bill becomes law.

US-119-S5642.s: This bill would require the Securities and Exchange Commission to write rules that add “CMC” to the ticker symbols of securities issued by companies on a list published by the Secretary of Defense. It would also require the modifier to be removed if an issuer is taken off that list. The change would affect issuers named on that list and their securities.

US-119-S5644.s: The bill would change federal banking rules so some cash reward payments by crime stopper groups would not have to be reported as currency transactions. It would affect nonprofit groups that give cash rewards for information about a crime.

US-119-S5645.s: The bill would direct the Energy Secretary to set up a Data Center Community Assistance Program within 180 days after enactment. It would give state, local, and Tribal governments plain-English help, data, and technical support on the energy, water, infrastructure, and economic effects of new data centers. It would also create a public toolkit for local officials and let the Secretary review a developer’s information if a government asks for help.

US-119-S5646.s: The bill would change the federal wage law to say that certain direct sellers and qualified real estate agents are not counted as employees. It would affect workers in those two groups under the Fair Labor Standards Act, which is the main federal law for pay and hours.

US-119-S5648.s: The bill would direct federal agencies to be open about when they use automated systems and AI to interact with the public or help make important decisions. It would require public lists of those systems, plain-language notices to people, a way to appeal adverse decisions, and guidance on privacy, civil rights, and public input. It would also set rules for chatbots and similar tools, including notice when someone is talking to an automated system and a way to reach a human worker.

US-119-S5649.s: The bill would make more federal land in Alaska available for selection under the Alaska Native Vietnam era veterans land allotment program. It would require the Interior Secretary to open certain wildlife refuge lands right away, and it would direct the Agriculture Secretary to identify more Forest Service land within one year. The changes would affect eligible Alaska Native Vietnam era veterans seeking land allotments.

US-119-S5650.s: The bill would change how the Strategic Petroleum Reserve is managed by repealing two federal rules that require some drawdowns or sales. It would also require the Energy Secretary to do a long-range review and send Congress a plan within 180 days after enactment. The bill would update reporting rules and make several technical changes to the law that governs the reserve.

US-119-S5651.s: The bill would create the National Institutes of Clean Energy as a new agency in the Department of Energy by January 1, 2030. It would fund clean energy and climate research, including projects on microgrids, energy storage, electric vehicles, and other advanced energy work, with priority for public colleges, land-grant schools, minority-serving schools, and areas with heavy job losses. It authorizes $400 billion for fiscal years 2027 through 2036 to set up and run the institutes.

US-119-S5652.s: The bill would direct the Housing and Urban Development secretary to accept certain paperwork made under a named process standard as enough proof that a housing-related funding recipient meets domestic content rules under the Build America, Buy America Act. It would apply to financial help handled by the Department of Housing and Urban Development. It would also let the secretary accept similar standards that give an auditable, checkable proof process.

US-119-S5653.s: This bill would change federal permitting rules for a wide range of projects. It would limit some environmental reviews, set deadlines for permits after reviews are done, and change permit rules under the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act. It would also change permitting for energy projects, including electric transmission, onshore oil and gas drilling on nonfederal land, renewable energy, geothermal, hydropower, and offshore energy projects.

US-119-S5654.s: The bill would block new oil and gas leasing, preleasing, production, and related work in the Eglin Gulf Test and Training Range. It would not change valid existing leases already in place when the change takes effect. The ban would end if the Secretary of War sends Congress a notice that the range is not of critical use.

US-119-S5656.s: The bill would create an FBI-run notice system for crime victims who register, so they can get alerts about certain firearm-related actions by the offender. It would also let legal guardians or other lawful representatives sign up for minors or incapacitated victims. The bill would set up a pilot program for states and tribes with victim notice systems to get reports about firearm check denials and status changes in some domestic violence cases.

US-119-S5658.s: The bill would ban building data centers on federal land. It would apply to national forest land and land managed by the Interior Department, with some Indian land excluded from that definition. Any later transfer of federal land would have to include a rule that the land goes back to the United States if it is used for a data center, unless Congress specifically allows that use.

US-119-S5659.s: The bill would create a competitive Education Department grant program for local school agencies and some partners to help each elementary and secondary school have at least one full-time reading or literacy specialist. It would fund hiring, training, retention, and other support for these specialists, with a focus on schools serving students who struggle with reading. Grant recipients would have to report each year on their progress and how the money was used.

US-119-S5660.s: The bill would direct the Education Department to give competitive grants to colleges and universities that set up academic counseling and other services for students who have survived sexual assault or other violence. It would affect eligible schools and the students who use these support services.
US-119-S5660.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-09-30)

US-119-S5662.s: The bill would tighten child labor rules under federal wage law, with a focus on children working in agriculture. It would raise some age limits, bar children under 18 from certain pesticide-handling jobs, and require reports to the Labor Department after serious injuries, serious illnesses, or deaths of workers under 18 in farm work. It would also increase civil fines and add possible jail time for some repeated or willful child labor violations.

US-119-S5663.s: The bill would create a National Science Foundation program that gives grants to colleges to repeat federally funded research. Schools could use the money for student tuition and stipends, materials, equipment, travel, and study costs tied to checking how repeatable the research is. It would also require reports to Congress on how many awards and students are supported and how the repeat studies compare with the original results.

US-119-S5664.s: The bill would create a Labor Department program to help workers who lost or were hurt by automation or artificial intelligence get career counseling, retraining, and other support. It would also require federal agencies to take certain steps when unemployment stays high, such as considering job effects for grants and loans and forming an emergency task force at higher levels. Some participants could get relocation help of up to $10,000 and monthly support payments.

US-119-S5666.s: The bill would require U.S. Customs and Border Protection to collect certain duties and interest on some solar cell imports that got duty-free treatment under a 2022-2024 solar tariff waiver. It applies to covered importers of crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells and modules that were entered during that period and are still under certain trade duty reviews. It would also require Customs to post a public list of importers who receive bills for these amounts, with payment status updates.

US-119-S5667.s: The bill would change immigration law to deny birthright citizenship to some people born in a U.S. territory. It would affect children born there when the mother is not lawfully present and the father is not a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident.

US-119-S5668.s: The bill would direct NASA to create a federal science plan for finding and measuring methane, using ground, air, and space tools. The plan would be due within 18 months after the law takes effect and would be sent to Congress. It would also guide future research and let state, local, academic, nonprofit, industry, and international groups use the data if they choose.

US-119-S5670.s: The bill would change rules on how federal budget money is set aside and used, so it has to be made available in time to be spent before it expires. It would bar delaying or holding back those funds in the last 90 days before they run out, including by adding conditions before the money can be used. It would also make the September 25, 2026 rescission proposal have no force or effect.

US-119-S5672.s: The bill would change how Medicare pays some doctors and clinics, especially those that provide primary care. It would create a temporary monthly payment model for services like care management, mental health support, office visits, telehealth, and phone calls for patients linked to a practice. It would also change a Medicare reward program by adding care efficiency measures and adjusting payment bonuses and cuts, and it would tie some yearly Medicare fee updates more closely to inflation.
US-119-S5672.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2026-09-30)

US-119-S5673.s: This bill would limit how car makers and other companies can collect, use, share, and sell consumer car data. It would require clear privacy notices, let people see certain data about them, and bar sharing or selling precise location data and most other car data without clear consent. It would also require companies to report their data practices to the Federal Trade Commission, which would then report to Congress and publish a summary.

US-119-S5674.s: This bill would bar people from making misleading recycled-content claims when they advertise, market, sell, or offer a product to consumers. It would also direct the Federal Trade Commission to update its green marketing guides and issue rules and guidance on when recycled-content claims are allowed, including the use of mass balance accounting under certain certification rules. The bill would apply federal rules to these claims and would let the FTC enforce them.

US-119-S5677.s: The bill would create the Lone Star Coastal National Recreation Area as part of the National Park System to protect and promote the natural, cultural, and recreation resources of the Upper and Middle Texas Gulf Coast. It would allow the Interior Secretary to work with Texas, local groups, landowners, and others to manage the area, use voluntary land deals, and set up a partnership and management plan. It also would let the federal government help fund some projects, with federal money matched by at least three non-federal dollars for every federal dollar.

US-119-S5681.s: The bill would change how the Federal Housing Finance Agency’s Inspector General pays for office expenses. It would let the Inspector General set those expenses on their own. This would affect the Inspector General of that agency.

US-119-S5682.s: The bill would change the foreign agents law so news outlets in the United States that are owned, run, or funded by a foreign government would generally have to register as foreign agents, unless they meet set independence rules. It would also require the Attorney General to give Congress a yearly report naming these outlets and saying whether they are registered. The change would affect foreign government-owned media operating in the United States and the Justice Department.

US-119-S5683.s: The bill would require the Defense Department to publish a guide for people who want to start and run Family Child Care homes on military bases. The guide would explain the steps, training, inspections, background checks, licensing, safety rules, emergency plans, and possible financial help. It would have to be made public online within one year after enactment, and the department would brief Congress within 18 months.

US-119-S5684.s: The bill would require federal agencies to bar some contractors from getting federal contracts if they are found guilty or get a civil judgment for wrongly sharing a client’s personal information. It would also require a temporary stop on contract eligibility if a contractor or worker is charged with that kind of crime. The rule would cover things like Social Security numbers, tax return info, health info, and trade secrets.

US-119-S5685.s: The bill would require federal financial watchdogs to turn over and post records tied to Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell, and related people or entities. It would also make those agencies start investigations into certain banks and other firms, and into senior executives at those firms, for possible banking, securities, money laundering, or criminal law violations. If they find wrongdoing, the agencies could seek bans, civil fines, and criminal referrals to the Attorney General.

US-119-S5686.s: The bill would bar Defense Department staff and others acting for the department from recording, broadcasting, or posting military executions for the public. It would also ban using federal money to create or share public recordings of any execution under military law or other federal law, unless Congress or a court allows it. The rules would take effect when the bill becomes law and would apply to executions carried out on or after that date.

US-119-S5687.s: The bill would set rules for how people ask the President for pardons, commutations, reprieves, or fine relief. It would keep an Office of the Pardon Attorney in the Justice Department, spell out how petitions are reviewed, and require notice to some victims. It would also make people who receive clemency report certain information, and it would require public posting of some clemency details.

US-119-S5688.s: The bill would change two mining law sections to increase the share of oil and gas lease money that goes to states from acquired lands. It would affect how revenue from those leases is divided between the federal government and states.

US-119-S5689.s: The bill would stop federal grants, loans, tax credits, and other aid for covered data centers, which are large sites built for artificial intelligence work. It would also add a federal tax equal to 100% of certain state or local aid that these data centers receive. The rules would take effect the day after final regulations are issued by the Treasury Secretary.

US-119-S5690.s: The bill would require the Interior Secretary to replace the plaque at the Lincoln Memorial that marks Martin Luther King Jr.’s "I Have a Dream" speech. It would also use the federal law for memorials and plaques to guide the new plaque’s design and placement. The department could accept donations for the work, and federal funds could also be used.

US-119-S603.s: The law makes the General George C. Marshall House in Leesburg, Virginia, part of the National Park System as an affiliated area, a site linked to the park system. It names the George C. Marshall International Center to help manage the site, and the Interior Department must sign an agreement that spells out each side’s role. Interior may also give technical help and enter agreements that can provide money for marketing, signs, interpretation, and preservation.

US-119-S616.s: It changes the federal charter for the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association and moves more of the group’s rules into its bylaws, which are its internal rules. It also changes where the office is set, limits political activity by directors and officers, and expands who cannot get loans from the foundation. The law also lets the group use its money to pay certain costs, and changes how any leftover assets are handled if it ends.

US-119-S629.s: The law changes two disaster aid programs for farms and private forest land. It widens who can get payments after natural disasters, including some wildfire damage, and it gives more ways to get money before work starts. It also lets people use the funds within 180 days instead of 60 days in some cases.

US-119-S675.s: The bill would let the Interior Secretary give up to $50 million in grants to help build the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora, North Dakota, but only after the project has at least $100 million from state or other non-federal money. The money could be used to preserve Roosevelt-related materials and to provide public education, but not to run or maintain the library. It would also allow federal agencies to loan museum items and other artifacts to the foundation for the library, and says the federal government would not run the library.

US-119-S700.s: The bill would let the Forest Service transfer about 232.9 acres in the Tonto National Forest in Arizona to Gila County if the county asks for it. The county would have to use the land to serve and support veterans, and the land would go back to the United States if it stops being used that way. The transfer would be done with a quitclaim deed, without payment, and the county would pay the costs of surveys, required reviews, and related work.
US-119-S700.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-02-25)

US-119-S723.s: This law sets deadlines for the Bureau of Indian Affairs to handle papers for home, business, land, and right-of-way loans on tribal trust land. It also requires faster title report updates, lets tribes and some federal agencies view the BIA trust records system in read-only mode, and creates a Realty Ombudsman in the BIA. It also calls for a Government Accountability Office report on digitizing mortgage papers for homes on Indian land.

US-119-S759.s: The law directs NOAA to set common rules for sharing map data about public recreation on federal waters, like boating and fishing. NOAA must work with states, local governments, tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations, and with other federal agencies, to make the data fit together. Within four years, NOAA must post a public website showing places with fishing limits, areas in the U.S. exclusive economic zone with limits on certain recreational boats, and federally protected areas.

US-119-S766.s: The law requires the Office of Management and Budget to gather yearly updates from federal agencies on certain projects that are far behind schedule or have gone at least $1 billion over the original cost estimate. Agencies must send details like project plans, dates, costs, delays, and any bonus payments tied to the project. OMB must then send a yearly report to Congress and post it online.

US-119-S789.s: The bill would direct the Interior Department to track critical minerals and rare earth resources around the world, including recycled materials, and report on their global ownership and supply. It would also create a process to help U.S. people who want to sell foreign mining, processing, or recycling stakes find buyers that are not controlled by North Korea, China, Russia, or Iran. Interior would also have to work with U.S. allies on mining and recycling technology and on ways to share related know-how.
US-119-S789.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-02-27)

US-119-S858.s: The law requires the memorial honoring Medal of Honor recipients to be placed within the Reserve on the National Mall, the main area that runs between the Capitol, Lincoln Memorial, White House, and Jefferson Memorial. It affects where the monument can be built. It became Public Law 119-104 on September 10, 2026.
US-119-S858.src: Congressional Research Service summary (Introduced in Senate, 2025-03-05)

US-119-S933.s: This bill would authorize NASA programs for fiscal year 2025 and set funding for NASA offices and missions. It covers space exploration, space operations, space technology, aeronautics, science, STEM education, and NASA policy. The bill would also direct NASA on work related to Artemis, the Space Launch System, lunar landing capabilities, and the use of commercial providers and international partners in some areas.

US-119-S98.s: The law requires the Federal Communications Commission to check the qualifications of people or groups that apply for certain broadband funding in high-cost areas, such as rural communities. Applicants must give enough details to show they can handle the project and have a solid plan. The FCC must make the check through a formal rule process, and only applicants that meet the standards can get money. It also must set penalties for applicants that default during review before they start getting support.

US-119-SJRES11.s: A joint resolution is a formal statement by lawmakers, and this one became law. It cancels a Bureau of Ocean Energy Management rule on marine archaeology for oil and gas plans on the Outer Continental Shelf. It also restores the older rule that let the agency ask for an archaeology report only when there was reason to think such remains might be in the lease area.

US-119-SJRES13.s: This law cancels a Treasury banking rule that changed how regulators review proposed bank mergers. It affects banks that apply to merge and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, which reviews those requests. The rule had removed some faster approvals and stopped using some simpler forms, and the law became Public Law 119-19 on June 20, 2025.

US-119-SJRES18.s: The resolution cancels a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule on overdraft fees at very large banks. Those banks would no longer have to follow the rule’s fee limits, including a $5 cap or other listed options for handling overdrafts. It became Public Law 119-10 on May 9, 2025.

US-119-SJRES200.s: A joint resolution is a formal statement by Congress. This measure would direct the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Iran unless Congress has given clear approval through a war declaration or other specific law. It also says the United States could still defend against attacks, gather and share intelligence, help partner countries with defense, and assist with the safety and departure of U.S. citizens.

US-119-SJRES216.s: This joint resolution would block a proposed U.S. military sale to Saudi Arabia. The sale includes thousands of bomb guidance kits, bombs, and related parts and support services. It would affect the U.S. government and the Government of Saudi Arabia.

US-119-SJRES221.s: Lawmakers would state that Congress does not favor the proposed civilian nuclear cooperation agreement between the United States and Saudi Arabia. The measure affects that agreement and the two countries involved.

US-119-SJRES28.s: The law cancels a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule about which payment app companies count as large enough for bureau oversight. It affects nonbank companies in the general-use digital payment app market with at least 50 million transactions a year that are not small businesses. The resolution became Public Law 119-11 on May 9, 2025.

US-119-SJRES31.s: This joint resolution became law and cancels an Environmental Protection Agency rule about reclassifying major pollution sources as area sources. It ends a rule that would have required some sources of hazardous air pollutants to keep using certain pollution controls when they change category. The change affects facilities that release persistent and bioaccumulative hazardous air pollutants.

US-119-SJRES80.s: This joint resolution nullifies a 2022 land-use plan for part of Alaska’s National Petroleum Reserve and returns to the 2020 plan. It would reopen some of the reserve to oil and gas leasing and remove protections that had closed about 48% of the area. It became law on December 5, 2025.
